en: Victorious is Śiva, the Lord of all sciences, the Sovereign of all souls,
the unbroken omniscient Guru of the world from its very beginning.
Having propitiated the Yajurvedic branch, I take refuge in the Śatarudriya;
having extracted the essence of the Rudras, a correct exposition is here provided for those who are armored with sacred ash and whose very selves consist of ash and rudrākṣa beads.
[She] who dwells daily at the feet of Him whose crown is the moon that sheds ambrosia;
(4th line) thus, I am the humble servant of those who have bowed to the Lord of the Gods through the pure meaning of the *Rudrapraśna*.
(5th line) Here indeed, the fact that the *Śrī Rudropaniṣad* is the essence declared by all the Vedas is well-established in the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, and *Itihāsa*. (6th line)
To explain: in the Jābālopaniṣad, it is said: "Then they said to that religious student, 'Tell us, by what recitation does one attain immortality?

(7th line). In response to this question regarding the means of liberation, Yājñavalkya replied: "By the Śatarudriya; for these are indeed the names of the Immortal, and by these one indeed becomes immortal. This refers to the Śrīrudropaniṣad, which is expressed by the term Śatarudrīya. (p. 4a, f. 1, b, 1st line)

Its status as the primary means for attaining liberation is contested. It is called *śatarudriya* because its deity is the hundred Rudras; according to the rule *sāsya devatā* (Pāṇini 4.2.24), under the governing heading, the rule *śatarudrāc cha ca* (Pāṇini 5.4.153) prescribes both the suffix *gha* and the suffix *cha* after the word *śatarudra* to denote the deity. Thus, since grammarians derive both forms—*śatarudriya* and *śatarudriyam*—the latter is established.

The "hundred-footed" refers to the supreme infinity, according to the Vedic revelation: "A hundred is infinite. And from the statement in the Mahābhārata: "The word 'hundred' denotes the universe, the thousand, and all that is imperishable. Furthermore, infinite turmeric plants are described: "Thousands..."

This is because of such scriptural declarations as: "The Rudras who are upon the earth by the thousands," and "And those Rudras who are heard of by the thousands all around the quarters upon this earth."

Their status as deities (*devatātva*) is due to their being the objects of worship through mantras, as stated in the *Nirukta*: "Deities are those who are expressed by mantras. Alternatively, [the term] *Rudrīya* is derived from *Rudra* with the suffix *-īya* according to the rule "from *vṛddha* [words]" (*Pāṇini 4.3.144*). Likewise, there is the suffix *-gha*; from the word *rudra* alone, the suffix *-gha* is applied in the sense of relationship and so forth, as seen in such examples as "O Agni, that body of yours which is *rudriyā*" (*yā te agne rudriyā tanūḥ*) and "for the sake of offspring, the *rudrīya*" (*yathā tokāya rudrīyam*).

Because it is seen [in the scriptures]. And thus, the term *rudrīya* refers to that which pertains to Rudra—the *Śatarudriya*, recited in a hundred branches, which has the *Śrī Rudropaniṣad* as its core. As it is stated in the *Sūtasamhitā* of the *Skanda Purāṇa*: "The supreme *Śatarudriya*, found directly in a hundred branches, liberates one from all sins merely by its recitation."

Bhaṭṭabhāskara has also stated: "One hundred [names] of Rudra are traditionally taught in the Yajurvedic scriptures. Therefore, these belong to Rudra; they are *rudriyāṇi*, that is, names of Rudra. Since there are one hundred—indeed, infinite—names of Rudra in this [section], it is called the *Śatarudriya*. And it has been said: "These, indeed, are the names of the Immortal."

In the *Kūrma Purāṇa*, the Blessed One himself says: "O sinless one, hear these secret names of mine. And in the *Droṇaparvan* of the *Mahābhārata*, the *Śatarudrīya* chapter is described. For therein, having first asserted the infinity of the Supreme Lord’s names with the words, "His names in the worlds are many and according to their true meaning," it continues: "And in the Veda, his supreme *Śatarudrīya* has been handed down."
The *Śatarudrīya* contained in the Vedas is cited as its supporting authority.

By that [text], the infinity of the names "Śatarudra" constitutes the ground for the application of the term *śatarudrīya*. Nor should it be argued: "How can these be names of Him, given that they have not been taught by [authorities] such as Naiṣkaṇḍuka as being names of the Supreme Lord? For [it is said]: "These indeed..."

Since it is possible to account for the inclusion of those [names] otherwise— given that the *Kūrma Purāṇa* states, "These are my favorite names," thereby identifying them as the secret names of the Veda, and thus making their non-inclusion in the *Nikhaṇḍu* established— and given that they consist merely of a few names employed in world-renowned poetry, drama, and so forth, rather than being the direct Vedic declarations such as "these are the names of the Immortal" (*amṛtasya nāmadheyāni*) which are cited in the *Nikhaṇḍu*.

For the followers of the *Naiṣkhaṇḍuka* [sect] do not rely upon the secret doctrines (*rahasya*) of the Vedas. Indeed, there are thousands of such Vedic names not accepted by the *Naiṣkhaṇḍukas*, such as: "That indeed is the name of this great Being," and "This is the secret name of the waters, namely *yadāyāvā*," and so forth. For in these cases, the status of being a name cannot be removed even by the non-acceptance of the *Naiṣkhaṇḍukas*.

On the contrary, it rather confirms their status as the secret doctrine (*rahasya*) of the Vedas. Now, if you argue that their identity with those [names] is understood from the application of such Mahābhārata passages as "Oṃ tat sat— thus is Brahman remembered as threefold" and "The *ātāna*, *taptā*, *lava*, and *vasaṅghā*," etc., then alas,
what a display of faith is this from the "Beloved of the Gods" (the King), who, lacking faith in what is declared in the Vedas, relies instead upon some historical narrative (*itihāsa*).
He does not accept that [position] based on the statement in the Purāṇa; for there is also such a statement in the Mahābhārata:
"In the worlds, his names are many, corresponding to their true meanings."
"And its excellent Śatarudrīya has been recited in the Veda"— as was previously cited—
and there are also individual ritual applications for each [of the names].
As in: "Just as Harikeśa said 'so be it,' so did the lord Dīrghadarśin";
"Not even by you, O Giritrin, Lord of all the worlds, Viriñca, Vaikuṇṭha, or the hosts of the lords of gods [is this face attained]";
"Then, having addressed Mīḍhvān"; and "Then, by Mīḍva, those who were delighted were addressed. (p. 7a, f. 3a, 1st line)
This is because such names as Harikeśa, Mīḍhuṣṭama, and others prescribed in the *Śrī Rudra* [mantra] are employed in the *Bhārata* and *Bhāgavata* passages cited above.

Therefore, let it suffice to say that there is no connection with the inhabitants of the Naimiṣa forest (*naikhaṇḍuka*) regarding names of this kind. The view of the "beasts" (the ignorant) is that the *Upaniṣads* are to be chanted as a means for attaining liberation (*mokṣasādhanajapyā*).

If, however, the true state of affairs is understood here by the religious students (*brahmacārin*), then the question becomes relevant; for [this discussion] does not apply once the *Upaniṣads* are understood to be chanted as a means for attaining liberation.

Once [the question] has arisen—"What should be chanted here as the reality?"—if it is not understood [that the Upanishads are the answer], then the response "by means of the Śatarudrīya" would lack coherence. For if one were to follow the actual state of affairs regarding the Upanishads—that they are the chanting which is the means to liberation—the response "by means of the Śatarudrīya" would not be appropriate to the question, "What is that reality which should be chanted for the sake of immortality? Rather, it is only logical that the response refers to the Upanishads themselves. Otherwise, [the text would be inconsistent].

According to the maxim that "the mention of a specific [item] is for the purpose of excluding the rest," there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that none of the Upaniṣads other than the *Śatarudrīya* could serve as a means to liberation through recitation (*japya*). This is just as when, in response to the question "Who is the learned man in this village?", the answer "Devadatta is learned" implies that others such as Yajñadatta and the like are not learned. Therefore, in this case, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the question and the answer.

It must be said: having determined generally that the Upaniṣads alone are to be chanted as the means for liberation, the question arises (line 3) as to which among them is the most excellent for chanting; likewise, [the text] states "composed of the Śatarudrīya. And as for the answer, when the doubt arises as to how the Śatarudrīya is the most excellent of all Upaniṣads, it is established here (line 4) by the statement, "These are indeed the names of the Immortal," which explains its superiority. These [names] recited in the Śatarudrīya belong to the Immortal, the eternally liberated (line 5).

The meaning is that these are the names of the Supreme Lord. [Objection: "Let that be so; what follows from it? To this he says: "He becomes liberated here" (line 6). The word "here" (iha) is used for the purpose of emphasis. It means that by these very names alone one becomes liberated—let alone the contemplation of the reality of Brahman as the Self. In this regard, those divine names of the Supreme Lord alone bestow liberation through mere recitation (japa). (Lines 7–8)

But in other Upaniṣads, this is not the case; therefore, the intended meaning is that [this work] possesses the status of being the most excellent among all Upaniṣads. By the phrase "or these here," its existence within hundreds of recensional branches (*śākhā*) is indicated, and by that, the following point is demonstrated: although all names indeed belong to the Supreme Lord—just as the Śruti says, "These songs [were offered] to Rudra for stability in the forest"—[this work stands out] because it brings the entire mass of words directly before one's perception.

It establishes that [the name] is a designation for the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*). For this very reason, after introducing Śiva, Āśvalāyana stated: "Indeed, all these are His names here. Nevertheless, because they are well-known as being recorded in hundreds of recensional branches (*śākhā*) and as being the means to liberation (*mokṣa*), the statement that "these are the names" is justified on account of their primacy. As it is said: "We are the thirty-six-day [sacrifice], and we are the twelve-day [sacrifice]."
Even though the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) is accomplished in thirty-six days, its constituent days are primary; thus, it is like an extension (*pradeśa*) of the *dvādaśāha*.

This entire point is demonstrated in the *Kūrmapurāṇa*. For therein, regarding the practice of the *gāyatrī* performed for a hundred years by the royal sage Vasumān—who had obtained a boon from Brahmā—the following is recited after he has approached the Supreme Lord who was pleased: "Then Mahādeva said... (p. 8a, f. 5a, 1st line).

With a joyful mind, he said to the king: "Listen to these secret names of mine; hear them from me. Chanted throughout all the Vedas, they bring peace to the cycle of worldly existence. O pure one, constantly offer salutations with these names.
This chapter, the Śatarudrīya, is the supreme essence of the Yajurveda."

Recite [this] with an undistracted mind, O you of virtuous intellect; as a celibate student, moderate in diet, established in the sacred ash, and composed in meditation, one should recite Rudra until death, and thereby attain the supreme goal. Here, since the status of this [text] as the best of the Yajurveda is already established by its being called "the essence of the Yajus," the word *uttama* (supreme) is used again to refer to it as the best of the Ṛgveda. And thus, it is the most excellent of all.

The injunction is that one should recite the Śatarudriya chapter. By this, the meaning of the phrase "with the Śatarudrīya" [from the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa*] is for the most part demonstrated. And here, in response to the inquiry as to how it possesses the quality of being the supreme among all, the qualification "the pacifiers of worldly existence" (*saṃsāraśamanāni*) is provided to establish that point. It is not merely through the act of recitation alone that my name liberates one from *saṃsāra*, nor simply by its being associated with the *kurumba* plant.
However, with the intention that such supreme status among all the Vedas is attained even by reciting [this] with my salutation, it was said:

"Worship constantly with these words of name. This is because the recitation (*japa*) of those mantras consisting of names, being composed of salutations, takes the form of vocal worship (*vācikanamaskāra*). The meaning is: "While performing the recitation, you will have performed salutations as well. And thus, they are not merely names alone...
If one pays homage even to those things which destroy the *saṃskāras*, what more need be said? The intended meaning is that they uproot the suffering of *saṃsāra*.

By this [explanation], the portion of the Śruti stating, "Having slain with these, one becomes immortal," is explained. Furthermore, by the phrase "these indeed are the names," the portion "these here are the names of immortality" is explained. Here, these...

The meaning of the word *amṛta* is "one who understands every single step" (*pratipadamimānī*); that is, one who understands every single step of the meaning of the word *amṛta*. The sense of the particle *vā* is "these [verses] have been sung by him in all the Vedas here. By the phrase "renowned as having a hundred branches" (*śataśākhāmnātatva*), his fame is demonstrated. By the word "secrets" (*rahasyāni*), it is stated that there is no room for fallacious reasoning regarding the secret meaning of the Vedas, nor is there any renown for [works such as] the *Naiṣkhaṇḍuka*. And by the word "sinless" (*anagha*), [it is implied that he has mastered] the *Gāyatrī* practiced for a full hundred years.

It is thus stated that for you, whose sins have been completely destroyed through worship, there is an unimpeded qualification for the Rudrādhyāya. (p. 9b, f. 6a, 1st line) Likewise, even though there exists this [Rudrādhyāya], which grants liberation through mere recitation, people sink into the cycle of worldly existence due to the fault of lack of faith. Alas! Such is the power of sin—this is the intended meaning. And these [details] are recounted in the Brahmottara-khaṇḍa. Therein: "From the recitation of the Śrīrudra, in all... (3rd line)

When evil has perished from the world, because of the total absence of the most wicked, the world—having been struck by Aśraddhā and Durmedhā, who were appointed by Brahmā after he was informed by Citragupta, Vaivasvata, and others who were themselves without office—is said to have become one whose face is Śrī Rudra; we shall cite those very words immediately below. Therefore, it is established that the Rudrādhyāya of the Jābāla Upaniṣad, as supplemented by the Kūrma Purāṇa, demonstrates its status as the supreme among all the Vedas.

This meaning is indeed heart-felt to the wise. The Jābāla Upaniṣad, for the sake of accomplishing the lack of ignorance, states with reverence the primary means for living beings: "Avimukta is my field; my name is supremely auspicious; the chanting of the Śatarudrīya, as well as the highest renunciation (sannyāsa). These are the words of the Parāśara Purāṇa. Furthermore, there are Vedic [passages]. Here, the knowledge of the Śatarudrīya—

Because it is stated explicitly that the meaning of the Jābāla Śruti is the status of being a counter-proof (*pratisādhanatva*). And here, "supreme" (*parama*) is a qualification of the one liberated while not yet departed (*avimukta*). The meaning is that it is supreme—that is, most excellent—by means of the mantra known as the *praṇava*. For there is a Śruti passage stating: "When the vital breaths (*praṇa*) of a living being are departing, Rudra explains the *tāraka* [mantra]. And thus, among all forms of meditation (*upāsanā*), the meditation on Avimukta is the best; and among those to be recited (*japya*), [the *praṇava* is the best].

Regarding the recitation of the *Śatarudrīya*, [the author] demonstrates through the words of the venerable Parāśara—that among the stages of life (*āśrama*), renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is the primary means for attaining knowledge—and shows that this is the supreme among all the Vedas. It is established that the *Jābāla-śruti*, which is supported by that [statement], is the authoritative source. Likewise, the *Kaivalya-upaniṣad* also [speaks of] Āśvalāyana, who had approached [him] for the sake of realizing Brahman.
After the Supreme Lord Brahmā had taught the Truth, this Śatarudrīya was handed down as its means of attainment: "He who studies the Śatarudrīya becomes purified by fire;

he becomes purified from the drinking of liquor; he becomes purified from the killing of a Brahmin; he becomes purified from the performance of malevolent magic (*kṛtyā*). Therefore, one should take refuge in Avimukta. Even one who has transcended the stages of life (*atyāśramī*) always attains knowledge through the single recitation [of it], [crossing] the ocean of saṃsāra."

Regarding the term "destruction" (*nāśana*): here, the first injunction is that one desiring the knowledge for crossing over *saṃsāra* should recite the *Śatarudrīya*. Here, having raised the doubt—"In this mass of the Vedas, which consists of the sections on ritual action (*karma*), worship (*upāsanā*), and knowledge (*jñāna*), what is the reason for the instruction that the *Śatarudrīya* alone is the means to knowledge, while everything else is to be abandoned?"—it is stated that it is because of its status as the supreme among all the Vedas. First, [the section on] ritual action...
By means of the passage beginning with "That which is the Śatarudrīya" and ending with "purified from his actions," it demonstrates its superiority in comparison to other sections (*kāṇḍa*).
And this has been elaborated upon in the Sūta-saṃhitā: "He who, endowed with faith, [recites] the Śatarudrīya daily..."

"One should practice [this]. Through this, one becomes purified from arson, the drinking of liquor, and likewise from the performance of forbidden acts (*akṛtyācaraṇa*), as well as from the killing of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*);

so say the followers of the Kaivalya branch. Here, by the phrase "from the performance of forbidden acts," the Vedic text—namely, "one becomes purified from what has been done and not done"—is explained.

That which is performed like a forbidden act is "forbidden-act-like" (*kṛtyākṛtya*); it means the performance of what should not be done (*akṛtyācaraṇa*). The meaning is that one becomes purified from that.

And thus, the intention of the Śruti is demonstrated that one who recites the Rudrādhyāya becomes purified not merely from the killing of a Brāhmaṇa or the drinking of liquor, but from every sin whatsoever; and this same meaning is established in detail in the Brahmottara-khaṇḍa,
for therein it is taught that prior to creation, in the lightless state, there was that which is partless (niṣkala), supreme, and consisting of consciousness and bliss.

That light is the Self, the absolute Śiva. Having first touched the *brāhmaṇa* aspect of his own nature—which is of the form of *rajas*—he bestowed the Vedas upon him who was appointed to the task of creation. Furthermore, the Lord of the world gave him the Rudrādhyāya, which is the singular compendium of the essence of the Self and the quintessence of all the Upaniṣads. This very [text] was upheld by the ancient sages, led by Marīci and Atri, together with the gods; and from them it was received by [the present teachers].

Having introduced the subject with the words: "The enemies seized a hundred arrows; these are the highest austerity. By the recitation of the Rudrādhyāya, even they immediately attain the supreme goal," it is read as follows: "Heaven is the fruit of meritorious action; hell is its opposite. The two lords of these two are those who bring about the journey [of beings]: Indra and Antaka (Yama). Likewise, desire, anger, greed, pride, arrogance, and so forth."

The sons of Adharma were all the leaders of Naraka; they were born from anger, as well as from the killing of their father and the violation of their mother. Furthermore, a single daughter was subsequently born, who was Brahmahatyā (the personification of the sin of killing a Brahmin). Then there were Gurutalpa (the violator of the teacher’s bed), Surāpāna (the drinker of liquor), and another, Pulkasīgama (the one who approaches a Pulkasī woman). These are proclaimed as the principal sons of Kāma. [And] Devasva...
The abduction of women, the theft of a Brāhmaṇa’s property, and the theft of gold—these are remembered as the sons of Loha.

Having summoned these Caṇḍālas, the leader of sins then bound them with a turban for the purpose of filling Naraka. Commanded by Yama, all those leaders of Naraka filled the hells with their own major and minor transgressions.

When the Rudrādhyāya, the direct means for attaining liberation, arrived upon the earth, all those leaders of sins fled in fear. O Lord, you have empowered them along with all the minor sins (upapātakas) to serve as attendants of Yama for the purpose of increasing the population of hell; now, O Master, we are no longer able to speak in this world.
(…) By the power of the *japa*, they have been utterly consumed and put to flight—
in every village, on the banks of rivers, and in sacred shrines.
Since we are fully protected by the recitation of the *Śrī Rudra*, how could we ever be harmed?
We are unable to count even a thousand atonements,
nor are we capable of performing the recitation of the Rudra-mantras even for a single moment.

"For us, who are the foremost among those guilty of great sins and for our dependents, the recitation of the Rudra-mantra is supreme and formidable; the recitation of the Rudra-mantra is supreme and difficult to overcome. Thus it is said.
Having been directly informed by the leaders of the sinners,
Yama approached the presence of Brahmā and reported everything to him.
Thus informed by Śikhaṇḍin, as if by Yama himself,
the Creator devised a stratagem for the purpose of obstructing the recitation of the Rudra-hymn.
He urged both faith and wisdom upon his two sons, for these two prevent ignorance among mortals.
When the world had been deluded by those two and had turned its back on the Rudrādhyāya,
he became as if his purpose were accomplished after half a month [spent] in the abode of Yama. Thus it is said.
Thus, this meaning has been elaborated everywhere in other Purāṇas as well;

all of that is not written here for fear of prolixity. In this way, what is established by the Śruti and proclaimed also by the Purāṇas—that the Rudrādhyāya serves as an expiation for all sins—the authors of the Smṛtis have forgotten. Just as, having drunk [liquor] today... the Guru... [the rest of the sentence is incomplete in the source].

"Having committed adultery with another's wife, having committed theft, and even having committed the murder of a Brahmin, one who recites the *Rudrādhyāya* while covered in ashes and lying on a bed of ashes is liberated from all sins"—this is the statement of the *Śātātapa-smṛti*. "Or else, by reciting the Rudras eleven times, the knower of Dharma, even if touched by great sins, is liberated from all taints"—this is the statement of the *Yājñavalkya-smṛti*. [Reciting] the Veda once...

"By reciting the *Rudraikādaśinī* immediately thereafter, one becomes purified; by reciting it, one is purified at that very moment"—this is the statement of Atri. (4th line) Other [passages] as well should be cited. "He who studies the *Śatarudrīya* becomes purified by fire; he becomes purified from the drinking of liquor; he becomes purified from malevolent magic (*kṛtyā*) and from what has been done [sinfully]"—thus [it is said regarding] the *Śatarudrīya* as the purifier of all sins. (5th–6th lines)

By stating that it is a cause of cessation (*nivartakatva*), its superiority over the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*) is demonstrated. For the ritual section does not provide assistance to knowledge (*jñāna*) except by generating the purity of mind (*cittaśuddhi*) required for it. And that purity of mind—which consists in the removal of sins produced by the performance of all the rites prescribed in the ritual section—is accomplished through the recitation of the *Rudra* alone; thus, its status as the most excellent of the entire ritual section is established. Nor is the *Śrīrudra* [merely] a ritual act...

This is because, while it produces the purification of the mind—which is like the fruit of the stalk—it does not produce heaven and other such results which are its own [distinct] fruits. How, then, can its superiority over those [other rites] be asserted? It must be said that it is so, according to the manner stated in the *Sūtasaṃhitā*: "Just as the branches of a tree indeed blossom when the root is watered, so too, when Śiva is pleased by the recitation of the Rudra-mantra, all other deities are likewise pleased. Therefore, through the recitation of the Rudra alone, devotion and liberation are accomplished."

For one who pleases the Supreme Lord, even if there exists a desire for insignificant fruits such as heaven—which are the results of pleasing deities like Indra and Agni who are His limbs—those very fruits will stand before him of their own accord through a competitive impulse (*ahamahamikā*). If one should recite [the mantra] there according to his wish, he obtains that; of this there is no doubt. This [is for] one seeking the destruction of sin, one seeking liberation from disease...

Because it is established by such scriptural statements as, "One who desires prosperity, one who desires peace, one who desires long life, and one who desires health— should perform this [recitation], and he shall obtain all these," he who recites the *Śatarudriya* while meditating upon Maheśvara obtains even more than that person who might give away land endowed with gold, together with its mountains, forests, and groves, and provided with medicinal herbs. (2nd line)

Thus, in such statements from the Śaiva Purāṇas, the preeminence of the recitation of the Śrī Rudra is established. This is because all forms of worship must be accomplished through the hardship of one-pointed concentration of the mind, whereas the Śrī Rudra is shown to produce its fruits without effort by generating the specific results of each respective rite as explicitly stated in the scriptures. Therefore, due to its capacity to generate the fruits of the entire *karmakāṇḍa*, the Śrī Rudra is supreme.

Therefore, indeed, even all rituals—namely the Agnihotra, Darśapūrṇamāsa, Paśubandha, Cāturmāsya, Jyotiṣṭoma, and those lasting a year—insofar as their fruits are included within Śrī Rudra, have been placed among his millions of limbs; let that suffice for now. As for the subject at hand: thus has the excellence of the Karmakāṇḍa of the Śatarudrīya been stated. Always... (p. 14b, f. 11a, l. 1)

He states the preeminence of the Śrī Upāsanākāṇḍa [section on worship]: "Therefore, one becomes a resorter to Avimukta" (*tasmād avimuktam āśrito bhavati*). By the word "therefore" (*tasmāt*), the study of the Śatarudrīya mentioned in the preceding sentence—namely, "having studied the Śatarudrīya"—is referred to. Thus, the meaning is as follows: "Because of the study of the Śatarudrīya, one becomes a resorter to Avimukta"; that is, one has performed that worship which consists in taking refuge in Avimukta.

"To obtain the fruit of worshipping Avimukta"—by this much, the fact that this [section] is the preeminent part of the *upāsanā-kāṇḍa* is established. For instance, the *Jābālopaniṣad* states: "Therefore, one who does not serve Avimukta alone becomes [liberated in] Avimukta. Worship [is performed] during the departure of the vital breaths; Rudra [reveals] the *tāraka* Brahman.

It has been stated that the fruit [of this practice] is that by means of it one becomes immortal and attains liberation; and that worship of the Unliberated (Avimukta) is twofold: internal (adhyātmika) and external (adhibhautika). Because [the Purāṇas] do not have another purpose, they do not provide ground for the suspicion that they have another purpose. By the statement, "One should supplement the Veda with the Itihāsas and Purāṇas," the Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsas, and Purāṇas stand in a relationship of mutual support and being supported— like the "forest and the elephant" analogy— and thus, being powerful, the meaning understood from them is unshakable.

And thus, just as in the case of the *agni* [fire] being the primary referent, so too in the case of *brahman* being the primary referent, there is an interpretation based on direct Vedic cognition (*sākṣād-vedana*). When there is doubt—such as "Is it *aghaṣṭe*? or "Is this a determination elsewhere?"—the *mīmāṃsā* will fulfill the portion concerning the necessity of establishing a systematic arrangement (*vyavasthā*).
Consequently, through the principles of *śruti*, *liṅga*, and so forth, the *Śrī Rudra* is understood to have *brahman* alone as its primary referent. Just as indeed...

"The Person the size of a thumb dwells in the midst of the self; he is the Lord of what has been and what is to be"—thus, by the force of the scriptural mention of "Lord" (*īśāna*) in the *Kaṭhavallī*, it is established in the *Sūtra* section titled "From the word alone, it is known" that this refers to the Supreme Lord and not to the individual soul (*jīva*). Even there, it is established by the force of hundreds of scriptural mentions of names such as Śiva, Śaṅkara, Bhava, Sarva, Paśupati, Rudra, and so forth.

The established conclusion is that the *Śrī Rudra Upaniṣad* has Brahman as its sole subject matter. This is just as [the conclusion was reached] regarding the passage "The ether, on account of its characteristic marks" (*ākāśas talliṅgāt*), "On account of the teaching of internal attributes" (*antastaddharmopadeśāt*), and "The inner controller is understood to be [Brahman] among gods and others, because of the designation of His attributes" (*antaryāmī devādiṣu taddharmavyapadeśāt*). Furthermore, regarding the passage beginning with "He who has visibility and other qualities" (*dṛśyatvādiguṇakaḥ*) according to the method of the stated attributes, there is a discussion concerning different loci (*vyadhikaraṇeṣu*).

[For instance, in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad]: "What is the goal of this world?"—to this he replied: "All these beings, indeed, arise from the ether" (*asya lokasya kā gatir ity āśā iti hovāca | sarvāṇi ha vā imāni bhūtāny ākāśāt*).

In this very way they arise. Just as the status of Brahman has been established for such scriptural passages as "He who is seen within the sun" and "the golden person," by the force of indicative marks (*liṅga*) such as being the cause of all beings and being the Self of all, so too here, by the force of indicative marks such as being the Lord of all, being the Self of all, being the one [cause], and being the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of all, the status of Brahman must be accepted.

For in the *Rudropaniṣad*, after first demonstrating the lordship over a single object within the phenomenal world through such passages as "Salutation to the Lord of the Quarters" (*diśāṃ ca pataye namaḥ*), the status of being the Lord of the entire universe is established by the statement "Salutation to the Lord of the Worlds" (*jagatāṃ pataye namaḥ*). Similarly, after first showing the individual self through passages such as "To those with arrows and to those who shoot" (*iṣumadbhyo dhanvāvibhyaśca*), the state of being the Self of all is established;

and likewise, through the passage beginning with "Salutation to the one who hears" (*namaḥ śṛṇvate ca*), the state of being the inner controller of all is established—all of which are attributes unique to Brahman.
Thus, the general form of the Supreme Lord, characterized by such attributes as having a blue neck, wearing matted hair, and holding a trident in his hand, has been described.
Other such indicative marks and characteristics are also to be understood; for qualities such as being the Lord of all are not possible in the case of fire.
Indeed, it is heard in the *Talavakāropaniṣad* regarding the ancient conflict between the gods and the asuras...

To dispel the pride of the gods—who were arrogant because they believed victory in battle had been achieved solely through their own greatness—Śiva appeared before them in the form of a yakṣa. When Agni, who was intoxicated by his power to burn the world, approached him out of a desire to know his true nature, Śiva placed a single woman before him; he was then rendered incapable of burning even her.

And in that very manner, having rendered even the wind incapable of moving it, they cried out in distress. Then, desiring to know who this divine person in the form of a *yakṣa* was, and wishing to behold his true form before the gods who were exerting themselves in vain, the Blessed Umā, daughter of Himavat and the presiding deity of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), appeared; for the Supreme Lord himself had manifested in the form of the *yakṣa*.

He taught that [the Lord] was the Virāj, and that even the gods do not fully comprehend the majesty of that Supreme Lord who is being praised. This narrative is elaborated upon in the Purāṇas; likewise, I shall explain this in accordance with the supreme Vedic texts such as, "The progenitor of Agni, the progenitor of Sūrya," and "From fear of him, Agni and Indra... he who is Rudra in the fire," and so forth. And thus, the Supreme Lord...

Because it is impossible for fire—which is subject to creation, whose power is dependent upon Him, and which is subordinate—to possess qualities such as being the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) or being the self of all;
therefore, that [creation] is the unique characteristic (*asādhāraṇaliṅga*) of the Supreme Lord alone, who is the creator and controller of the entire world including Agni, Indra, and the rest.

That very same [characteristic], supported by scripture (*śruti*), indicative marks (*liṅga*), and other means of proof, is established through reasonings reinforced by the knowledge derived from the *Itihāsas*, *Purāṇas*, *Arthaśāstra*, and *Dharmaśāstra*.

Because [the text] is supported by the *upabrahmaṇas* and is thus unshakable in its meaning; for instance, in the case of the *ayanāni* of the Sun and others—namely, the *saṃvatsarasattras*—since they share the commonality of being a collection of days (*ahargaṇatva*), the conclusion of the injunctions for the *dvādaśāha* applies by virtue of internal similarity (*antaraṅgasādṛśya*). Just as it is accepted that the conclusion of the injunctions for the *gavāmayana* must be adopted because of internal similarity, so too should the meaning of the *Upaniṣads* be understood.

In the case of a definitive conclusion (*nirṇaya*), only that which has been explained in the *Upaniṣads* is to be accepted, because of its internal similarity; however, an explanation provided in the *Karmakāṇḍa* is not [to be accepted], due to the excellence of proximity and the necessity of acceptance. Thus, whatever is prior to the *Agniṣomīya* sacrifice—such as the injunction "they proceed with the *upāṃśu* [muttering]"—is merely a commendatory passage (*arthavāda*) intended for praise, since it possesses an alternative scope (*sāvakāśa*).

Since it is possessed of scope, whereas the other [text] is devoid of it and thus possesses greater force by virtue of being without scope, it is established—by way of the explanation in the Jābāla-upaniṣad, "These indeed are the names of the Immortal"—that this Śatarudrīya refers exclusively to the Supreme Lord. This is so even though there exists, within the context of the injunction and explanatory passage (arthavāda) for the Śatarudrīya oblation in the Agnicayana, the statement: "This Agni is indeed Rudra."

The commentary, for the sake of establishing that the meaning [of the mantra] is realized through its specific application (*adhikaraṇa*), explains that the *Śatarudrīya* mantra is applied to the fire with the intention that the fire is identical in nature to Rudra, who is the subject of that mantra; such is the extent of that exposition. Therefore, it is established that the *Śatarudrīya* does not have the fire as its referent in accordance with the principles of direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) or indicative mark (*liṅga*).

Since a mantra employed for a specific purpose lacks an inherent (svārasika) cognition [of that meaning], even if it manifests that meaning through some means such as secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), metaphorical usage (*gauṇī*), or supplying missing words (*āhāra*), it lacks "intentionality" (*tatparatva*) toward that meaning; it is with this very intention that the *Vārttika* states, "whether it be metaphorical or indicative. Therefore, in the case of the injunction, "With the *aindrī* [verse], one worships the *gārhapatya* fire," the *gārhapatya*...

Even when there is an application (*viniyoga*) based on the context (*sthāna*), it is not accepted that the *aindra-ṛca* verses refer to the *gārhapatya* fire. For this very reason, the *puruṣasūkta* [is applied] to the south of the sacrificial person (*puruṣa*). And according to the *Āpastamba-sūtra*, "with the Puruṣa [hymn], [one worships] Nārāyaṇa," and likewise in the *Puruṣamedha* sacrifice, where it is used for the praise of those animals designated as victims, [it says]: "In front, one piles up the form of a person facing westward."

Regarding the statement, "The head of the Puruṣa becomes the fire," one should perform the placement of the form of the Great Puruṣa upon the Mahāgni; then, according to the Āpastamba Sūtra— "Having placed [the image] with the verse 'A thousand heads has the Puruṣa,' the sacrificer worships it with the Puruṣa Nārāyaṇa"— one should worship with the *Puruṣasūkta* during the ritual service for the sake of the Puruṣa.

One should worship Varuṇa, who possesses all forms; one should worship the Giver of Wealth (Dhanada), who possesses all forms—with these words from the *Śātātapa-smṛti* and other texts, although there is an application (*viniyoga*) for the worship of Varuṇa, Dhanada, and others, it does not have them as its ultimate purpose (*paratva*). This is the extensive scope of this [text]. Therefore, just as the heart of a devoted wife remains fixed on her husband even when she sees many things and speaks much, so too [the mind] remains fixed on [Brahman] through many statements.

Furthermore, although the venerable Śrī Rudropaniṣad was being led away from there, its heart remained fixed solely upon the glorious Sāmba Parabrahman; thus, those such as Rāmānuja and others—who, desiring to turn it away from that [Supreme Reality], set out to make you, O Sītā, their own, like the most wicked Rāvaṇa—let them be for now. However, by means of your purificatory rites and the signs of prayers for the attainment of the desired and the avoidance of the undesired...
Because [this passage] is primarily devoted to the praise of Rudra, his status as the Lord of All and the Inner Controller of All is established as its true meaning.

For in the world, a prostration is invariably prompted by the excellence of the one to whom homage is paid, as is observed in common experience. Furthermore, this is supported by the etymological definition of the word "namaskāra" provided by the authors of the scriptures, who state that "namaskāra" is a mental disposition (*bhāva*) preceded by the contemplation of the excellence of the one to be propitiated.

In the case of the excellence of salutation (*namaskāra*), since it is impossible to abandon the excellence conferred by the specific qualification of the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) and instead adopt another excellence, the reality of the Lord’s status as the Sovereign of All and the Inner Controller of All—conferred by those respective qualifications contained within the *namaskāra* mantra—is established.
Thus, how could there be any doubt regarding its reality? Even though people are seen to offer salutations out of fear of excellence and the like, or even out of fearlessness.

In the Śruti as well: "Obeisance to you, the destroyer; obeisance to you, O Sovereign; obeisance to you, the radiant one. May your weapons burn away from us; be auspicious toward us. Likewise, this obeisance is prompted by fear due to the Supreme Lord’s nature as the Terrifier. Even though such an alternative explanation might be suspected, nevertheless, obeisance is offered to him through various means.

[The act of salutation] is not possible without [the recipient's] excellence. For this very reason, it is said: "Obeisance to your heat, to your radiance. Indeed, having performed obeisance, people conduct themselves toward one who is more excellent. In that *Mantra* and *Brāhmaṇa*, it is described that the abandonment of one's own excellence—which is inherent in the context of an act of obeisance—is not required. Even though obeisance is in fact prompted by both [parties], there is no deficiency; for the *Śrī Rudra* possesses an abundance [of merit] resulting from its preponderance of obeisances that are not shared by others.

Since the indication of excellence is unavoidable, the abundance of fear is indeed a characteristic mark (*liṅga*) of Brahman; for the Śruti says, "From fear of Him the wind blows," and "Great is the fear, the raised thunderbolt," and so forth. Therefore, prostration is not a characteristic mark of praise. Although the prayer for the avoidance of the undesirable and the attainment of the desirable is a characteristic mark of praise, nevertheless, while such a prayer might be directed toward someone other than the Supreme Lord, it is not so directed toward the Supreme Lord. This being the case, [the passage] forms a single syntactical unit within the *Puruṣasūkta*.
In the *Uttaranārāyaṇa-anuvāka*, within the verse beginning "Born from the waters during the heat," there is seen a prayer:
"May I desire this; may I desire that; may I desire all. Since this shows that even the *Puruṣasūkta* is intended as a hymn of praise, one might object:

"Then would not the sovereignty, the cessation [of creation], the creative power, and so forth, presented therein, also be ultimately real? To this, what is the answer? Therefore, let this be considered as something trivial. Let it rest.

This is the detailed account. Thus, the supremacy of the Śrī Rudra among all the Vedas, as well as its essential purport, has been explained at length through the authority of the Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsas, and Purāṇas. Now, for the benefit of those who perform recitations (*japa*) and other rites, the Great Nyāsa of the Śrī Rudra as taught by Bodhāyana is being expounded according to the traditional lineage.

"Now, therefore, we shall explain the procedure for the recitation, fire-oblation (*homa*), worship, and consecration (*abhiṣeka*) of the five-limbed Rudras, preceded by the ritual placement (*nyāsa*). (2nd line)

Now, this is the meaning of the term *pañcāṅga-rudra-pada*: those for whom there are five types of limb-assignments (*aṅganyāsa*) and so forth are the *pañcāṅga-rudras*. To explain: first, there is the assignment of thirty-one limbs, beginning with the crest-lock (*śikhā*) and ending with the weapon (*astra*);
second, there is the assignment of ten limbs, from the head down to the feet.
The third five-limbed assignment (pañcāṅganyāsa) is from the feet to the head;
the fourth five-limbed assignment is from the private parts to the top of the head;
the fifth five-limbed assignment is from the heart to the weapon (astra).
Therein, he shows the first [mantra] and not another:
"O Rudra, having gone... for the tuft; "In this great ocean... for the head; "Thousands... for the forehead; and "The swan dwelling in purity... between the eyebrows.
One should recite "tryambakaṃ yajāmahe" over the two eyes; "namassṛtyāya" over the two ears;
"mānastoke" over the nose; "avatatya" over the mouth;
"nīlagrīvau dvau" over the neck; and "namaste astvāyudhāya" over the two arms.
"yā te hetiḥ" [is recited] over the two upper arms; "pari no rudrasya hetiḥ" over the two wrists; "etīrthāni" over the two hands;
the five *anuvākas* beginning with "sadyojātam" over the five fingers; and "namo vaḥ kirikebhyaḥ" over the heart.
"Salutation to the hosts"—on the back;
"Salutation to the golden-armed one"—on the two sides;
"The bow is strung"—on the belly.
"Hiraṇyagarbha" at the navel;
"miḍuṣṭama" at the hips;
"ye bhūtānām adhipatayaḥ" at the genitals.
"Ye anneṣu" is for the two testicles;
"saśirā jāta" is for the anus;
"mā no mahāntam" is for the two thighs.
And "This is your portion, O Rudra" (6th line) [is recited] over the knees;
"The winner of the encounter" [is recited] over the shanks.
"viśvaṃ bhūtam" at the two ankles;
"ye pathām" at the two feet;
"addhyavocat" for the armor.
"Salutation to the one with the helmet"—this is the minor armor (*upakavaca*). "Salutation to the blue-necked one"—this is the third eye.
"Releasing from the bow"—this is the weapon (*astra*).
"And those who are so many"—this is the binding of the directions (*digbandha*).
The meaning of this is as follows: having recited the mantra beginning with "O Rudra, that auspicious form of yours which is not terrible," one should touch the crest-lock (*śikhā*) and other parts.
Regarding the phrase "the two blue-necked ones on the throat": one should sequentially place the two *nīlagrīva* mantras on the northern and southern portions of the throat.
By the word *upabāhu*, the portion above the wrist is denoted.
Having recited the mantra *sadyojāta*, one should place [the mudrā] with the two thumbs, saying "namaḥ" to the two thumbs.
Having recited the *vāmadeva* mantra, [one should place it] with the two index fingers, [reciting] the syllable *jātavedas* from the beginning of the head.
The supreme state, the essence extracted from the Vedas, is expressed by this mantra:
"To Jātavedas, the Head, Svāhā!
Thus, by this [mantra], that which is called the Śiras-mantra, beginning with "Jātavedas," is declared. This is the traditional teaching regarding the vow-conquered [state].
"Sahamānam" (the mantra beginning with this word), along with "ete mantrās tvaṃ (sva) śirājātavedāḥ," and "upakavacāya huṃ"—one should assign these [to the respective limbs].
"Namo'stu... (seventh line).
One should perform the placement (nyāsa) with "To the blue-necked one" for the third eye, and with "Obow,

release [your arrow]" for the weapon-mantra (*astra*), saying "phaṭ. This is the first placement, beginning with the crest-lock (*śikhā*) and ending with the weapon, accompanied by the binding of the directions (*digbandha*).
Now he states the second placement (nyāsa).
One should perform the placement of salutations with "Oṃ namo bhagavate rudrāya. Having placed the syllable Oṃ on the head, one places the syllable Na on the nose and ears.
One should place the letter *mo* on the forehead and the letter *bha* in the middle of the mouth.
One should place the syllable *ga* in the region of the throat and the syllable *va* in the heart;
one should place the syllable *te* in the right hand and the syllable *ru* on the left.
One should place the letter *drā* at the region of the navel and the letter *ya* on the feet. The meaning of this is as follows:

immediately after the first [mantra] accompanied by the previously mentioned *digbandha* (binding of the directions), one should utter the mantra "Oṃ namo bhagavate rudrāya," and having paid homage—saying "namo mūrdhne" for the head, "namo nāsikāyai" for the nose, and "yaṃ pādyābhyāṃ namaḥ" for the two feet.
Thus one should place [the mantras] on the two feet; this is the second. Now he states the third:

Having immediately placed [the mantra] on the two feet, one should place Vāmadeva between the two thighs; having placed Aghora on the heart, one should place Tatpuruṣa on the face; having placed Īśāna on the head, [one becomes] Sadāśiva, whose name is Haṃsa.

Having performed the ritual of placement (*nyāsa*) in this manner, one should then begin the *sampuṭa* (encasement): *trātāram indram*, *tvaṃ no agne*, *suganno panthām*, *asunvantam*, *tat tvā yāmi*.

Having performed the "Rudrīkaraṇa" by placing the following *sampuṭa* (enclosing mantra) in the directions starting from Indra: "ā noniyudbhiḥ," "vayaṃ soma," "tam īśānam," "asme rudrāḥ," "syonā pṛthvī," one is liberated from all sins through one's skin and bones. One becomes unconquerable among all beings. Then, all afflictions and harms caused by *bhūtas*, *pretas*, *piśācas*, and so forth, are [destroyed] by the blazing [mantra].
The meaning of "paśyantu" (may they see) is as follows: having recited the *sadyojāta* mantra and saying "namas padbhyām" (salutation to the feet), one should touch the feet.

In this same manner, having performed the sequence starting from *vāmadeva* up to the head (*mūrdhan*), one should thereafter say "haṃsa haṃsa" and touch the head. That which is called "haṃsa" is indeed Sadāśiva; thus, by acting in this way, one becomes known as "haṃsa," for Sadāśiva is famously known as "haṃsa."

Thus it is. He states the subsequent ritual arrangement: "Then one should begin the *sampuṭa*. Having formed the *añjali-mudrā*, which is denoted by the word *sampuṭa*, he first makes his face [the opening] and utters the mantra: "Aṃ, to Indra the protector, to Indra the savior. Then he should say: "Raṃ, obeisance to Agni. In this manner, he should proceed from the southern direction down to the nadir.
Immediately after that, he should perform the *raudrī-karaṇa*. That is of two kinds: beginning with "Thou art the pervasive one, the impeller," and so forth, up to "Thou art the serpent, O wise one."

Thus, even in the case of the *raudra* mantras, there is one method of performing the *raudrīkaraṇa* by means of the suffix "pāhi mā agne" ("protect me, O Agni") and so forth; another, however, is the *raudrīkaraṇa* consisting of the installation of the deities within one's own body according to the traditional practice (*sampradāya*), beginning with "O Brahman, established in the organ of generation" (*prajanane brahmātiṣṭha*) and ending with "surrounded by garlands of flames, may they all remain and protect me," as will be described below.
The fruit of all this is stated by [the passage] beginning with "having gone to the skinless [state], one is liberated from all sins"; this is the third nyāsa. Now he speaks of the fourth:

The meaning is that one should perform self-protection by touching the secret parts, the navel, the heart, the throat, the mouth, and the head with the mantra *mano jyotiḥ* and the verse *bodhyagnir agniḥ mūrdhānaṃ divo marmāṇi te jātavedāḥ*. Having recited the *mano jyotiḥ* mantra and said "Homage to the secret parts (*guhyāya namaḥ*"), one should touch the secret parts.

In this manner, one should touch the body from the feet up to the head with the mantras beginning with *evamabodhi* and *agni*. This consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) is designated as "Self-Protection" (*ātmarakṣā*).
This is the fourth placement (*nyāsa*).
Now, he describes the fifth placement.

The *Śivasaṅkalpa* is the heart; the *Puruṣasūkta* is the head; (5th line) the *Uttaranārāyaṇa* is the tuft (*śikhā*); the *Pratiratha*, beginning with "āśuḥ śiśānaḥ," is the armor (*kavaca*); the *Patipuruṣa* is the eye (*netra*); (6th line) the *Śatarudrīya* is the weapon (*astra*); and "bhūrbhuvaḥ suvaḥ" is the binding of the directions (*digbandha*). Its meaning is as follows: "By which this past, the world, and the future... and so forth. (7th line)

The thirty-sixth [chapter] consists of the essence of the mantras. Having recited the *Śivasaṅkalpa-sūkta*, one should touch the heart while saying, "Hṛdayāya namaḥ" (Salutation to the Heart). Having recited the *Puruṣasūkta* up to the end with the verse "Sā santi devāḥ," one should touch the head while saying, "Śirase svāhā" (Svāhā to the Head). Having muttered the *Uttaranārāyaṇa* section beginning with "adbhyassambhūtaḥ," one should say, "Śikhāyai vauṣaṭ" (Vauṣaṭ to the Tuft), and touch the tuft. [Then follows] the *Apratiratha* hymn beginning with "āśuśśiśāna... (2nd line).

Having recited this *anuvāka*, one should touch the base of the arm with the mantra "For the armor, *huṃ*. One offers cakes on single potsherds for each person, [reciting] the *anuvāka* beginning with "One [cake] is left over. He offers cakes on single potsherds for each person, [reciting] the *anuvāka* beginning with "As soon as born, he offered food to his offspring. And there is the *Śatarudrīya*. Even though the two grounds for the application of the *Śatarudrīya* mentioned previously—namely, "O Agni, you are Rudra"—are not present here.

Nevertheless, regarding the mantra "viśvadevadeva" (the god of all gods), [it is argued that] because of the phrase "dyumnaṃ praṇītavuṣya sa" (his splendor has been brought forth), it belongs to Viṣṇu due to its connection with the term "vaiṣṇava"; just as the mantra "utbuddhyasva" (awake! is considered to have Budha as its deity merely through its connection with the nominal stem "budha," and just as mantras such as "śanno devīḥ" are considered to have Śani as their deity because of the presence of the nominal stem "śani," so too does Agni possess divinity.

Regarding the passage "agnerudra," some consider it the *Śatarudrīya* merely because of its connection with the word "rudra. In reality, however, the *Śatarudrīya* designation for that [section] is due to the fact that it is a hymn of praise (*stuti*) to Agni—whom the *anuvāka* beginning with "tvamagne rudra" (p. 34b, f. 31a, 1st line) sets forth—in his capacity as the *Śatarudrīya*. As for the *anuvāka* beginning with "devā deveṣu" (2nd line), since the thirty-three gods are mentioned three times, there is a certain partial meaning (*avayavārtha*) therein through the presentation of the term "śatarudra" (3rd line).
The status of being the Śatarudrīya should be understood from the accompanying [text]. Having recited these two Anuvākas, one should perform the placement with "Astrāya Phaṭ.
This is the fifth Nyāsa.
Now, after the five-limbed Nyāsa, he states the subsequent rite: "The five-limbed [Nyāsa] once... (5th line).

One should recite. One should prostrate with the eight limbs; one should recite once the five-limbed form consisting of the five mantras beginning with *sadyojāta*. One should perform [the prostration] according to the measure of the eight limbs. He states those very eight mantras: *hiraṇyagarbhaḥ yaḥ*, *prāṇataḥ*, *brahmajajñānam*, *mahī dyauḥ*, *upaśvāsaya*, *agne naya*, *yā te agne*, and *imaṃ yamaḥ*—this is the eight-limbed prostration like a staff (*daṇḍavat praṇāma*);
this is another view. After that, he states the ritual action: "Then one should meditate upon oneself in the form of Rudra."
Resembling pure crystal, with three eyes and five faces,
bearing the Gaṅgā, ten-armed, and adorned with all ornaments.
With a blue neck, wearing a serpent as a sacred thread,
with a tiger skin as an upper garment, and clad in an elephant hide for clothing.
He is the most excellent, the bestower of fearlessness, endowed with a water-pot and a sacred thread;
he is the granter of boons, tranquil, gracious, and holds a trident in his hand.
He is blazing, bearing aloft a mass of tawny matted locks.
He was anointed with nectar, joyful, and bearing Umā as half of his body;
seated upon a divine lion, endowed with divine enjoyments,
possessed of the three eyes, and saluted by gods and asuras.

Having thus meditated correctly upon Rudra— who is eternal, everlasting, pure, firm, imperishable, undecaying, all-pervading, the sovereign Lord, and indeed the universal form— the practitioner of the vow should then begin the recitation.
Thus he has explained the procedure for the consecration (*abhiṣeka*).

Now, therefore, we shall explain the procedure for the bathing, worship, and consecration of Rudra. Having first bathed at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) and emerged, having put on a fresh garment, being pure and self-restrained, a celibate student (*brahmacārī*) wearing clean clothes, having fashioned an image of Īśāna, [one should place] its south...

One should establish him, facing forward, within the Self in the inner region. May Brahmā abide in the organ of generation; may Viṣṇu abide in the feet; may Hara abide in the hands; may Indra abide in the arms; may Agni abide in the stomach; may Śiva abide in the heart; may the Earth abide in the belly;
may the Vasus abide in the throat; may Sarasvatī abide in the mouth; may Vāyu abide in the two nostrils; and may the Moon and the Sun abide in the two eyes.
May the Aśvins abide in my two ears; may the Rudras abide in my forehead;

may the Ādityas abide upon my head; may Mahādeva abide on my crown; may Vāmadeva abide in my tuft of hair; may Pinākin abide at my back; may Śūlin abide in front; may Śivā and Śaṅkara abide at my two sides; and may Vāyu abide everywhere around me.

On all sides, outside, let there be a fire with flames encircling it on every side; let all the deities abide in all their limbs according to their respective places and protect me. Having touched the limbs according to the indicative marks [of the mantras], such as "Agni is in our speech" (*agnir no vāci śrutaḥ*), one should then worship oneself with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings, both physical and mental. Then, one should propitiate him.
You have been propitiated by humans, by the Siddhas, and by the gods, Asuras, and others;
I propitiate you with devotion—grant me your grace, O Maheśvara!
With the mantra "Tryambakam" and so forth, after the worship of the self in this manner,
he describes the method for external worship.

One should invoke him with the mantra, "May all the Rudras lead you hither. Once he has been established, there is no further invocation. Then one offers him a seat with the mantra, "To Sadyojāta. The water for the feet (*pādya*) is offered with "In every birth" (*bhave bhave*). The water for respectful reception (*arghya*) is offered with "Salutation to Bhava-Udbhava. The water for sipping (*ācamanīya*) is offered with "Salutation to Rudra. Then one bathes him with the hymn beginning with "O Waters, you are indeed... (*āpo hi ṣṭhā*).

Having performed the ritual purification (*mārjana*) with the three verses beginning "The golden-colored, pure ones" (*hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ*), with the entire Anuvāka beginning "Pavamāna, who dwells in heaven" (*pavamānaḥ suvarjanah*), and with the verse "With what [help], O Indra? (*kayā naścitra ābhuvat*) and the verse "Waters indeed this... (*āpo vā idam...*), he offers the cloth with "Salutation to Vāmadeva," the sacred thread (*upavīta*) with "Salutation to the Eldest" (*jyeṣṭhāya namaḥ*), the water for sipping (*ācamanīya*) with "Salutation to Rudra," the ornament with the *praṇava* (Oṃ), the rosary with "Salutation to Kāla," and the unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) with "To Kalavikaraṇa."

With "Salutation to the one who causes the transformation of power," he offers a flower; with "Salutation to the one who crushes power," incense; with "To the subduer of all beings," a lamp; and at the proper time, with "To the one who transcends the mind," he presents the food offering (*naivedya*). Then, with these eight mantras beginning with "Salutation to the god Bhava," he offers eight flowers.
Thereupon, his [the deity's] body appears before him. He should then mutter the *Rudra-gāyatrī*: "From the non-terrible ones, from the terrible ones... and so forth.

Having recited "tatpuruṣāya" one hundred times, or ten times, or three times, he then utters this benediction: "īśānaḥ sarvavidyānām. Then, having sprinkled him on the head with the water from the jar while reciting "namaste rudra manyave," he should mutter the eleven sections beginning with "sarvo vai rudra. [Then] "imā rudrāya... [is recited].

One should recite the twelve verses beginning with *sthirayanvanebhiḥ* and other Rudra-mantras; then, one should mutter the eleven sections (*anuvākas*) dedicated to Agni and Viṣṇu. One who desires the destruction of sin, liberation from disease, prosperity, peace, or long life should perform this. By doing so, one obtains all these benefits and offers the great oblation (*mahāhavis*) consisting of milk and other ingredients. Then, one gives the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), which consists of eleven cows.

"In the absence of that, one should offer a single-limbed [oblation]," thus said the venerable Bodhāyana; this is the meaning. Because the Śrī Rudra removes all sins, yields the fruit of all forms of worship, and bestows knowledge through mere recitation once, the purport of the entire Veda—consisting of the sections on ritual action (*karmakāṇḍa*), meditative worship (*upāsanākāṇḍa*), and knowledge (*jñānakāṇḍa*)—as well as the *Śruti*, *Itihāsas*, and *Purāṇas*, and renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), has all been established herein.

Now we shall explain the Śrī Rudropaniṣad according to its meaning. Herein there are eleven sections (*anuvākas*). Among them, in the first, there is the propitiation of the Blessed One; in the eight beginning with the second, there is the salutation to the Blessed One in His forms as the Lord of All and so forth; then, in the tenth, there is the prayer to the Blessed One; and the eleventh is the prayer to the host of Rudras who are portions of the Blessed One—such is the meaning of the Śrī Rudrādhyāya consisting of eleven sections.

In this regard, first of all, for the sake of exhausting his own sins, he propitiates the Lord by means of salutation: "Salutations to you, O Rudra. O you who are bowed to by Rudra, [this is said] regarding your wrath (*manyu*); salutations to your anger. And it should not be asked how there can be an attachment to defects in the Blessed One, who is an ocean of all auspicious qualities that have been cast away; for in one whose nature consists of the suppression of the wicked and the favoring of the virtuous, the anger directed toward those objects to be suppressed is merely a semblance (*alīkāra*).

Because [the Lord] possesses defects. Nor should it be argued that this entails the consequence of partiality (*vaiṣamya*) and cruelty (*nairghṛṇya*); for since He performs restraint and grace in accordance with the respective karma of each living being, those faults do not apply to Him, as has been explained at length in the *Brahma-mīmāṃsā*. In this regard: "The Lord who causes us to flow away from the cause of suffering is called Rudra; therefore, Śiva is the supreme cause."

This has been explained by the authors of the Purāṇas. Thus, the sense is as follows: since you are the one who dispels the suffering of those who bow to you and the sins that cause that suffering, it is indeed appropriate for you to avoid anger toward me, who am bowed before you, which would otherwise be caused by my sin. In this way, the vocative "O Rudra" (rudra-pada) should be understood as intended as an address in the subsequent passages as well.
Having thus propitiated the Blessed One, he now propitiates his weapons as well with salutation, [saying] "uta" (and also), which means "moreover. (p. 38a, f. 34b, 1st line) (2nd line)

O Rudra, let there be salutation to your arrow, to your shaft; likewise, let there be salutation to your bow, which serves as the instrument for that arrow. Furthermore, let there be salutation to your two hands, which are occupied with the bow and arrow. When the Supreme Lord becomes enraged toward a most wicked person who transgresses his own command in the form of the Śruti and Smṛti, he stands ready with an arrow for the purpose of striking him; at that moment, one’s gaze should be fixed upon that bow equipped with its string and arrow.

Then, for the purpose of grasping the bow and arrows, the arms are extended and held; thus, from the act of grasping, there is a sequence. By this sequence, the order of salutation is established here. Since the forms of the Lord—which are to be worshipped—manifest as the divine play of the Infinite and Variegated Power, they are [designated as] the *iṣṭa* (desired) and so forth; therefore, there is the salutation and prayer to them. This is indeed appropriate, for it is heard in the *Mahābhārata* regarding one who has forgotten the *Pāśupata* [observance].

Regarding the knowledge of the methods for wielding and withdrawing weapons, while Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna were on their journey to Mount Kailāsa, they were commanded by the Supreme Lord (Śiva): "Bring that weapon from there to this place. Having gone for that purpose, they found the Pāśupata weapon there; it was exceedingly terrifying, made formidable by the flames of poison vomited from the mouths of many hoods [of serpents]. And that [weapon] was [subdued] by the power of the Śatarudrīya chapter of the Blessed Śrī Kṛṣṇa.

It should be understood here that [the mantra], having become peaceful in form, came into his hand. Now, the ṛṣis, meters, and deities are shown here. For it is forbidden to mutter a mantra without knowing its [ṛṣi, meter, and deity]; therefore, the meters (chandas) are studied. "He who, indeed, without knowing the ṛṣis, meters, and deities... [etc.]

A Brahmin sacrifices with a mantra, or teaches speech, or avoids a stump, or falls into a pit, or is carried away by a current, or becomes shallow; therefore, one should know these [consequences] regarding each mantra. Regarding the mantra "O Rudra, homage to your wrath" (*namas te rudra manyave*):

The seer (*ṛṣi*) is Ātreya. The meter (*chandas*) is Anuṣṭubh. The deity (*devatā*) is Śrī Rudra. As for its visualization (*dhyāna*): One should meditate on the goddess of the arrow, blazing, upon a bow drawn back to the ear, with the arrow shining like the twilight.
One should meditate upon Maheśa, whose appearance is majestic, who is united with the Goddess, whose body is that of yoga, and who is youthful.

Preceded by the performance of the *prājāpatya* penance, the perfection (*siddhi*) of this mantra is attained through eleven thousand recitations. By means of this mantra, through circumambulation and prostration, there arises the grace of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), the destruction of sins, and the state of being a follower of Gaṇapati. As for the variations in its application:

The *Rudrakalpa* and *Arṇapāda* [commentaries] should be consulted; they are not written here for fear of prolixity. This is the first mantra. Having thus addressed the Blessed One with the first mantra, one prays for one's own welfare with the second: "O Rudra, that arrow of yours which was most auspicious has become terrible toward me, the most sinful, but through my salutation it has become peaceful. This is the first mantra. Thus, having praised the Blessed One with the first mantra, one prays for one's own happiness with the second: "O Rudra, that arrow of yours which was most auspicious previously has become terrible toward me, the most sinful, but through my salutation it has become peaceful. This is the sixth line.

This is the meaning. Likewise, that bow of yours which became auspicious (*śiva*), that form of yours which became peaceful (*śānta*), and that which was your *śaravyā*—which became *a-śaravyā*—is a specific type of weapon that is the cause of harm and poison. This is because of the Vedic revelation: "O *śaravyā*, when discharged toward the distant enemy, sharpen the *brahman*. Alternatively, from the verbal root *śṛ* (to injure), with the suffix *u*, we have *śaru*; those who possess *śaru* are *śaravaḥ*. That which is beneficial for them is *śaravyā*.

The quiver—this is an elliptical expression for the arrow-case as well. With that bow and with that [quiver], O Archer, be gracious to us; bring us happiness. Here, the seer is Atri; the meter is Anuṣṭubh; the deity is Śambhu. One should meditate upon the smiling God, shining with splendor together with the Goddess, adorned with arms bearing the bow and arrow, heroic in form, and being praised by hosts of gods. By reciting this continuously for twelve days—at times other than midnight, provided there is no conflict with one's obligatory duties—one performs the *puraścaraṇa* (preliminary rite).

Success! Thereupon, one becomes fit for the ritual application (*prayoga*). The *dharmamantra* is for the warding off of famine, civil unrest within the kingdom, and so forth. Thus, having sought worldly happiness by means of the second [mantra], one seeks the knowledge that is the cause of liberation by means of the third:
"O Rudra, that body of yours which is heard of as the auspicious one... [and] "these two bodies of yours are the terrible and the auspicious. (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 4.5.1)

The Brahmins who know the Vedas understand that the Lord has two forms in Bhārata: one is terrible (ghorā), and the other is auspicious (śivā). Furthermore, regarding the question "What is that [form] there which is non-terrible (aghorā)?": it is not merely non-terrible in the sense of being devoid of the quality of causing fear through weapons; rather, it is auspicious (śivā), meaning it brings about well-being and bestows happiness. It does not merely provide worldly pleasure, but rather the supreme human goal (paramapuruṣārtha).

He says that she is the bestower of the knowledge that is the cause of liberation for all beings. Regarding the term "apāpakāśinī" (the illuminator of the sinless): by the word "sinless" (*apāpa*), the knowledge of the reality of the Self as Brahman—which is the opposite of sin—is meant. As it is said: "Just as a tuft of reed placed in a fire is consumed, so too are all the sins of this person burnt away," according to the Śruti which states, "they are burnt away. This means [she is the giver] through knowledge; for the Śruti also states, "The realization of the Self is the light."

With that body of yours which is of such a kind—tranquil and consisting of unsurpassed bliss—look upon us from every side; make us endowed with light on all sides. For, according to the Śruti: "When this [Brahman] is known, all this becomes known," the non-dual reality of Brahman as the Self is to be manifested everywhere. Furthermore, the word *kāśī* is used here with the intensive (*yaṅluk*) suffix to express the sense of intensity (*bhṛśārtha*), indicating a frequent or intense action.

The meaning is that [the Lord] has been shown to be unobstructed and to cause those endowed with direct realization of the imperceptible to act. By the phrase "He gazes with his most peaceful form" (3rd line), it is demonstrated that the Supreme Lord has consciousness and bliss as His very nature. Anticipating the objection that one might desire liberation through mere prostration to His body—given that [liberation] is attainable only through many means such as hearing, reflection, meditative absorption, and sitting [in yoga]—He provides this instruction (5th line).

He is *riśantaḥ* because, abiding in the speech consisting of the *Girirudrādhyāya*, which pacifies fear (*bhīti-śānti*), He extends the bliss of liberation (*śam-mokṣa-sukham*). Even without the superimposition of hearing [the text], one who possesses the desire for liberation through the mere recitation (*japa*) of the *Śrīrudra*—which consists of divine names formed by salutations (*namaskāra*) alone—becomes immortal; for thus says the Śruti: "By these, indeed, one becomes immortal. This is the second invocation.
The natural meter of this mantra is Anuṣṭubh;

its deity is Śambhu. One should meditate upon the Lord of Creatures, the Sovereign, who has the moon for his face, who is adorned with the crescent of the moon, who bears the Gaṅgā, who is accompanied by the Daughter of the Mountain, who possesses three eyes, and who is adorned with ashes and serpents. (2nd line)
By reciting [the mantra] continuously for three nights without contradicting one's daily obligatory duties (*nityakarman*), the accomplishment of *puraścaraṇa* is attained.
This mantra bestows fruits such as the pacification of cattle; the desired accomplishment of the second and third [mantras] has been prayed for.
(3rd line) Now, with the fourth mantra, one prays for the removal of the undesirable, beginning with "yāmīṣum. (4th line) On the mountain...

He who, dwelling on Kailāsa, spreads welfare for the worlds is Giriśantaḥ. O Giriśanta, why do you carry—that is, hold—in your hand this arrow (iṣuṃ) for the purpose of casting it? [The word] *astave* is used in the sense of the infinitive suffix *-tum*, according to Vedic usage (*chandasi*). Make that arrow auspicious; O Śivakara ("Bringer of Welfare"), it behoves you to make the arrow auspicious—this is the intent of the address. As to what constitutes the auspiciousness of the arrow, he says: "Do not harm me"—that is, our person in the form of sons, grandsons, and so forth.

Likewise, our world—consisting of cattle, buffaloes, and so forth, as well as houses, gardens, fields, and the like—is [to be offered] by us. The intention is that this very thing constitutes the making of the world auspicious (*śivatvakaraṇa*). Here, since the purpose is already fulfilled by the term *giriśantī*, we shall demonstrate that the further address *giritra* conveys an additional meaning, indicating a specific distinction: "If even one who performs non-immortal deeds should worship me... (p. 41b, f. 38a, l. 1–3).

"I shall certainly protect [them]," such is the promise of the Supreme Lord. For this very reason, in the *Upānuvākya-kāṇḍa*, having introduced the theme that Manu divided his inheritance among his sons, beginning with Sanābhānediṣṭha and his vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), Rudra approached him as he was tending the cattle on the sacrificial ground (*yajñavāstu*). He said, "These cattle are indeed mine. [Manu] replied, "They are not for me; they are for you. He did not agree.

"He indeed has power over it," he said; "it is lost upon my sacrificial ground, or rather, it belongs to me. Therefore, [the sage] said, "Let there be [peace] through the sacrificial ground. Having spoken thus, Nābhi did not give it up. "Do not harm me at the sacrifice, nor harm my cattle"—this is the vow of the Blessed One that is heard. And in the Purāṇas and Itihāsas, there are many such statements concerning this subject; and so it is stated [on page 42a, folio 38b, line 1].

Regarding the speech in the form of the "Mountain-vow" (*giripratijñā*): the intention of the address is that, by abiding in it, one should worship [the Lord] as *Giritra*—the protector from the mountain—and that even though he is devoid of action (*akṛtyakāruṇa*), he would protect me, Nābhānediṣṭha, who worships him, just like [he protected] the cattle and so forth; this is the fourth [verse]. Thus, having offered salutation with "Obeisance to you, O Rudra," the attainment of the desired and the avoidance of the undesired were prayed for in the third and fourth [verses]; now, preceded by praise, both of these [are sought].

He prays with auspicious words; by the word *giri*, the Vedas, which are of the nature of mountains (*giri*), are denoted. Regarding this, the Śruti says: "He made those three mountain-like [Vedas] visible to the ignorant" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.4.3.3), introducing them with the words "These are indeed the Vedas. Thus, because He dwells (*śete*) or abides (*tiṣṭhati*) within the Vedas, which are of the nature of mountains, He is *Girīśa*. O *Girīśa*, You who are the subject of the Vedas—O Unfading One, due to Your stainlessness—we speak of You with auspicious words; that is to say, we praise You.

Regarding what kind of praise [is appropriate] there, he says: "In whatever manner (*yathā*)—by means of such praise (*stutyā*) performed—our entire world (*sarvam api jagat*), consisting of moving beings such as cattle and sons, may become free from disease (*ayakṣmam*), healthy (*arogam*), well-disposed (*sumanāḥ*), endowed with cheerfulness (*saumanasyopetam*), and happy; in that manner we shall praise. Here, by the term *girīśanta*, it is indeed appropriate to offer a hymn to the one who is the subject of description in all the Vedas.
Thus it has been shown there that one should not suspect impurity on the part of the Supreme Lord due to His connection with the speech of a sinner; therefore, He addresses [the disciple] again:

(3rd line) "Even when there is a connection with the speech of a defiled person, there is never any harm to Him who is eternally faultless. For the water of the Gaṅgā does not become sinful through contact with the water of a street; on the contrary, by association with the Gaṅgā, the street water itself becomes purifying, [just as it overcomes] the water of the Yamunā. (5th line)
The intention behind the address is that one indeed attains non-distinction [from the Lord] when the mind and speech are thus fixed upon the supremely purifying Blessed One;

and just as my speech becomes honored by the world like the Veda, so too, with this in mind, even my words— once fallen into the Śaiva [tradition]— attain the very nature of Śiva due to their extreme excellence, just as water from a street gutter falling into the current of the Gaṅgā acquires the status of the Gaṅgā itself.

"By auspicious speech"—thus it is said; these two mantras, the fourth and fifth, constitute a single mantra when joined. The seer (*ṛṣi*) of this mantra is Gautama (line 9), the deity (*devatā*) is Rudra.
[It refers to him] shining forth with a form suited for battle.
One should meditate upon the enemy of Tripura, the Lord of the gods, who possesses a gentle smile;
who desires to consume the Daityas; who holds the bow of the Lord of Mountains in his hand; and who is mounted upon the chariot of the host of immortals.

Through these two mantras, the avoidance of untimely death and other benefits are attained. By reciting [them] continuously for twenty-one days, the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) is perfected. Fifth.
Now, even though I have been thus propitiated by these salutations and hymns, [what of] Vaivasvata, Citragupta, and others who are exceedingly difficult to subdue? Fourth.

And because he feared that other gods, who had become witnesses to his sin, might prevent the removal of his misfortune through their power, [the text] says "He spoke," implying that even though they were well-disposed, they were all unable to help him. Regarding the partiality [of the gods], it is said:
"When two Brahmins come to question a Brahmin... (7th line).

Because it is heard [in scripture] that "he should speak," the meaning is as follows: He is the one whose nature is to speak *adhi* (above/superiorly) to those who are devoted (*bhakta*) and those who are not; he is the first, the primary, that is to say, the most excellent. He is *daivyaḥ*, meaning he exists among the gods (*deveṣu bhavaḥ*), that is, he is the inner controller (*antaryāmī*) of the gods. He is the physician (*bhiṣaj*), the healer of all diseases such as illness, sin, the suffering of saṃsāra, poverty, and so forth; for there is a scriptural passage stating, "I hear him as the physician, the supreme physician. Thus, being possessed of such qualities, he spoke *adhi*.
