"Let him speak out according to the Vedic usage; that is to say, let him employ the *laṅ* in the sense of the imperative (*loṭ*)—let him show partiality toward this [man], thinking 'this is mine'. (Third line) What is he doing? He is "driving away" (*nyarvān*) even those who are manifestly harmful, such as serpents, scorpions, thieves, tigers, and the like. And all the *yātudhānyas*—that is, the species of *yātudhānas* appearing in the forms of *rakṣases*, *piśācas*, diseases, and epilepsy—all those who are harmful in ways that are not immediately apparent. (Fifth line)

"Crushing and destroying, he has spoken over [them]"—in this regard, how can there be a statement of partiality toward you regarding the Blessed One who is entirely impartial? For if that were so, it would entail the consequence of inequality and cruelty. To resolve such a doubt, it is said: "He has spoken over [them]. For speaking over devotees is prompted by the act of devotion; therefore, it does not bring about any fault in the Lord. This is because [the Lord's action] takes into account [other factors], and thus there is no inequality or cruelty.

The meaning is that this is according to the aforementioned principle (*nyāya*). Even though the Blessed One is partial [to his devotees], one might raise the doubt: "Why would the experience of the fruits of sin not still occur for him when prompted by other deities such as Vaivasvata? To dispel this doubt, the word "first" (*prathama*) is stated. [This refers to the mantra: "He who is the first among the gods, the Great Seer Rudra who transcends all; him, the supreme Maheśvara among lords, him, the supreme deity among deities; he who is the god of all... (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 10.1.1).

The meaning is as follows: since there are thousands of Śrutis, Smṛtis, and Itihāsas stating that "in the Vedas [He is called] Mahādeva" and "the deities stand aside for one who offers salutation to Him," when my partisan—who possesses the status of being the foremost among all deities known through these sources—is present, there is no room for the fear of suffering caused by other deities who depend upon Him. Not only is there no suffering caused by other deities for me...

On the contrary, because he is merely a being, he is even worthy of worship by all deities; for, as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of that [being], the Blessed Lord has become a partisan of my side. This is shown by the word *daivya*, which denotes the state of being the inner controller of the deities. By the word *bhiṣaj* (physician), [it is meant]:
for a physician who knows the cause of a disease, when employing violence toward a patient, there is no cruelty whatsoever; rather, it is compassion itself in this case.

That [the Lord] is the instigator has been established by the *Śivapurāṇa* through the illustration of the physician. By stating that the Blessed One possesses supreme compassion, it is demonstrated that He indeed spoke regarding those who harm living beings, such as the *yātudhānīs*. Just as a skilled physician, although his application of caustic [alkali] causes immediate suffering through burning, brings about the ultimate benefit for those people by removing their wounds in due course.

Because he brings about happiness, there is no loss of his compassion. By stating "jambhayan" (crushing) instead of "jambhayan" (crushing), and by not using the word "addhā" (truly/certainly), the Lord’s unimpeded sovereignty is demonstrated. For if he were himself unable to restrain the *yātudhānas* and the deities of death who incite them, he would indeed have entreated him [Yama], saying, "My Yama must be harmed. This is the implication of that conciliation.

The Blessed One, liberating the prostrate [being] from the *yātudhānīs* of the past, spoke, saying, "May he crush [them]," thus praying for [his] protection. While they were thus restraining him, by first destroying the *yātudhānīs*, he protected the prostrate one. Then, when the gods arrived and asked, "Who is this most wicked one who has been protecting [him]? he offered a partisan reply, saying, "This is mine; how could he have committed sin?"

For this very reason, when the Supreme Lord, wishing to lead even great sinners such as the Kirātas and others—who were not His soldiers—to Himself, caused them to fall [from hell] by means of His own messengers and brought them to Kailāsa, Yama, Citragupta, and the others reported the matter accordingly at the end of their discourse. Then, by His own will, the Blessed One declared: "These, who have performed prostrations and other rites with as many as ten million *bilva* leaves, are Mine; the Blessed Ones [the gods] have no authority over them. Thus it is said.

It has been said that this story is frequently recounted in the Purāṇas. With this in mind, [the author] first presents the "looking" (*vīkṣaṇa*) with the words, "O God, speak for our protection and for our superiority," and subsequently establishes the "speaking over" (*adhivacana*).

This mantra is the *viśajvarakṣa* (the protection against the fever of the people); it averts all afflictions caused by Piśācas and other malevolent beings. For this very reason, its name is "Kavaca" (Armor), as he says:
The Blessed Bodhāyana declared: "This is the armor. Kaṇva is its seer; Anuṣṭubh is the meter; Śambhu is the deity.

One should meditate upon the three-eyed God, who has the crescent moon as his crest-jewel, who is the enemy of Time (Death), who wears a serpent as his sacred thread, and who resembles a blazing fire.

Success in one's purpose is achieved through fifty thousand recitations (*japa*). Now, the Lord who is the witness of all actions, whose essence is the Sun, having been directly entreated by the six mantras, is propitiated and petitioned with two verses beginning with "asau yastāmra" (He who is copper-colored). The meaning is that the Lord previously mentioned is indeed "this very one," the Sun who is being perceived directly before the eyes. He is seen directly.
He thus demonstrates that form through its qualifiers: "Copper-colored, ruddy, and brown, most auspicious.

At the time of rising, it is intensely red and thus *tāmra*; immediately after that, it is slightly red and thus *aruṇa*; and beyond that, it is tawny (*piṅgala*) in color. As it has been said: "The tawny (*piṅgala*), the mongoose (*nakula*), the bald man (*khalati*), and the *miṣa* and *aṭura*—these four, according to etymologists, are called *babhru*."

Thus it has been proclaimed. And that [light], because it is the cause of the world’s happiness by warding off darkness, cold, and so forth, is most auspicious (*sumaṅgala*). For the underlying sense is that when the Blessed One is in the form of the Sun, the world seized by darkness and the like would indeed become auspicious. Such is the Blessed Lord Rudra, whose nature is the Sun; or rather, those other Rudras who, having become one with the Sun, have been invoked for this [earth] on all sides in the quarters, by the command of the Supreme Lord.

And they, stationed in the eastern and other directions, exist by the thousands—countless in number—as those Rudras who will be mentioned later in the passage beginning with "sahasraśo ye rudra adhibhūmyām. They perform favor and restraint toward people in accordance with their merit and demerit;
[this refers to] the very anger [of these deities] whose forms are like the sun, caused by the performance of what is enjoined or the practice of what is forbidden.
"By means of great praise, prostrations, and so forth, we approach you; may you be gracious toward us"—this is the meaning. Thus ends the seventh [verse].

Having thus propitiated [the deity] in the seventh [verse], in the eighth he prays for the attainment of lost success (*naṣṭasiddhi*): "He who glides along for you... [and] "those who are blue-necked, three-eyed, and blue-throated. (Eighth verse)

"He who is known as 'the Tranquil' (praśānta) according to the Vedic revelation is indeed this very one who is 'deep red' (vilohita), being exceedingly red, he moves forward. For what purpose does he move? To this he says: 'And him...'"—that is, they saw that Supreme Lord in the form of the Sun. "The cows"—meaning those who first carry away ignorance—"saw him. Likewise, "the water-carriers" (udakahāryaḥ)—those who fetch water—even from the cowherds saw him.

How much of the object to be designated do the ignorant perceive? Indeed, all beings—even cows, buffaloes, and so forth, as well as all those who possess the knowledge of Brahman—perceive Him. Thus, in order to gladden everyone through His own vision, the Supreme Lord, whose self is the Sun, moves forth; for it is heard [in scripture]: "As He rises, all creatures rejoice in Him. This is the singular conclusion of the Vedānta.

One should attain that which is of the nature of pure consciousness, bliss, and non-duality, which is extremely difficult to discern. It is to be perceived by the worshippers through the grace of the Guru, like the manifestation of Kailāsa and other [realms]. Therefore, this [reality] is directly perceptible to all; everyone who has performed their duty (*kṛtakṛtya*) should approach the Blessed One—thus says the Brāhmaṇa. Herein, for the verse beginning with "asau yaḥ tāmrā," the meter is *āstārapaṅkti*; for the verse beginning with "asau yo avasarpati," [the meter is...].

The metre is *jagatī* with six feet. The seer (*ṛṣi*) for both [verses] is Marutvat. The deity is the Blessed One in the form of Āditya. One should meditate upon Him who is situated within the solar orb, golden-hued, radiant, nourishing, and possessing a pure smile; fierce, with undiminished brilliance, and served by thousands of sages. If one recites this continuously for sixteen days preceded by the performance of the *kṛcchra* penance, success is attained. This is the method for averting drought.

Having propitiated the form of Āditya with the seventh and eighth [verses], let him propitiate the venerable Nīlakaṇṭha-mūrti, who dwells on Bhūkailāsa, with the ninth [verse] and pay homage: "Salutation be to the blue-necked one, the venerable Kaṇṭha-mūrti; salutation be to him. Of what nature is he? To the thousand-eyed one (*sahasrākṣāya*). The word *vāci* refers to speech that is immeasurable. According to the traditional teaching (*smṛti*), "the universe consists of a thousand [parts]"; therefore, he is the thousand-eyed one (*sahasrākṣāya*) because he possesses a thousand eyes.

The meaning is "those whose vision is undivided. By this, it is stated that even those residing on Kailāsa are within the range of my vision as "I" and "mine. Furthermore, to what kind of one? To the *mīḍhuṣe*, the showerer of the desires of those who bow; by this, the quality of bestowing the fruit of salutation—which consists in the accomplishment of all desired goals—is demonstrated. And by the term *nīlagrīvāya*, the sense is "to the one possessing a blue throat due to the swallowing of the *kālakūṭa* poison"; it is not a [mere] quality.

The wise one, accepting faults, praises with his head the former [the moon], while the Lord of Kailāsa keeps the latter [poison] in his throat; thus the celebrated greatness of the Blessed One is remembered. Therefore, the Supreme Lord, having restrained within himself the entire web of faults which is like the *kālakūṭa* poison, praises even a mere fraction of virtue with his head.
Even though he is easily accessible, he is being worshipped. Having paid homage to the one Lord, one then pays homage to his attendants with the words "atha u" (and then).
Furthermore, there exist the first groups of beings who are devoted to residing near this Nīlakaṇṭha form;

for these divine hosts of manifold forms are well known in the Purāṇas and other scriptures as the attendants (*pārṣada*) of the Blessed Lord, and in the Sāmaveda they are referred to as *adhipādāya*.

By the passage beginning with "for the protection of the field" (*kṣetrāpātāya*), they are described as possessing universal sovereignty; likewise, in the *Sauṣuptika* section of the *Mahābhārata*, it is said:

"The Siddhas, who are the lords and masters of the three worlds, whose hands bear the letter *ka*, who are eternally blissful, joyful, masters of speech, and free from envy; those who, having attained the eightfold sovereignty (*aṣṭaguṇamaiśvaryam*), do not even feel wonder; and before whom the Blessed Lord Bhava himself is constantly filled with wonder by their deeds."
"By means of sacred learning, celibacy, austerity, and self-restraint, those who, having approached the trident-marked [form], attained union with Bhava.
(5th line) Thus, in the *Drauṇaparvan*, his various divine forms as attendants and so forth are elaborated upon through such passages as "O Lord, he assumes the earth," and so on.
(6th line) Furthermore, in the Purāṇas, there are statements regarding his greatness numbering in the thousands, such as in the verse "therein, thousands upon thousands. (7th line)
How much more could be cited? Thus, to those who are his foremost hosts of beings, I have paid homage; I have made obeisance; I pay homage.
(Line 8) The seer and deity of this mantra are the Blessed One himself; the meter is *triṣṭubh*.
With the radiance of the autumn moon, [he possesses] a cool splendor like that of Puṣan. (p. 48b, f. 45a, line 1)
One should meditate upon Śiva, seated upon a lion-throne together with Umā.
This mantra bestows the attainment of beautiful leaves. All the *puraścaraṇa* mantras are to be seen in the *Arṇava*.
Thus ends the ninth [chapter].
Now, with the six verses beginning with the tenth, [the author] prays for the withdrawal of the weapons.

(3rd line) Although it was already prayed for by the words "O Śiva, O Aṅgiras, perform the vow, do not harm us," and so forth, nevertheless, because of fear, it is prayed for again through the Lord. (4th line) Therefore, there is no room for the suspicion of redundancy. "Release [them]," etc. (5th line) O Blessed One!

O Blessed One, since the term *bhaga* is defined as the possession of the six qualities— complete sovereignty, valor, fame, splendor, knowledge, and dispassion— you, the Fully Awakened One, are endowed with these six attributes such as complete sovereignty mentioned in that statement. O Lord, from the tips of the ends of your own bow— that is, from those [ends] belonging to your bow— [by means of which...]

"Release the maurvī-string; slacken it! For no one other than you is able to string this bow, which is endowed with complete sovereignty and other such powers, according to the Vedic revelation: 'Thou didst fasten [the string] upon the bow for Umā-Rudra in the forest. Therefore, the meaning is that you alone, having become gracious, must lower the bow.
Indeed, even when the string has been lowered, the arrows appear as if they are still coiled."
Therefore, O Blessed One, turn back those arrows which are in your hand; this is the tenth [chapter].

Having thus prayed for their turning back, those arrows—finding no relief from fear even through their mere color—were cursed to have blunted tips. In this way, the words "hundred" (*śata*) and "thousand" (*sahasra*) denote infinity;
O thousand-eyed one, O infinite-eyed one, [the meaning is] those among hundreds who possess infinite quivers, because of the infinity of the arrow-receptacles.

Having thus performed the sacrifice, even archery is said [to be surpassed]. In the world, an archer possesses limited vision and a limited quiver; when his field of vision is obstructed or his arrows are exhausted, he is unable to shoot. However, one who possesses unlimited vision and infinite arrows can never be thwarted. You, moreover, possess unlimited vision and infinite arrows; you cannot be thwarted in any way whatsoever.

Therefore, since this purpose of my means [of attainment] is difficult to avoid, you yourself must unstring your bow, fix the string upon it, and shatter the tips of the arrows—their points—rendering them blunt and useless as if they were mere quivers.
Even when this has been done, if the piercer remains cruel, he does not leave even the mind undisturbed; "Śiva" thus refers to one who possesses a gentle appearance.
May our mind be well-disposed toward beautiful acts of homage.
Thus ends the eleventh [chapter].

Now he expresses his desire to see even those arrows that have become blunt: "The stringless," [says] Kapardin; the bow of the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara) is without a string—this is the sense of the ellipsis. Furthermore, the quiver is "without arrows," meaning it is devoid of shafts.

Even though he is free from arrows, the poet describes the piercing [of his enemies] by means of arrows remaining elsewhere: "They have vanished" (*aneśan*)—the arrows of this Kapardin have vanished; that is, they have reached destruction in the form of an incapacity to pierce. Regarding the verb *naś*, the present tense (*laṭ*) is used in the Vedic sense of a benediction, and there is also the suffix *ki*. Furthermore, "his quiver" (*niṣaṅgadhīḥ*) refers to the sword-sheath. They say: "May it be slightly capable"—meaning it is only capable of rusting the sword, not for the purpose of cutting, nor even sufficient to withstand the drawing of the sword.

This is the meaning. Here, the three verses beginning with "pramuñca dhanvanaḥ" constitute a single mantra; its seer is Nārada, its meter is Anuṣṭubh, and its deity is Śrī Rudra. [The visualization is:
[He] possesses a splendor like that of ten million rising suns and a form ablaze with fire. (Fifth line)
One should meditate upon Rudra, adorned with terrifying serpents and wielding various weapons.
"By this [weapon], enemies shall perish"— this is the twelfth [verse].
Thus,
having requested the withdrawal of the weapons with three mantras, he now prays for his own protection by means of them.

"O most bountiful one, [protect us] with that weapon of yours"—this is an address containing a reason (*hetugarbha-sambodhana*), meaning "you who rain down the fulfillment of the desires of your devotees. Regarding the phrase "that weapon of yours" (*yā te hetiḥ*): it refers to your sword and other weapons; furthermore, it should be understood as "that bow which has been in your hand," by means of which weapon—namely, this bow which is the cause of health for your devotees (*ayakṣmayā*)—you, O Lord, protect and preserve us from all misfortune on every side. Thus.
The thirteenth.

Having thus prayed, he again pays homage: "Omnis salus tibi" (*namaste*). O Blessed One, let there be homage to your weapon. Of what kind? To the extended (*tata*), that is, to that which is raised up to strike; and to the unextended (*anātata*), that is, to the other [weapon] not so raised. To the bold (*dhṛṣṇave*), capable by its very nature of striking—homage to it. Furthermore, let there be homage to both your arms. By the use of the dual number in the word "arms," [the two are intended].

Although the duality [of arms] is already established, perceiving that both arms are raised to shoot, he speaks again out of fear and extreme agitation: "Thus, salutations to your two arms" (the fourteenth verse). Then, having offered salutation, he prays once more: "From all sides, from your bow...
O Blessed One, regarding your bow—that is, your archer's weapon—whatever weapon is mounted upon it, such as this... (the eighth line).

May that weapon in the form of an arrow, that missile, ward us off from every side—from all affliction; that is to say, may it exclude us [from harm] and protect us. Furthermore, while this heap of evil exists, how can there be for you an avoidance of affliction? To this he says: "Moreover, that quiver of yours, wherein sharp arrows abide—may that [quiver] be far away from us, from our kin."
"Place [it] in the heap, in the mass of evil; establish it—meaning, destroy it.
Thus ends the fifteenth mantra.
Regarding this [verse] beginning with "atra yāte hetih" (the fourth line):

the meter is *anuṣṭubh*. The seer (*ṛṣi*) and the deity (*devatā*) are the Blessed One himself. One should constantly meditate upon him whose lotus-feet are reddened by the pollen of the flowers from the garlands on the crowns of tens of millions of prostrating gods, who is accompanied by Bhavānī, who has come along with him, and who holds the *pināka* bow in his hand.
This mantra is primarily intended for the destruction of enemies.
The first section (anuvāka) is completed.

Thus, in the first section (*anuvāka*), having propitiated the Blessed One along with his retinue by means of fifteen mantras, he has been petitioned. Now, in the second [section], with eight verses, intending to pay homage to you in the form of the Lord of All, the Self of All, and the Inner Controller of All, he first—

Beginning with this [verse] and ending with "Obeisance to you, the dogs and the lords of dogs," he pays homage by virtue of his being the Lord of All; indeed, all these mantras consist of double obeisances.

Furthermore, every mantra begins with "namas" and ends with "namaḥ," such as: "Obeisance to the golden-armed one, the leader of the army, and to the lord of the quarters; obeisance, obeisance. In the same way, it continues further on; therein, each individual object included within the phenomenal world [is addressed].
Having established the Lord’s sovereignty preceded by the proof of His preeminence, he begins to offer salutation:

"Salutation to Hiraṇyabāhu. To Hiraṇyabāhu means to Him whose arms are adorned with golden armlets (*keyūra*) and other ornaments; and the mention of the "arms" is illustrative, signifying that He is covered from head to foot with divine golden armor and decorations.
The Śrutis proclaim that the entire divine, auspicious form (*divyamaṅgalavigraha*) of the Blessed One is, by its very nature, of golden color (*kanakavarṇa*). [They declare:

"Obeisance to the one with golden arms, to the golden-colored one; from the tip of the nails, all indeed should be of [golden] color. [And: "When the seer sees... [and] "the offering (*arpaṇa*)," etc.; and [passages such as] "the form of the limbs, perceivable by the intellect of those who sleep," and "shining like beautiful gold," etc.—these are the scriptural authorities (*āgamas*).

The *senāni* is so called because he leads (*nayati*) the armies (*senāḥ*). The army (*senā*) consists of multitudes such as gods, asuras, siddhas, elephant-skins, humans, and so forth; he is the commander-in-chief (*senāpati*).

For it has been stated by Āśvalāyana, after invoking Śiva: "Indeed, all these names here belong to him—'all the armies' and 'all the exalted ones'. To that *senāni*, the lord of the directions beginning with the East, [be] homage.

In order to dispel the doubt that the status of being a guardian of the directions (*dikpati*) belongs only to Indra, Agni, and others, it is stated [in the text] "the commander of the army" (*senānī*); by this qualification, it is shown that the sovereignty over the directions belongs to the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) alone as the sovereign of the entire host of deities, whereas Indra and the others—

By his command, [the mantra] is shown to be the presiding deities of those respective [spheres]. In response to the inquiry as to how the Supreme Lord can possess lordship over Indra and the others, he is specified as "Hiraṇyabāhu" (Golden-armed). For by that [mantra], the form of the Supreme Lord to be meditated upon in the Antaryāditya-vidyā is expressed: "That golden person who is within the sun. Precisely for this reason, the application of the mantra "Salutation to Hiraṇyabāhu" has been established in the Purāṇas and other texts for the meditation on the Inner Sun. And likewise, "those who go beyond him... (ye cāmuṣmāt parāñcaḥ).

In the passage beginning with "Beyond this world are six worlds of the gods and of desires" (*muṣmānte ṣaṭñceṣṭendeva kāmānām*), which describes the sovereignty over the enjoyment of the heavenly worlds and so forth mentioned in the *Antarāditya* section,

the phrase "with golden arms" (*hiraṇyabāhavaḥ*) demonstrates that it is appropriate for Him— who establishes the nature of the Supreme Lord— to possess lordship over those [worlds], such as heaven and their enjoyments and sovereign powers. Furthermore, the lordship of the Supreme Lord is well-known.
Having heard that Indra and others hold sovereignty over the realms of Śruti and so forth, and that all this—including Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra—is produced from Him;

and that "He is the cause, the cause of causes, the one endowed with all sovereignty, Śambhu who is to be meditated upon"—as well as the scriptural passages such as "From fear of Him, fire and Indra [tremble]"; and as it is stated in the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, for example in the Mahābhārata: "He alone bestows [the fruits of action] upon men, and He alone takes them away again."

And among the gods beginning with Śakra, his alone is said to be sovereignty; thus it is stated even in the *Bhāgavata*. Furthermore, that which is elaborated upon in the *Śiva-purāṇas*—namely, that Brahmā and the others are "those who carry skulls made by him"—is likewise [established] here. Thus, having first established the salutation to the Supreme Lord as the possessor of all the quarters, distinguished as the world-protectors such as Indra and the rest, now follows the second mantra: "Salutation to the trees," wherein [the phrase] "to the Lord of beasts" occurs.

First, the syntactical connection (*anvaya*). Here, the word "paśu" does not refer merely to cows and the like; rather, it refers to those with two feet and four feet. Since these [terms] refer to all common living beings in general, [the Lord is called] Paśupati. This is because of such scriptural passages as, "Of beasts, both those that are four-footed and those that are two-footed," and "These indeed are the beasts: those with two feet and those with four feet," and so forth. And thus, [He is] the entirety...

The meaning is "the lords of living beings. In that regard, when the inquiry arises as to how the state of being a sacrificial animal (*paśu*) pertains to living beings, and how the Blessed One possesses the status of their lord (*pati*), the phrase "to the tawny-haired trees" (*vṛkṣebhyo harikeśebhyaḥ*) was stated to explain this. Here, "tawny-haired" refers to those whose hair consists of *palāśa* leaves; [the meaning is] "salutation to the Rudras who possess such [hair]. Likewise, another has explained it as: "and salutation to Paśupati."

In this interpretation, because this [tree] lacks the capacity to establish the state of being a Pāśupata, there is no connection with the phrase "lords of the animals" (*paśūnāṃ patayaḥ*). Nor is there any relevance for the statement "the manifestation of the nature of a tree" within the context expressing universal lordship (*sarveśvaratva*). Furthermore, there is some purpose for the qualification "to the tawny-haired ones" (*namaḥ harikeśebhyaḥ*), and later [it says] "homage to the trees" (*namo vṛkṣebhyaḥ*).

Since it will be stated later that the tree-nature belongs to [the one] "named Harikeśa," there would be a redundancy; therefore, the specific meaning must be considered. We shall demonstrate this: "Having its origin in the Unmanifest as its root, nourished by that very [Unmanifest], with intellect, the aggregates, and mind, and with the senses as its hollows; having its roots above and its branches below, the eternal tree of the world; and here too, the threefold state."

With the foremost mantra, "Obeisance to the Lord of the worlds, the cause of existence," there is the consecration of the Supreme Lord; and because the tree of *saṃsāra* is manifested [through] the weapons such as the axe (*ṭaṅka*), even the term *harikeśa* indicates the three qualities (*traigunya*) characterized by the color green, which are the leaves consisting of the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*). Furthermore, the Vedas, whose domain is the three qualities, are characterized by their remaining hairs.

According to the traditional teaching (*smṛti*) that "the *chandas* are its colors," just as there are protective coatings for a tree, so too the *chandas*, consisting of the ritual sections (*karmakāṇḍa*), serve to protect the tree of *saṃsāra*; for they teach the rituals that cause the growth of *saṃsāra*. And because they are infinite like the hairs on the head, they are described as being hair. Thus: "Obeisance to the trees."

The meaning of the mantra portion "to Harikeśebhyaḥ" is a salutation to the Supreme Lord, insofar as he constitutes the tree of transmigratory existence permeated by the various impurities of karma. This concludes [the explanation].

By this, the two questions—"How is there the state of a bound soul (*paśutva*)? and "How is there the state of the Lord of Beasts (*paśupatitva*)?"—are answered. The state of being a bound soul for living beings consists in their being bound by the fetters of transmigratory existence; thus, the explanation of these two questions is concluded.

Because He causes them to perform their respective functions, the Supreme Lord possesses the status of a "Lord" (*pati*) by virtue of attaining that meaning; this very point is clearly elaborated in the *Laiṅga Purāṇa*:
"From Brahmā down to the lowest [beings], all are proclaimed to be 'bound souls' (*paśu*) of the trident-bearing God of gods, subject to the power of transmigratory existence.
Because He is the Lord of those [souls], Śiva, the Lord of Devas, is remembered as Paśupati. By means of the bonds of impurity (*mala*), *māyā*, and so forth, [He binds] the bound souls..."

"Having bound [them] with these nooses, Maheśvara, the Lord of lords, himself causes them to perform their duties. He alone is their liberator, when he has been properly worshipped with devotion. Thus, statements from the Skanda, Śiva, and Kūrma Purāṇas should also be cited here. Having stated that [the creation] begins with Brahmā and ends with the stationary beings, the inclusion of "bipeds and quadrupeds" in the mantra "He is the Lord of those... refers to the entirety of conscious beings.

Thus, it is explained that [the world] is characterized by conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). Just as cows, horses, buffaloes, and so forth, are bound with ropes by their owners, brought under control, and then employed in various tasks dependent on the capacities of those respective objects—either as a means of serving [the owner] or for his own utility—so too is the state of being cattle (*paśutva*) established for all beings from Brahmā down to the immovable [plants], while the Supreme Lord possesses the status of their master (*pati*). This is further confirmed by the Vedic revelation: "He said... (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.18).

Deluded by the knowledge that "I alone am the supreme prostration and the lord of all beings"—a boon obtained from the Blessed One in the Pāśupata [tradition]—the world, being incapable of distinguishing between the bound soul (*paśu*), the fetter (*pāśa*), and the Lord (*pati*), is unable to offer salutation on its own. Therefore, out of compassion, [the Lord] made his own Pāśupata nature manifest in the world under a different guise; this is thus established as self-evident within the Śiva Purāṇas.
"Your state of being bound and even your animal-like condition—I shall today make these firm through the excellent amusements of bondage. By such [verses], the intended meaning is explained.

This is appropriate because, since the animal-like state consisting of the bonds of *saṃsāra* is beginningless, the state of being bound—which consists of being a binder of that [state]—is also beginningless, due to its connection with the attainment of activity. For a bond cannot exist without a binder; this is established by the self-evidence proclaimed in the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, and other sources.

Regarding the state of being the Supreme Lord, [the objection that] the Blessed One’s acceptance of the Pāśupata vow, the acquisition thereof, and the existence of some bestower of that boon upon him are in any way inconceivable—let them be set aside for now. Now, as for the third [mantra]: *namassasphiñcarāya*. Here, *saspati* refers to young grass; *piñcara* means a color mixed with yellow and red; and *sasphiñjara* is that which is like young grass in its *piñcara* color. To Him, the radiant one (*tviṣamāne*).
The literal meaning of the phrase is: "Salutation to the Lord of the paths, the possessor of light," referring to the Vedic and Tantric paths.

Here, by the term *tviṣīmataḥ* ("possessing splendor"), the light that is knowledge (*jñāna*) is expressed; by this, two doubts are dispelled. For such is the doubt: "How is it that the Tantric paths were revealed by the Supreme Lord, when they are Smṛtis outside the Veda? (6th–8th lines).

"And whatever views exist here, they are all fruitless; for their final goal after death is indeed *tāmasī* (of the nature of darkness), because they are [merely] constructed. To this, the reply is: it is true that the Tantric paths are censured; however, that censure applies only to those who are outside the Vedic fold (*vedabāhya*), whereas for the followers of the Vedas (*vaidika*), the Tantric paths themselves are beneficial. This was considered by the Omniscient Supreme Lord.

In this regard, these [Tantric] systems were established; for if they did not exist, then those outside the Vedas—who are most wicked, who turn their backs on the Vedic path, who do not know the means to the highest good or other scriptures, and who are driven solely by the force of their own habitual conduct—would surely have perished. Therefore, the initiation into the Tantric path was intended [for them]. This very point is stated in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:

This has been clearly explained: the sage Gautama, having understood through some cause that their lineage was born of illusion—like a cow [of low origin]—cursed them most severely, saying, "They shall become excluded from the three Vedas and equal to great sinners. Thus, being cursed by Gautama for their wickedness and exclusion from the Vedas, they all departed and approached Lord Śaṅkara and the imperishable Viṣṇu.
"May we be like servants who are honored with various hymns of praise"—with these words and others, they presented their petition to Śaṅkara in the presence of Viṣṇu.

Then, being thus well-urged by Mādhava, the enemy of Mura, Rudra said: "Therefore, for the sake of protecting those outside the Vedas and for the delusion of the sinful, we shall compose scriptures. Thus he acted.

"Even Keśava, impelled by Śiva, [revealed] delusive scriptures: the Kapāla, Lāṅgula, Guḍa, Śākta, Bhairava, Pūrvapaścima, Pāñcarātra, Pāśupata, and likewise thousands of others. These are the Tantras such as the Pāśupata and Pāñcarātra for the protection of the most wicked among the outsiders.

It is said that the path has been set forth for the sake of delusion; this is the meaning of that statement. Furthermore, there is a presentation of doctrines contrary to the Vedas in the *Pāśupata*, *Pāñcarātra*, and other *tantras*, such as the doctrine of an Ishvara who is a mere efficient cause (*nimitta*), and descriptions of the Lord (*pati*) as distinct from the individual soul (*jīva*). Regarding those [texts], there is a censure of the Veda; and it has indeed been established by all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that their lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) in those specific parts is determined in the *Brahma-mīmāṃsā*.
And the purpose of censuring the Vedas and describing that which is contrary to them among those [works] is to delude those who,

though being Vaidikas, develop a lack of faith in the Vedas due to the power of sin; and that delusion is for the sake of favoring them, for those haters of the Vedas remain [only] within independent [treatises] that contain censures of the Vedas.

Those who, though highly esteemed by the Śruti, perceive the Tantric path as a means for the realization of the Veda, do not worship the Supreme Lord according to the prescribed injunctions. Due to that fault of hatred toward the Veda, they fall into a state of transgression; yet, through the merit [of their practice], they shall attain steadfastness in the Veda in a future birth. Now, as for those belonging to the Vedic fold, such as Śāṇḍilya, having abandoned steadfastness in the Veda, they resort to the Pāñcarātra and other such systems.

In the *Vāsiṣṭhalaiṅga*, it is heard that those who worshipped Viṣṇu according to the rite of initiation (*dīkṣā*) were granted a boon by the Lord Vāsudeva, who said: "You shall go by way of the twice-born Vedic path preceded by censure. [He continued: "By resorting to my own system alone, even the worship of me has been performed by you;
however, I am not pleased by that. O Śāṇḍilya, though it was performed by you through a wrong path, this worship of mine is dear to me."

Therefore, after a long time, you shall attain the path of the Vedas. Regarding the delusive power of the Supreme Lord over the most wicked, there is no fault, because—just as with His appearance in that context—His intent culminates in grace toward them. For this very reason, the delusive power of the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa is frequently proclaimed in His incarnations as Buddha and others.

"For Pūṣan does not belong to him. All this—even the scriptures intended for delusion—is what is meant by this [statement]. There are many other such statements on this subject; all of them have been taken up by us in the *Pāṣaṇḍagajakesarī*, and they should be consulted therein. Thus, for the protection of those outside the Vedic fold, the Omniscient One [established] the great Tantric path.

The phrase "set in motion" (*pravartita*) has been demonstrated by the term "of the Radiant One" (*tviṣīmataḥ*). Following that, having raised the objection regarding the fault of partiality and cruelty on the part of the Supreme Lord toward certain qualified recipients of the Veda and others excluded from the Veda, this is resolved by the term "to the Tawny One" (*saspiñjarāya*). This term denotes a specific mixed caste and, by indicating the state of being dominated by the three *guṇas* in such a manner, removes that [objection]. It is beginningless...

The meaning is that for the Creator who creates in such a manner according to the specific qualities and actions accumulated through knowledge (vidyā), there is no possibility of partiality or the like; for the Śruti states: "One becomes virtuous by virtuous action, or sinful by sinful action," and so forth.
Now begins the fourth [chapter].

*Namo babhruśāya*: He who bears the Supreme Lord is *babhru*. [The term] *vṛṣabhaḥ* [is derived from] the root *bhraṃś* by means of the rule beginning with *kṛvṛdṛc* etc. When there is the suffix *kvip*, followed by reduplication (*dvirvacana*) and the substitution of *yaṇ* for the root vowel, and upon the prohibition of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* due to its being *kit*, the form *babhruḥ* is established. Because he lies or stands upon *babhru* (the tawny one), he is *babhruśaḥ*; [thus] the Bull-vehicled One (*vṛṣavāhanaḥ*). In the reading *babhruśaya*, the letter *la* [in the suffix] should be explained as *babhruḥ* being simply *babhru*. Specifically... (third line).

The meaning is: "He who pierces" (*vivyādhī*) refers to the Lord (*svāmī*) of the objects that are the arrows—namely, food (*anna*), the inedible (*abhakṣya*), the chewable (*bhojya*), the lickable (*lehya*), and the suckable (*śoṣya*); [the phrase] "salutation to him" (*tasmai namaḥ*) is the intended sense.

Here, by the term *babhruśāya*, it is demonstrated that he is the Lord who presides over the bull which is the form of Dharma, for it is taught that food is the effect of Dharma: "From sacrifice comes rain; from rain, the production of food. (6th line)

By the phrase "they pierce with food" (*vivyādhina*), it is understood from the Vedic scripture that for those who pierce [others] regarding food, food itself becomes their arrows; and since it is heard [in the text], one is pierced by food as an arrow. Thus, the state of being a lord of food (*annapati*) is appropriate, because that which is to be controlled is indeed subject to that [piercing]. This is another reason. This concludes the fifth [section].

"Salutation to Harikeśa. (8th line) [The text] refers to one who has blue locks on his head, who is accompanied by the Unborn (aja), who possesses golden hair (*harikeśa*), and who is "youthful" (*yuvan*). He is "wearing the sacred thread" (*upavītī*), meaning he possesses the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavītin*). He is the "primordial Brāhmaṇa" (*ādibrāhmaṇa*) in the Veda.

Having introduced him with the words "You are Virūpākṣa" and "the collyrium for the teeth," [it continues]: "Among the gods you are a Brāhmaṇa; I am a Brāhmaṇa among men. Indeed, a Brāhmaṇa approaches a Brāhmaṇa. (2nd line)
"I approach you; speak, O you who hear the Veda! One should worship Īśāna as the primordial Brāhmaṇa, and not the other [form of] Brahman.
(Third line) "Because the Lord Śiva is the Brāhmaṇa who is superior to all—superior to the Kṣatriya power of the king and the origin of the Vaiśya.

(Fourth line) This is according to the statement in the *Parāśara-saṃhitā*. And the word "puṣṭa" (nourished/prosperous) refers to the sovereignty and other qualities [of Śiva], just like those of Devendra and others. (Fifth line)

[The term] *paripūrtimat* refers to speech. Those who are nourished among all beings from Brahmā down to the stationary objects—He is their Lord; the meaning is "the Master of the Nourished. In this regard, since the Supreme Lord, the primordial Brāhmaṇa, is necessarily the object of worship for everyone beginning with Brahmā, He favors His own worshippers by bestowing nourishment upon them; thus, His status as the "Lord of the Nourished" is established.

By the phrase "upavīti na" (he wears the sacred thread over the left shoulder), this is demonstrated: he who is himself nourished bestows nourishment upon another. Since the senses and other faculties of the Supreme Lord are eternally youthful, it is appropriate that He should grant them [nourishment] from the eternally perfected worlds; thus, the power of the thing itself (*vastusāmarthya*), in the form of propriety (*aucitya*), is manifested through the word "harikeśe" (in the golden-haired one). In this way, the Lord [is described] preceded by a demonstration of His sovereignty over various objects such as the *pahimantra* and *aidīgā*.
Now, following the homage preceded by the words of sovereignty, the sixth mantra is for the purpose of paying homage to him as the Lord of the World (*jagatpati*).
"Homage to Bhava": *bhava* is cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*); the *heti* is the weapon for its destruction—that is, [the weapon] against cyclic existence.

The tree is the object to be cut; salutation to Him, the Lord of the worlds of moving and non-moving beings, the Master of the universe. (6th line) Although the status of being the Lord of the entire universe, from Brahmā down to the stationary entities, was already stated in the phrase "Lord of animals" (*paśūnāṃ pati*), nevertheless, there is a distinction: that was stated as the cause of binding with the fetters of *saṃsāra*, whereas here [He is described] as the liberator from *saṃsāra*. This applies to both as well. (8th line)

Because he possesses the nature of Brahman, it has been stated thus. In order to further establish his status as the Lord of the World (*jagatpati*), following the maxim of "running until one's exhaustion," he begins once more to pay homage to the Blessed One by means of [the verses] beginning with the seventh, starting with *namo rudrāya*. *Rudra* is so called because he causes the suffering of *saṃsāra* to run away (*drāvaka*). For this very reason, he is an *ātatāvī*, one who protects (*avati*) by means of a drawn bow (*ātatena dhanuṣā*). "Fields" (*kṣetrāṇi*) refers to bodies; for there is a traditional teaching (*smṛti*) stating: "This body, O son of Kuntī, is called the field. Of those...

The meaning is: "Salutation to Him who is the Lord, the Master of the fields. For in the world, the lords of regions protect those dwelling in their territories from various calamities; and they also endow those dependent upon them with specific forms of happiness—so too does the Lord of the field.
The Supreme Lord likewise protects those situated within the field. Indeed, there is no protector other than the Supreme Lord who causes those not yet born to live.
For this very reason, it is indeed prayed for in the Śruti: "May she, who is free from disease, enjoy us on all sides.

This has been stated in the Vivada: "To the dying person, Rudra explains the saving Brahman; having become immortal, he indeed becomes liberated," according to the Śruti. Furthermore, one should observe that the word *kṣetra* possesses a particular natural aptness when it refers to sacred fields such as Avimukta.
Now the eighth [verse]:

"Salutation to Him who is called the Charioteer, the driver of the machine of the world; the Lord of all beings stands in the region of the heart, O Arjuna, causing all beings to revolve, mounted upon the machine by means of Māyā"—so says the Smṛti. The meaning is: "Hantya" refers to one who cannot be slain (*ahantavya*); he is the lord and master of the *araṇyas*, that is, of the forests; salutation to him.

His status as the Lord of the Forest (Vanaspati) indicates his role as the Controller of the Universe, which is shown by the word "Sūta. Furthermore, the fact that even as the Controller of the Universe he is not afflicted by its transformations is made known by the term "Ahantya" (the Unslayable).
Now begins the ninth [chapter].

"Salutation to Rohitāya": *rohit* means "red," referring to his red color. He is a *sthapati* because he is both a *sthātṛ* (one who stands) and a *pātṛ* (one who protects). It belongs to the *vṛṣodara*-class [of compounds]. Thus, for him who has become such, the meaning is "the Lord (*pati*) of trees. By the word *pati* used here, the reason for his lordship over the trees is stated: by abiding within the trees, he [protects] the trees.
Because his lordship over that [tree] is inconceivable, the form of the Supreme Lord, who presides over the tree, is expressed by the word *rohita*.
(Line 8) This will be stated later: "Those which are on the trees, the *sphijara*s, blue-necked and crimson.
Now begins the tenth [section].

"Salutation to the Mantrin. Forest thickets and the like are the objects that are exceedingly dense; their master is the Lord of the Bushes (*kakṣāṇāṃ patiḥ*). "Salutation to him"—this is the first syntactical connection. Now, one might object: "Surely, the sovereignty over such impenetrable places would belong to Īśvara [the Lord God]. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "He conquers the multitudes of merchants (*vāṇijaḥ*)," meaning those who desire to trade. Just as a merchant (*vaṇik*)...

Having distinguished all the worldly conventions of every land, he illuminates them; likewise, this [knowledge] also [illumines] the entire collection of objects—this is the sense that nothing remains difficult for him to penetrate. By means of the principle of *kaimutika* (the "how much more so" argument), he establishes his status as the Lord of the divisions (*kakṣā-patitva*).
By the word "mantra," the seven crores of great mantras are meant; likewise, the Upaniṣads, which are the essence of the other Vedas, are all [included].

They are also called *guptavādāḥ* (secret teachings). Their master is [the Lord], just as one is called a "wealthy man" (*dhanī*) because he is the owner of wealth (*dhana*). For people do not refer to a carrier of wealth as "wealthy" merely by virtue of having a connection with it. Likewise, what need is there to mention his lordship over these profound [teachings], given the Vedic revelation: "He is the Lord of all sciences"?
The sense is that if this is so, what more need be said regarding his status as the Lord of the *kakṣās*?
Now begins the eleventh [chapter].
"Salutation to Bhuvanti. He is called *bhuvanti* because he extends (*tanoti*) the world (*bhuvaṃ*).

To him, the "provider of space" (*vārivaskṛtāya*): those who perform service (*paricaryā*) for him are the "space-makers" (*varivaskṛtaḥ*), meaning his devotees; he dwells among them, thus he is the "provider of space" (*vārivaskṛtaḥ*).

Although the Supreme Lord is omnipresent, through his presence among his devotees, there is [the attainment of] grace and liberation. Indeed, it is for this very reason that, through immersion (*samāveśa*) in him, one becomes like him.
It would be so for me alone through that treasure, yet not for you alone; for what indeed can be done by men toward Śiva, who is perfectly complete?

Whatever is done for the devotees of Śiva, that is done for Śiva himself. "He is bodiless, yet he is the body of his devotees," and so forth—such words from the Purāṇas are heard. The meaning is: "Obeisance to Him, the Lord (patiḥ), the master (svāmī) of the bulls, the rice-grains, and so forth. Herein...

By the phrase "O Lord" (*bhagavan*), the reason for being the master of medicinal herbs is stated; for since the circle of the earth has been sprinkled [with ghee], the mastery over the earth, the sacrificial cakes, and the medicinal herbs belongs to its Master, the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), as a matter of course. Furthermore, by the expression "for the sake of the water-maker" (*vārivaskṛtāya*) and the statement that he resides within the body of the devotee, I do not [offer this] to the people of Damayantī at the sacrifice of oblations (*havirvitāna*). Rather, let this be offered, drenched in ghee, into the mouth of the Fire-god (*hutabhuj*), so that it may reach the Brahmin.

"Vyāsa, who moves before my face, is satisfied by the ripening of his own past actions performed with focused attention toward me. Thus, as stated in the *Bhāgavata* through the mouth of a devotee, the Lord's status as the enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*) is revealed. By this, it is implied that even through His enjoyment of medicinal fruits, the Supreme Lord possesses ownership of those herbs; for He is the owner of that which is enjoyed by the enjoyer. In this way, because it takes the form of the Supreme Lord’s meal, whatever is offered by the worshippers is indeed a meal [for Him].

"It was not made by others"—thus the Self is proclaimed by the Śruti, Smṛti, and other authorities. Just as people seek Rudra within with supreme wisdom, they grasp him with their speech. It is heard in scripture: "He becomes one who eats only sin; he becomes one who eats only [the pure]. Those who always seek Rudra, who is worthy of worship, and grasp him with wisdom through their speech, [attain] food that is filled with essence and the water of nectar.
"Those who inwardly desire Bhava, Rudra, accompanied by Bhavānī, they hold him as their very essence with their tongue; of this there is no doubt. Such are the words from the Parāśara Purāṇa.
Thus ends the twelfth [chapter].

*Nama ucchairghoṣāya*: "Salutation to the one of loud roar. In battles and the like, he whose roar is loud is *ucchairghoṣa*; to him, the one who causes [the enemy] to cry out—that is, to the one who causes the enemies to weep or brings about their destruction—namely, to the lord of foot-soldiers (*patti*), meaning to the master of those who go on foot. Here, by the expression "lord of foot-soldiers," the dependence of the Lord upon the feet and so forth is indicated.

Regarding "valor" (*śauryam*): it was stated that he "rushed forward" (*ākramyata*) in order to demonstrate his own capacity to destroy the enemy himself, rather than merely warding off what had been obtained [by others].

Furthermore, it was stated that he "roared loudly" (*uccairghoṣāya*) to show that weapons, retinues, and so forth are mere ornaments; even for the destruction of an enemy, there is no dependence on battle, but rather [the victory] is achieved by a mere *hum*-sound.

And likewise, the sense is that because he has destroyed Tripura, Manmatha, Yama, and others by means of his mere ornaments such as weapons and retinues, or even by the syllable *huṃ*, or by smiles, glances, nails, and so forth, there is no dependence upon those [other deities].
|| Now begins the thirteenth [chapter]. ||(8th line)

*Namaḥ kṛtsnavītāya*: salutations to Him by whom the entire world is pervaded (*kṛtsnavītaḥ*) as its substrate and as its inner controller (*antaryāmin*). To Him who runs after—that is, follows behind—His devotees in order to protect them, according to the scriptural statement: "The cows run after the running bull. Salutations to the Lord (*pati*), the Master (*svāmin*) of *satvas*, meaning those who are His own. Here, the phrase "runs after" is stated as the reason for His being the Lord of the *satvas*; He follows behind them according to the analogy of a cow and its calf.

Because it is appropriate for the Lord to protect those who are devoted to him, he goes toward them; by the phrase "to one who has gone everywhere," that very running is established. Since it is possible to follow the devotees from the left of the all-pervading one, this indeed is the Lord’s quality of protecting on all sides in his entirety, as heard in the *Gṛhya* of the Vājasaneyins. Indeed, he deliberates upon what is to be entered into the cave: "Homage..."
"O Rudra, dweller in the waters, grant me well-being; lead me safely across the month," [he says] when about to ascend a path. Indeed, he recites the mantra: "Homage to Rudra, dweller in the waters;

O God, grant me well-being; lead me safely across the month. When about to enter a forest, he consecrates himself with the mantra: "Homage to Rudra, lord of the forest; O God, grant me well-being; lead me safely across the month.
Therefore, whatever he may be doing, he should perform it all with the words "Homage to Rudra"; for in all cases, [it is] "Rudra."
According to the Śruti, this [hymn] beginning with "citti" constitutes a single mantra-anuvāka. Its seer is Maṇḍūka, its metre is Mahāgāyatrī, and its deity is Rudra.
One should meditate upon Hara, whose every limb is adorned with pearls, who bears the moon and the Gaṅgā, and who sits comfortably at the foot of the Kalpa-tree together with Umā.

This mantra is primarily concerned with the attainment of sovereignty through the destruction of enemies, subjugation, and so forth. Thus ends the second section (*anuvāka*). Regarding the word "second":
in the third [section], at the beginning, he is saluted as the Lord of All by means of eight mantras, starting with "Obeisance to the Conqueror" (*namassahamānāya*). To the Conqueror...

The meaning is: "to him who overcomes enemies," or "to him who forgives the offenses of his devotees. Regarding the phrase "to the lord of those who pierce thoroughly" (*nivyādhinīnāṃ pataye*), the term *sahamānāya* ("to the enduring one") and *nivyādhiṇe* ("to the one who pierces thoroughly") are epithets containing a causal implication (*hetugarbha*). This is because, among those who pierce, he who pierces most thoroughly and possesses the power to overcome all insults is the most excellent; thus, by designating him as such, it is appropriate to establish his status as a sovereign (*svāmitva*). Therefore, the word *sahamāna* [is employed]. (p. 64a, f. 60b, l. 1)

Even though its purpose is to endure the offenses of devotees, its natural significance (*svārasya*) should be understood in this way: [Objection: If the Supreme Lord is, by his very nature, the most excellent creator of piercing (*vedha*) among all things, and the Lord of those who cannot be pierced, then all the worlds would be as good as consigned to their fate; for since even one free from sin would be subject to offense due to being a mere living being, the state of the Supreme Lord would have to be avoided, as stated in the verse.

He says that this doubt does not arise regarding the Blessed One, whose nature is to overcome all others (*sahamasvabhāva*). [The phrase] "to the overcoming one" (*sahamānāya*) is used. Now, the second [salutation]: "Obeisance to Kakubha" (*namaḥ kakubhāya*).

To Kakubha, the Great One (*mahate*), the quiver-bearer (*niṣaṅgiṇe*), the lord of thieves (*stenānām*)—that is, of secret robbers (*guptacorāṇām*)—obeisance. Here, because there is a requirement for the application of the greatness expressed by the word *kakubha*, it refers specifically to those thieves mentioned within its own sentence.
The connection is through the state of being a *yogin*; thus, "greatness among thieves" indicates the cause for the ownership of theft. This is expressed by the words "to the great Kakubha.

By the word "to the quiver-bearer" (*niṣaṅgin*), the possession of the necessary implements required for the activity of stealing is demonstrated. Now, as for the third [interpretation]: "Homage to the quiver-bearer"—the *niṣaṅga* is the arrow held in the hand to be joined with the bow; the *iṣudhi* is the quiver bound to the back to hold arrows. [This refers] to those thieves who are equipped with both.

Salutation to the master of the open thieves. Here, the epithet should be connected [to the name] for the purpose of demonstrating a form consistent with their lordship over robbers. Now, the fourth [name]: "Salutation to the masters of the *pañcata*. Those who, having become their own [servants], steal property while remaining unknown to others—they are the *stāyavaḥ*; salutation to their master. To establish that very state of being *stāyavaḥ*, [the text says] "*pañcate*."

Regarding the qualification "paripaṃcat" (one who deceives): having become a trusted person to a master, one who steals any kind of property whatsoever from him in any transaction whatsoever—whether involving his goods, actions, or transformations—is called a *paṃcan*. In all such transactions, one who acts as a deceiver is called a *paripaṃcan*; the meaning is "to that which has such a nature. Now, the fifth: "Namo..."

Regarding the term *niceravaḥ*: those who exist in the forests (*araṇya*) as thieves are the "forest-dwellers" (*āraṇyāḥ*). Homage to their lord, who brings about the service of the single deity. The phrase "homage to *niceru*" means "to the one who wanders about" (*paricarāya*). With respect to the forest-dwelling thieves, in the context of worldly usage, he is called *niceru* because his nature is to move about constantly among them. Likewise, with respect to them, he is called *paricara* because his nature is to move about everywhere in order to plunder; for he is the most excellent among such [thieves].
The sense is that ownership is appropriate for you.
Now begins the sixth [section].

"Salutation to those who do not release [their prey] by means of a *sṛka* (a hook or snare)"—thus, *sṛkāviṇaḥ* refers to living beings who desire to kill, that is, who wish to strike (*jighāṃsantaḥ*). To those of both these types, such as thieves and the like who seize heat in fields and other places, [there is] salutation to the Master; here too, there is the state of being a protector for those who steal at the proper time, through self-protection.

The two qualifiers "of the clever one" (*caturasya*) and "of him who desires to strike down that which is opposed to it" (*tadvirodhino jighāṃsata eva ca*) apply [to the subject], while the plural number is Vedic (*chāndasa*), because otherwise the relationship between qualifier and qualified would be untenable; the same applies to the subsequent mantra.
Now, the seventh [mantra]:

"Salutation to the Simas!"—thus [is the mantra]. "Asi-mantra" refers to those who carry swords; "naktañcarāḥ" means those who roam at night, that is to say, those who employ such means. Having slain [their victims], they take away the sins [of others]; they are the thieves (*caura*). To their master (*svāmin*), salutation! Here, two qualifiers are provided to demonstrate his essential nature (*svarūpa*) as it accords with his status as the master under discussion.
Now begins the eighth [chapter].

"Salutation to the Uṣṇiṣins": those who pluck (*luñcanti*)—that is, seize away—the earth (*ku-bhūmim*), which consists of fields, orchards, and so forth, are *kuluñcas*. Salutation to their lord. There are two kinds of *kuluñcas*: some are *uṣṇiṣins* who, by residing in villages, seize the fields and property of the weak through their oppressive conduct; others, however, being powerful, take refuge in mountains, forests, and the like.

The fact that [the deities] "seize away the fields of the worlds" is demonstrated respectively by the two qualifying epithets, "to the one with the *uṣṇīṣa*" and "to the one who moves on the mountain. The sense is that for such a being, sovereignty over the *kula* is appropriate. Thus, with the twenty-one mantras beginning with "Homage to the golden-armed one" (*namo hiraṇyabāhave*), which demonstrate his sole lordship over the directions and so forth, [he is addressed as] "the Lord of the worlds" (*jagatāṃ pataye*).
Having stated that the Blessed One is the Lord of the entire universe— well-known from the Śruti texts which declare, "He is all this," "He is the Lord of the worlds"—

he now begins to offer salutation by describing the Blessed One’s nature as the Self of all through His oneness with his own self, starting with the words, "Salutation to those who possess arrows" (namo iṣumatbhyaḥ). Those who carry arrows and bows even for the sake of the worlds are the "possessors of arrows and bows" (iṣudhanvāvinaḥ), and they exist in the world in the forms of gods, asuras, and humans.
Salutations to you all, as many as exist in those forms—those who are portions of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) and, in reality, non-different from Him.
Because there is a plurality of Rudras of terrible form, the plural pronoun *vaḥ* is used with the intention of addressing them; thus says the Brāhmaṇa:
"These Rudras are most terrible, who are saluted on both sides; whereas these Rudras are more peaceful, who are saluted on one side."
"Salutations to those who do not pay homage. Now follows the second [verse]: "Salutations to those stretching [their bows]," meaning those who are stringing their bows.
"Stretching" (*ātanvānāḥ*) refers to those who are fixing arrows upon their drawn bows; and to all those of that nature throughout the world, salutations to you—as before.
Now follows the third [verse].
*Nama* (the eighth line):

*āyacchadbhyaḥ* means those who are drawing [the bow]; that is, those who are pulling [the bowstring] while making it bend, and those who are releasing—that is, discharging—drawn arrows. The remainder is to be understood everywhere as before.
(p. 66b, f. 63a, l. 1) || Now, the fourth [chapter].
"Salutation to those who have gone forth" (*namo'stvyabhyaḥ*): the "going" (*ayana*) of a released arrow reaching as far as the target; its agent is the one who has discharged it.

The "piercing" (*vedha*) is the entry of that arrow, which has reached the vicinity of the target, into the target itself. The end of the piercing is indicated by the words "salutation to those seated" (*nama āsīnebhyaḥ*) and so forth, ending with "and to the horse-riders" (*aśvapatebhyaś ca namaḥ*).

These five mantras are clear in meaning. Thus, this [chapter] consists of a collection of seventeen intermediate mantras, characterized by salutations at both the beginning and the end. It is the third [chapter].
The third *anuvāka* consists of a single mantra. Its seer (*ṛṣi*) is the Blessed One himself; he alone is the deity (*devatā*). The meter (*chandas*) is *bṛhatī*.
The meditation (*dhyāna*) is:
[the deity] in embodied form, endowed with beauty and youth.
He resembles the crest of a blossoming *aneka-puṇṇāga* and mango tree;
his crown has the form of a peacock made of the twenty-five lunar mansions;
and his face is like the stainless, full orb of the autumn moon.
In the morning, the sage Carmaṇvat, adorned with garlands worn over both his left and right shoulders, wearing a garment as radiant as a pure lotus,
and with a cluster of kadamba flowers from the earth hanging down to his navel, moved slowly.
Even by enemies, she was to be gazed upon with longing, for her shanks were beautiful to behold;
she was auspicious, worthy of honor, possessed of lovely limbs, and adorned with the ornaments of maidenhood—
her form a mirror to the beauty of all embodied beings, and her appearance stainless compared to other forms.
Having placed a bow and a single stainless arrow into her hand,
he grasped her second arm firmly with his left hand.
Repeatedly inhaling the clusters of fragrant flowers with his hand,
he gently fanned himself with a branch bearing forest foliage.
Accompanied by children and charming dogs,
as they go and come, the Teacher of the Worlds should be meditated upon when seen—
He of such form, possessed of great splendor, the Lord who has assumed the body of a Kirāta.
This mantra bestows fruits such as the subjugation of one's own kingdom and the destruction of enemies.

By reciting it five thousand times, preceded by the Prājāpatya rite, this mantra becomes perfected; thereafter, it becomes fit for ritual application. This concludes the third section. Just as in the third, in the fourth as well, the Blessed One is saluted as the soul of all.

Among those, the first: *nama āvyādhibhyaḥ*. "To the *āvyādhis* (female archers)" refers to women capable of piercing from all sides; "to the various *viddhyanyas*" refers to women capable of piercing in diverse ways.
And they are those who dwell within the world (*jagatī*), the *āvantyas*, and the *asanatīs*; "to those of such forms, *namaḥ*"—as before.
Now, the second:
"Salutation to those of fierce hosts (*ugagaṇyābhyaḥ*).

Those who possess superior hosts, such as the Seven Mothers (*saptamātṛkā*) and others, who are likewise capable of destroying [obstacles]—the fierce deities (*ugradevatāḥ*) such as Durgā and the rest—to those whose forms have been entrusted [to the practitioner], as before.
Now begins the third [section].
"Obeisance to the Gṛtsas": the *vrātās* are associations of various kinds; their lords are the *vrātapatis*.
(4th line) Now begins the fifth [section].
"Salutation to the Gaṇas"—the Gaṇas are the Pramathas; their lords are Nandikeśvara and others.
(Fifth line) Now begins the sixth [chapter].
"Salutation to the Virūpas": the Virūpas are those of deformed form (*vikṛtarūpa*), universal form (*viśvarūpa*), and manifold form (*nānārūpa*).
Alternatively, they are those who, though praised by Brahmā, have in the ultimate sense transcended form due to their changelessness.

According to the principle that "an object becomes possessed of form through the form of that which is superimposed upon it"—just as silver is [superimposed] upon mother-of-pearl—that which is superimposed upon Brahman [is likewise devoid of form].
"Viśvarūpa" means those whose forms are universal.
Now begins the seventh [section].

"Salutation to the Great Ones" (namo mahadbhyaḥ): the "Great Ones" are those endowed with the eightfold sovereign powers (aṣṭaiśvarya), such as atomization (aṇimā) and so forth; their daughters are the "Lesser Ones. Now begins the eighth [chapter].

"Salutation to the chariot-riders (*namo rathibhyaḥ*). Those who possess chariots are the chariot-riders (*rathinaḥ*). There are nine mantras ending with "to the lords of horses" (*namaścāśvapatibhyaḥ*), beginning from the ninth [mantra]. Their meanings are clear. Among them, the chariot-drivers are the charioteers (*sārathayaḥ*) and the attendants (*kṣattāraḥ*); they themselves restrain the chariot. The *saṅgrahītāraḥ* are distinct from the chariot-makers (*takṣan*) because of the difference between a carpenter and a chariot-maker. The *karmārāḥ* are ironworkers (*lohakārāḥ*). The *ghātukāḥ* are those who kill flocks of birds.

The *puñjiṣṭhas*, the *niṣādas*, the *vacas*, those bound by dogs, those holding nooses, and the dog-keepers— the rest is clear. Thus, with these twenty-six mantras ending with "to the possessors of arrows" (*iṣumatbhyaḥ*), by demonstrating each individual element within the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), [the text] explicitly states through the direct voice [of the mantra], "to those of universal form" (*viśvarūpebhyaḥ*), that the Blessed One possesses the nature of the entire phenomenal world consisting of both the sentient and the insentient.

This has been described. This [phrase] "Salutation to the Eldest" (*namo jyeṣṭhāya*) indicates, as will be explained hereafter, the state of being the self of all (*sarvātmakatva*). By that, the non-duality of Śiva (*śivādvaita*) is expressed. And thus it is heard in scripture: "They consider the cessation of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), which is non-dual, as the fourth [state]; neither existent nor non-existent, Śiva alone is absolute. "Rudra indeed is all. "I alone existed first, I exist now, and I shall exist in the future; there is no other whatsoever distinct from me."

"Smṛtis are Śambhu, the elements are Śambhu, the worlds are Śambhu, the forests are Śambhu, and the mountains are Śambhu"—such are the [scriptural passages]. Regarding the nature of that [Śambhu] as consisting of both the sentient and the insentient: according to the principle of the *ārambhādhikaraṇa* and others, He is the locus of superimposition (*adhyāsādhiṣṭhānatva*). Since the existence of that which is superimposed apart from its locus is observed in cases such as nacre-silver, just as the nacre—the locus of the superimposition of silver—is not itself of the nature of silver, so too is the locus of the superimposition of the world [not of the nature of the world].

Because Brahman is the very self of the universe—this has been explained in detail in the *Brahma-mīmāṃsā*—the doubt raised by the statement "to dogs and to dog-owners" (6th line), namely, how identity can be taught with such lowly beings as dogs, is thereby dispelled. What is expressed by the Vedic text through the word "dog" (7th line) is non-difference characterized by the body; however, that which is indicated (*lakṣya*) by it—the consciousness of the individual soul (*jīva-caitanya*)—is superior when [considered] in relation to its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). (8th line)
The fact that the Supreme Self persists within bodies that have fallen into low states is clearly elucidated by the Blessed One himself in the *Gītā*:

"The wise perceive the same [Self] in a Brahmin endowed with learning and humility, in a cow, in an elephant, in a dog, and even in an outcaste. Nevertheless, there is not even a trace of the defect of those limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) in the Supreme Lord; for it is not as if the reflection [of the sun] in the Gaṅgā, a pond, wine, or urine [is affected by the defects of those receptacles].

The Sun (Āditya) is connected to the qualities and defects of those limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*); thus, everything is faultless. This fourth section (*anuvāka*), which consists of a collection of intermediate mantras comprising seventeen sacrificial verses (*yajus*) and takes the form of a salutation on both sides, constitutes a single mantra.
Its seer (*ṛṣi*) is Durvāsas; its meter (*chandas*) is Mahāvirāṭ; and its deity (*devatā*) is Śambhu.
In meditation,
one should contemplate the Lord Hara, mounted upon his bull and accompanied by Gaṇeśvara, with all his limbs smeared with ashes and adorned with a circle of matted locks.

This mantra removes diseases such as consumption, fever, derangement of the humors (*sannipāta*), and leprosy. Its mastery is attained through one thousand recitations preceded by the *prājāpatya* penance.
Thus ends the fourth section (*anuvāka*).

Thus, having offered salutation in the fourth [verse] by way of [the Lord’s] being the self of all, the Blessed One has been saluted. Now, beginning with the description of His unique majesty—whose nature is the various [powers] belonging to the Blessed One—he begins to offer salutation to Him.
From this point up to the word *drāpaḥ*, there are salutations in the singular; everywhere, a single mantra begins with a salutation.

Just as in the case of "Salutation to Bhava and Rudra," other [names] should also be understood in this way. Therein, first, by means of two [verses], he offers salutation to Him while contemplating His universal form common to the Supreme Lord, which consists in performing the fivefold cosmic acts known as creation, maintenance, dissolution, concealment, and liberation. "Salutation to Bhava": He is called Bhava because He brings forth (*bhavati*) this entire world. By this... [all this].

"Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are produced from Him"—by such passages, the Lord's status as the cause of the world's birth, well-known from the Śruti, is demonstrated. "In Rudra there shall be an end to the suffering of saṃsāra; Rudra explains the liberating Brahman"—by this, His status as the cause of liberation, well-known from the Śruti, is stated. [He is called] Śarva because He hears and destroys everything; by this, [His status as] the withdrawer [is shown]. (p. 70a, f. 66b, l. 1)

The Lord’s role as the destroyer of the universe is stated by the phrase "to the Great Devourer" (*mahāgrāsāya*) and so forth, as established in the Śruti. By the word *paśupati* (Lord of Beasts), His role as the cause of the bondage and maintenance [of the world] is expressed; for the word *paśu* denotes the bondage of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), while the word *pati* denotes the protection thereof. Thus, it is stated that He is the cause of the maintenance and bondage of the universe, as well as its liberation, as established in the Śruti by such passages as "the cause of the bondage and maintenance of the world. By virtue of being the cause of these fivefold activities (*pañcakṛtya*), He is the Blessed One (*bhagavān*).

The salutation (*namaskāra*) is the meaning of the two mantras. Here, in order to show the connection of the word *namaḥ* with each of the two words ending in the dative case, they are recited together with their meanings; by that, the connection becomes "salutation to Bhava" and "salutation to Sarva.
This should be understood in the same way everywhere hereafter.
Now begins the third [chapter].

"O Nīlagrīva!"—he whose neck became blue (*nīla*) by swallowing the *kālakūṭa* poison is *nīlagrīva*. Before that swallowing, he whose neck was white (*śiti*) was *śitikaṇṭha*; because of that swallowing, he became *nīlagrīva*.
By this [epithet], it is shown that [Śiva], disregarding the defect of blueness caused by the *kālakūṭa* upon his naturally white neck, swallowed the poison for the sole protection of the world.

By [the fact that] the Blessed One swallowed [the poison], it is demonstrated that his compassion for all the world is well-known—as in the verse beginning "The Arhat protects the universe," and so forth.
|| Now begins the fourth [chapter]. ||

"Salutation to Kapardin"—*kaparda* refers to the mass of matted hair (*jaṭākalāpa*) of the Supreme Lord; one who possesses that is *kapardin*. With this [mantra], [one says]: "Slay Dakṣa’s sacrifice! You are the leader of his soldiers; O Rudra, let there be no grief for my matted hair. This is the intention of the Blessed One. It is well known that the Blessed One's matted hair is remembered as the conclusion of Vīrabhadra’s vow, and by that [it is said]: "The gods indeed excluded Rudra from the sacrifice; he pierced the sacrifice," and so forth.

The greatness [of Śiva] well-known from the Vedas, namely the destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice, has been displayed; he is "Vyuptakeśa," one whose hair is shorn or cut off. (6th line) He is a Paramahaṃsa wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*). For there is a Vedic text stating: "Now, the wandering mendicant wears a single garment, is shaven-headed, uses his stomach as a bowl, has knowledge for his crest-lock (*jñānaśikhin*), and has knowledge for his sacred thread (*jñānayajñopavītin*)," and so forth. By this, Dattātreya, Dūrvāsas, and others are established as well-known in the Jābāla Upaniṣad. (8th line)

And in the Kali age, Śaṅkara will descend along with four disciples. This refers to the venerable Śaṅkarācāryasvāmin, whose nature as an incarnation of the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara)—well-known from the Purāṇas through such passages as "Śaṅkara shall come with Satātapa"—is intended by the phrase "to him who is of that form. By this, his status as the founder of the tradition of Brahman-knowledge among the Brahmins, as famously declared in the passage "the Lord of Brahmā, the master of Brahmā," is expressed.
Now begins the fifth [chapter].
"Salutation to the thousand-eyed one"—by this, his thousand eyes, which are infinite, are indicated.

His universal sovereignty, such as being "the thousand-eyed one" and "the omniscient," is shown as established by the Śruti. "A hundred bows, whose ends are infinite"—his bows, in the form of the Vedas, the *praṇava*, Mount Meru, and so forth, are likewise described as "a hundred bows. Having spoken thus, and having made Viṣṇu the supreme arrow, [he made] Śalya...

Having likewise made Maheśvara the lord of the great [bow], and having joined the bow with the *praṇava* (*oṃ*) and the *Sāvitrīs*, the meaning is: "to the one endowed with many bows such as Meru and Pināka," as stated in the *Mahābhārata*. By this, the greatness of the destruction of Tripura—well-known from the *Śruti* that those Asuras had three cities—is demonstrated. Now, by two [verses], [his] nature as the Trimūrti and his transcendence over the universe [are shown].

He demonstrates this: "Salutation to Giriśa"—*giriśaḥ* means Kailāsa; because it belongs to him, he is *giriśaḥ*. According to the rule beginning with *lomādi*, the suffix *śa* is used in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*). Thus, the meaning is "to Him who has that [Kailāsa] as His form. *Śipiviṣṭa* is Viṣṇu, according to the Vedic scripture: "That Viṣṇu is Śipiviṣṭa. Thus, the meaning is "to Him who has the form of Viṣṇu. *Mīḍhuṣṭama* means one who most excellently pours forth vigor; Hiraṇyagarbha, the creator of the world. Thus, the meaning is "to Him who has that [Hiraṇyagarbha] as His form. By this [it is shown]: "He is Brahmā, He is Śiva, He is Indra, He is the Imperishable, the supreme self-ruler. (pp. 71b, 68a, lines 1–3).

Thus, it is stated that [the Lord] possesses the nature of the three forms (trimūrti) well-known from the Vedas. Regarding the term *iṣumān* ("possessing arrows"), it is used in the sense of praise (*praśaṃsā*). One should observe what is stated in the Śruti regarding the preparation of the arrow by Manu and others: "The arrow was made excellent, Agni its shaft, Soma its point, and the people its feathers," and so forth. By this, the supremacy of the Blessed Lord over all the gods even in the destruction of Tripura is inferred, as in the passage: "He who among the gods... (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 10.1).

The state of being superior to the universe— well-known from such scriptural passages as "He is the source and the origin, Rudra who is superior to the universe, and the other deities are His limbs"— has thus been demonstrated.
Now begins the eighth [section].

"Salutation to Hrasvāya": [the term] *hrasva* refers to one of small stature in body; by this, even there, the fact that the body is an object of meditation (*upāsya*) through the *vidyā* [of the Lord], as established in such Vedic texts as "The heart is the sky, free from sorrow," and so forth, is demonstrated. [The phrase] "by means of the form of Mahāgaṇapati," whose limbs such as the feet are contracted, is the meaning. Regarding Mahāgaṇapati, his status as the direct Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) is [attested] in the mantra-scriptures, Purāṇas, and so forth.
By this [verse], the greatness well-known from such Vedic texts as "O you who are the Lord of the hosts" (*gaṇānāṃ tvā gaṇapatiṃ*) is demonstrated.
