Now begins the ninth [section].

"Salutation to the Great One" (*namo bṛhate*): the meaning is "to the Supreme Brahman" (*bṛhate parabrahmaṇe*), as established in the *Brahmamīmāṃsā* that Brahman-hood consists in being devoid of the threefold limitations (*pariccheda*) of space, time, and substance. Now, why is it called the "Supreme Brahman"? [Because] according to the *Atharvaśiras-śruti*, by this [mantra], "the Truth, the Reality, the Supreme Brahman... [is signified].

The state of being the Supreme Brahman, as declared in the Śruti passages such as "Truth, Knowledge, Infinite is Brahman," is thus demonstrated. By the phrase "endowed with all excellences" (*guṇaiḥ samṛddho varṣīyān*), the divine qualities and majesty mentioned in the Śruti—"His power is heard to be manifold indeed, and innate; [consisting of] knowledge, strength, and action"—are displayed, namely that He is one whose desires are true and whose resolves are true.
Now begins the tenth [chapter].

"Salutation to the Elder (*namo vṛddhāya*). [The word] *vṛddha* refers to one who is superior in age relative to all others; such a person is himself worthy of worship by all, yet there is no one else whom he must worship. Thus, he is the lowest [of the three]. For this very reason, it is heard in the Purāṇa (p. 72b, f. 69a, l. 1): "Whoever has the power, let him speak! O Proddhāṅkara, place your finger before me. Who would be honored by you, O Moon-crested One? (l. 2).

By the words "But the Lord of Beings was not praised by the cooked offerings," it is stated that He— to whom obeisance is due— is the Head (*mūrdhan*), as established in the Śruti by the passage "the head is dharma" (*yasmai namastacchiro dharmah*). Although this is heard in general terms as "that to which obeisance is due is the head," nevertheless, after introducing the Supreme Lord with the words "you are the best among beings," the conclusion is reached with "all obeisance is yours."

By stating that every act of salutation belongs to Him, it is determined—even though the opening question "to whom [is] the salutation?"—that the Supreme Lord alone is the object of the salutation. This is because it is appropriate to describe Him as the primary support in the form of the dolphin (*śiṃśumāra*) which is His own power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), and as the principal head of that [form]. Other deities do not possess such a form.

Because [the Lord] is designated separately by his respective names according to the form of the head, jaws, heart-center, feet, and tail—as explained at length elsewhere—[He is praised] with unique hymns and prostrations: "May you, who have grown great through the *vardhī*, *saṃvṛdhī*, *mātvā*, *rudra*, *cukrī*, and *mā* [mantras], and through our *namas* [prostrations];

may you, the bull, not be harmed by our invocation; O Hero, grant us vigor and medicines! I hear that you are the physician, and that the healers are yours; through well-spoken praise and true eulogy..."

"O you whose action is equal to that of the horse, we do not become angry with you, O one saluted by all the gods"—this, being well-known from the Śruti and the Purāṇas, demonstrates that [the Lord] is the object of praise common to other deities. Now, the eleventh [verse]: "Salutation to the foremost. He is the foremost because he exists prior to the origin of the world; even while the world remains, he remains as the foremost. This state of being foremost is expressed in the mantra: "Hiraṇyagarbha came into being in the beginning."

According to this scriptural statement, he therefore qualifies [the Lord] as "the first-born" (*prathamāya*), meaning He is prior even to Hiraṇyagarbha; the sense is that He is the cause even of him. For the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad states: "In the beginning, He brought forth Hiraṇyagarbha. By this, His status as the cause of the universe—well-known from such scriptures as, "That wherein there was neither darkness, nor day, nor night, nor the existent, nor the non-existent: Śiva alone existed"—is demonstrated. Although [this is not explicitly stated] by the phrase "salutation to Bhava" (*namo bhavāya*)... [text continues].
Even though that has been stated in this way, nevertheless, it is precisely that [Brahman] which is appropriate here, by virtue of being the progenitor of Hiraṇyagarbha, the origin of the world.
Now begins the twelfth [section].
*Nama* (second line):

*Āśave* means "to the swift," derived from the root *aś* (meaning "to reach" or "to pervade") with the prefix *āṅ* and an *auṇādika* suffix, signifying that which reaches or pervades. (Third line) *Jagat* means "pervading the world. The reason for this is *ajirāya*, meaning "to the one skilled in movement"; by this, [the nature of] Rudra—(fourth line)
By the word "annāt" (from food), the pervasiveness of the entire universe, as established by the Vedic revelation, has been stated.
Now follow the thirteenth, fourteenth, and fifteenth [mantras].
"Salutation to Śīghriya": that which exists swiftly in the waters is Śīghriya; that is to say, the inner controller (antaryāmī) thereof. In the swift flow of water...

That which exists in swift currents (*śībhyaḥ*) among waves and ripples is *ūrmya*. That which exists in water devoid of sound (*avasvana*) is *avasvanya*. That which exists in a stream or flow (*srotasi*) is *srotasya*. There is a distinction between these based on the magnitude or smallness of the swift current and the stream. That which exists on an island (*dvīpe*) is *dvīpya*. [This is established] by such passages as: "Homage to the one who is in the river (*nādyāya*) and to the peaceful one (*śāntāya*), homage to the one in the puddle (*sikatyāya*) and to the one in the flow (*pravāhyāya*), homage to the one in the wave (*ūrmyāya*) and to the one in the sun (*sūryāya*)," and so forth. (p. 74a, f. 70b, l. 1)

This will be explained in the section concerning the various roles of the waters, such as being the internal controller within the swift-flowing currents and so forth. Nevertheless, the Śruti states: "The waters indeed are this all; the waters are all beings; the waters are breath; the waters are cattle; the waters are food; the waters are Virāj; the waters are Samrāj; the waters are the meters;
the waters are the luminaries; the waters are truth; the waters are all the deities; the waters are Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Suvaḥ; the waters are Om," and so on.

In order to demonstrate that all the well-known majesty of the waters belongs solely to the Supreme Lord who dwells within them, the power residing within the water—which will be discussed further on—is here restated. For it is heard [in scripture] that one aspect of the majesty of the Supreme Lord, who possesses manifold powers, sustains a single form of power, just as it is said: "One sun alone sustains my manifold majesty."

The word *dvīpa* also refers specifically to that which stands within the water; for in the sense "water is divided (*dvidhā*) in this place," by the rule *īndrādibhyaḥ* [Pāṇini 5.2.113], the form *dvaya-* arises, and after the substitution of *ī* for the *a* of *sva*, the long vowel *ī* is formed by *savarṇadīrgha*. Then, by the rule *ṛkpūrabdhūḥpathāmānakṣe* [Pāṇini 5.4.74], the suffix *a* is added as a compound-final (*samāsānta*), whereby the word *dvīpa* is established. Alternatively, by the word *dvīpa*, which denotes the seven islands such as Jambū and Plakṣa, everything [is included].
And the world is perceived in that manner; thus, the meaning should be understood as follows: the Supreme Lord is the inner controller of all excellence existing in all the continents and worlds.
The fifth section is completed.

The Blessed One has been saluted by virtue of being endowed with five kinds of greatness; now, in the sixth [verse], He is saluted by way of His being the Self of all and the Inner Ruler of all: "Salutation to the Eldest" (*namo jyeṣṭhāya*). By means of the stages of life (*āśrama*) such as that of the student (*brahmacarya*), He is superior (*jyeṣṭha*) to them, yet inferior (*kaniṣṭha*) to them; thus He is both.

The meaning is "for the sake of form" (*rūpāya*). That which exists previously, such as the material cause (*mṛd-ādi-karaṇa*), is the "prior-born" (*pūrvaja*); that which exists subsequently, such as the effect (*ghaṭa-ādi-kārya*), is the "subsequent-born" (*aparaja*); the meaning is "for the sake of that which consists of those two. The "intermediate one" (*madhyama*) is the youth (*yuvan*), whose faculties (*indriya*) have fully developed through the growth of his inner strength (*sattva*) despite being timid (*avagalbha*); the meaning is "for the sake of that which has the nature of both. The [mantras] beginning with "Homage to the lowest one" (*namo jaghanyāya*) are intended to establish [the Lord's] status as the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*); "in the hindquarters" (*jaghane*) means "behind" (*paścāt*).

That which exists in the upper portion (*bhāga*) is *jaghanya*; that which exists at the base or root (*budhna*) is *budhya*. That which exists between both is *sobha*, the world of humans; for according to the Śruti, "By merit one leads to the world of merit, by sin [one leads] to the world of humans.

That which exists there is *sobhya*. *Pratisara* means that which moves back or goes forth; it is the moving about, the manifold expansion (*prapañca*). That which exists therein is *pratisarya*, existing in the world of Yama.
That which exists in the south is *yāmya*; that which exists in heaven is *svargīya*; that which exists in verses—that is, in Vedic mantras—is *ślōkya*.

That which exists at the conclusion (*avasāna*)—that is, in the Vedānta—is *avasānya*. That which exists in the forest is *vanya*. That which exists in the thickets or bushes is *kakṣya*. Now, he pays homage with the entire meaning by means of the words beginning with "namaḥ śravāya"; for it is heard, thus it is *śravaḥ*.

*Śabdaḥ* means an echo or resonance. *Āśuṣeṇaḥ* refers to one whose army moves swiftly (*āśu*). Similarly, *āśurathaḥ* means one with swift chariots. *Śūraḥ* means one possessed of heroism. (Line 8) *Avabhindan* means one who shatters. *Brahmadviṣām mūrdhno bhettā* means one who splits the heads of those who hate the Brahmanas. *Varmī* means one equipped with armor (*kañcuka*). *Varūtha* is the place of protection for the charioteer. (Page 75b, Folio 72a, Line 1) *Bilamaṃ* means provided with a hollow; it refers to a helmet that protects the head in battle. *Valmīkavacaḥ* means one possessing a body-protecting suit of armor (*kañcuka*), like the protective covering of an anthill. (Line 2)

Kavacin, Śruta, Prasiddha, Śrutasena, and Prasiddhasena; whoever among gods, asuras, or humans stands as Āśuratha; or the hero who pierces [the enemy], being armored and protected by a chariot-fender—[this refers to] one renowned for an armor made of anthills, or one known as Śrutasena, meaning "one who approaches with those means.
Thus ends the sixth section.
The Blessed One is the seer (ṛṣi) of this [mantra], he himself is the deity; in sequence, the meter (chandas) is Mahāvirāṭ and Mahāpaṅkti.
As for the meditation (dhyāna): [He is] one who has placed upon the lotus-hand of Gaurī a golden mountain serving as a bow.
One should meditate upon [the deity] holding a sugarcane stalk in his hand, mounted upon a chariot, and possessing the body of a man and a woman.

This mantra bestows the fruits of victory over enemies, long life, the increase of the kingdom, and the attainment of sons. Success is achieved by eating sacrificial porridge (*caru*) for three nights and reciting [the mantra] continuously for eleven days. Like the sixth [mantra], it is saluted in the seventh [chapter] by virtue of its being the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of all fruits and its being the self of all (*sarvātmakatva*).

*namo dundubhyāya*: "Obeisance to Dundubhya. He exists in the drum (*dundubhi*), thus he is *Dundubhya*. That by which something is struck or beaten is a striker (*āhananya*). A staff is for the purpose of striking the drum; that which exists therein is the striker (*āhananya*). "Obeisance to Dhṛṣṇu," and so forth—these are salutations to the Blessed One as the Self of All. In the world, *dhṛṣṇu* means one who is bold or impetuous (*pramṛśat-ṛghāya*). *Dhṛṣṇu* refers to one who does not flee in battle; *pramṛśa* [refers to] one who is resolute.

The account of the enemy army: the spy (*parāmarśaka*) is the messenger (*dūta*), a messenger skilled in knowing the news of that [enemy]. Urged by his master (*vrīhitaḥ svāmipreritaḥ*), he is among those men who carry quivers.
(3rd line) The two wise ones (*dhīvantau*) have been explained; one who has sharp arrows is *tīkṣṇeṣuḥ*; one who possesses many weapons is *āyudhī*;
one whose weapon is excellent is *svāyudhaḥ*. One whose bow is excellent is *sudhanvā*. By terms such as *namassrut*, the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*) is expressed. (5th line)

*Sruti* refers to a narrow path suitable only for the movement of feet; *srutya* refers to a broad path suitable for the movement of chariots and the like. *Pathin* is a great road; that which exists there is *pathya*. *Kaṭa* is a place with scanty water where one wanders in dejection (*kaṭati*); that which exists there is *kāṭya*. A place where water falls due to its own nature is *nīpa*; that which exists there is *nīvya*. *Sūda* means mud; that which exists there is *sūdya*.

That which exists in a lake is *sāraḥ*; that which exists in a river is *nādyaḥ*; that which exists in a small pond (*veśanta*) is *vaiśantaḥ*; that which exists in a well (*kūpa*) is *kūpyaḥ*; that which exists in a pit (*avaṭa*, *gartta*) is *avaṭyaḥ*.

That which exists in rain is *varṣyaḥ*; the absence of rain is *avarṣaḥ*; that which exists in that [absence] is *avarṣyaḥ*. The meaning is one who impels both rain and its absence. That which exists in clouds is *meghyaḥ*; that which exists in lightning is *vidyutyaḥ*. *Īddhra* means shining with purity.

*Śaradabhṛm*: that which exists there [in the autumn]. *Īdṛhyaḥ*: that which is to be protected (*ātavya*) from fear (*īdṛha*). *Reśmaḥ*: where living beings perish (*riṣyan*) or disappear, that is *reśma*;

the time of dissolution (*pralayakāla*) existing there is *reṣmyaḥ*. *Vāstavyaḥ*: that which exists in the dwelling (*vāstu*), such as cattle and so forth; or, the earth intended for the construction of houses is *vāstu*, and he who stands there as its protector is *vāstupaḥ*. This very one, consisting of sixteen *yajus* mantras in the form of salutations arising from the mind, constitutes the intermediate [section].
The seventh section (*anuvāka*), consisting of a composite form, is a single mantra. Its seer (*ṛṣi*) is Romaśa, its meter (*chandas*) is Mahānuṣṭubh, and its deity (*devatā*) is Rudra.
May he, who bestows fearlessness, dance with his hanging matted locks.
One should meditate upon the pure, smiling God, adorned with a tiger-skin.
This mantra bestows the fruits of intelligence, nourishment, health, prosperity, sons, knowledge, and liberation.

Success in the mantra is achieved by reciting it one hundred times preceded by a single fast. Thus ends the seventh [chapter]. In the seventh, [the Lord is worshipped] through His nature as the Self of all and His state as the Inner Controller of all.
O Blessed One, [the Lord] is saluted.

In the eighth [chapter], however, the Blessed One is saluted with seventeen [verses] by means of His uncommon attributes—which are the causes for being worshipped by all the worlds—and by virtue of His nature as the Inner Controller (*antaryāmī*). Among these, since the Supreme Lord alone is the bestower of liberation, He alone is thus [approached] by those seeking liberation.
The first mantra, "To Soma... (*ataḥ somāya*), is intended to show that [the Lord] is to be worshipped by all. Here, the primary grammatical connection is "Salutation to Rudra" (*rudrāya namaḥ*).

He is called Rudra because he causes the suffering of *saṃsāra* to fall away (*drāvayati*)—that is, he makes it disappear. For it is heard in the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad*: "When men shall roll up space like a piece of leather, then, having known Śiva, there will be an end to suffering."

The absolute impossibility of the cessation of suffering without the Supreme Lord—likened to [the existence of] space—is established by this very [qualification]: "Salutation to Soma" (*namaḥ somāya*). He who is accompanied by Umā is *soma*; *umā* is the Supreme Power (*parāśakti*), whose form consists of the transposition of the letters of the *praṇava*.

As stated in the *Laiṅga*, the *praṇava* is a divine designation; by that [designation], the Supreme Goddess, the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) who is the presiding deity of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), is expressed.

Furthermore, since the cessation of the transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) caused by ignorance is to be accomplished through the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), it is well-known in the Vedāntas that Umā, the Supreme Power (*parāśakti*), is the presiding deity (*adhidevatā*) of such knowledge of Brahman. For instance, in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad, after the proponents of Brahman have introduced the question, "What is the cause?
From what was Brahman born?", they say: "Thus, following [the truth] through the yoga of meditation, they beheld the divine power of the Self by means of its own qualities."

By the passage beginning with "nigūḍhāṃśu" and so forth, it is further established that the great sages who were exponents of Brahman attained certainty regarding the reality of Brahman solely through the grace of Umā. This is also corroborated in the Śaiva Purāṇa, where it is said:
"In former times, certain sages who were exponents of Brahman, though possessed of minds shrouded in doubt, [sought liberation]..."
They reflect upon reality as it truly is: "What is the cause? From where have we arisen? By what do we live? And into whom shall we enter? Thus it was said to you.
(8th line) Having entered into the yoga of meditation, they behold directly the sovereign power (*aiśvarī śakti*) that severs the bonds, though it is hidden by its own qualities.
(p. 78a, f. 74b, 1st line) With their bonds severed by that [power], they behold Mahādeva, the possessor of power (*śaktimant*), the cause of all causes, through the eye of knowledge. (2nd line)
In the *Kūrmapurāṇa* as well, having introduced the passage: "The high-souled sages, exponents of Brahman, gathered together and engaged in many discourses," [it continues]:

"Thus, to those others who had attained the yoga of meditation, O Great Goddess, Gaurī, the daughter of the Mountain King, appeared. Within that interval, they beheld Śambhu, the Supreme Lord, the cause of all, being gazed upon by his consort."

"Rudra, the great Puruṣa, the ancient one, the creator of the poets"—thus [it is said]. Likewise, in the *Talavakāra Upaniṣad* as well: "He came to that very same ether, accompanied by Umā, who was exceedingly beautiful; she was the daughter of Himavat, the Vācākī. 'This Yakṣa is indeed Brahman,' he said—or rather, 'It is Brahman. 'Rejoice in this victory of Brahman!'—and so on, [as told] of old to Śakra and the others."

It is related in the *Kaivalyopaniṣad* that Brahmavidyā was born from Umā’s grace: "When one meditates upon the Supreme Lord, the Master, who has Umā as his companion, the three-eyed, blue-throated, and tranquil one, then Manu goes to Him—the source of all beings, the witness of all, beyond darkness. Thus, the Supreme Lord is to be meditated upon precisely in the company of Umā, as the bestower of liberation.

This being stated, it leads to the understanding that Umā is the presiding deity of the supreme Brahma-vidyā; for the Śruti has declared, due to their identical purpose: "O Pārvatī, the Supreme Goddess is the bestower of Brahma-vidyā. Therefore, those who behold Śiva in their hearts together with His innate Power (Śakti)—for them alone does eternal power exist, and not for others. This is the Śruti and so forth, which follows the injunction for worship.

The Lord’s status as the pinnacle of liberation alone is due to his association with Umā; however, every aspect of his majesty—consisting of omniscience, universal sovereignty, being the inner controller of all, and being the cause of all—is indeed the manifestation of the Supreme Power (parā-śakti).
As it is said: "His supreme power is heard to be manifold; [it] manifests as his own nature, consisting of knowledge, strength, and action," and so forth. (p. 79a, f. 75b, l. 1)

The experts proclaim in the *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas*: "Thou art Power (*Śakti*), the body, the presiding deity, the inner self, the cause of knowledge and action, the multitude of seats, will, sovereignty, the abode, and the veils. What else could Thou direct? O Goddess, [Thou art] the one whose crest is the moon. For if it were not so, the Lord would certainly not be capable of even a slight movement; therefore, indeed, [Thou art she] of such majesty.

In the *Taittirīya Upaniṣad*, there is an extraordinary and superlative excellence regarding Umā, as stated in the passage beginning with "to the Lord of Ambikā" and followed by "to the Lord of Umā"; thus, the Blessed One is honored as her husband. Let that suffice for now; furthermore, because he manifests effortlessly before all beings in the form of the Sun and bestows every form of ultimate welfare (*śreyas*), [he is the supreme].

The second mantra, *namas tāmrāya*, signifies that the Supreme Lord alone is to be worshipped by all. At the time of rising, his color is intensely red (*tāmra*); immediately thereafter, he is slightly red, *aruṇa*; and above the eyes, he is tawny (*babhru*). The meaning is: "Salutation to Him"—the specific form consisting of the Sun (*sūrya*) belonging to the Blessed One who possesses these eight forms (*aṣṭamūrtti*). In the world, this is practiced by those observing fasts with great discipline.

When worship has been performed for a long time, immediately thereafter the deity manifests; however, the Lord Āditya manifests of his own accord and without effort before the entire multitude of living beings every single day in the form of the sun and so forth. For it is said: "The cowherds saw him as he went to fetch water," and thus he manifests. Therefore, even for the sake of bringing about his direct presence—
No effort is required; for the Blessed One rises spontaneously, appearing directly before every individual.

It is heard that, therefore, everyone thinks, "He has risen up toward me. Thus, while He remains manifest by Himself as if intent on bestowing boons, even one who merely extends the thought, "This is the Supreme Lord," [attains Him]. Entirely...
One attains the highest good (*śreyaḥ*). And thus says the Śruti: "A Brāhmaṇa who meditates upon [the sun] as it rises and as it sets, performing [his duties], attains all that is auspicious" (p.

80a, f. 76b, 1st line). "That Āditya is Brahman"—therefore, the intention is that the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), who effortlessly bestows all human goals (*puruṣārtha*), is to be worshipped. In the Śruti passage, "upon [the sun] as it rises," meditation is enjoined specifically upon the copper-colored [sun] delimited by the time of rising.

In this context, however, it is not possible for everyone in the world to observe the rule at the time of sunrise, because of their abundance of negligence and laziness. For the sake of favoring those who are unable to meditate at the time of sunrise, and for those who are unable even at that subsequent time when the sun is reddish (aruṇa), and for those who are unable even then when the sun has become brownish (babhru) in color, [the text] prescribes meditation upon Brahman; thus it is said: "Salutation to the copper-colored one and to the reddish one."

Oh, how supreme is the compassion of the one seated upon Śrī Rudra! Now, indeed, in order to show that the Supreme Lord alone is to be worshipped by those seeking all forms of happiness because he is the bestower of bliss, there is the third mantra: *namaśśaṅgāya*. Here, *śam* means happiness; he who causes [beings] to attain that is *śaṅgaḥ*.
The reason for this is "the Lord of Beasts" (*paśupati*); he is the master and protector of "beasts," including both the mobile and the immobile. And thus, it is the Blessed One alone—

The meaning is that [He] is the cause of the happiness for which the world yearns, because the protection of those who seek protection depends upon Him. (Second line) Now, the fourth [verse] is intended to show that the Supreme Lord alone is the object of universal worship because He transcends the universe: "Obeisance to the Fierce One" (*nama ugrāya*).

(Third line) In this sense, [the word *ugra*] means "the most excellent" (*ugra-śreṣṭha*), derived from the root *ud-gam* in the sense of "rising up" or "becoming superior," according to the *Uṇādi-sūtra* rule beginning with *bhaga-agre*. (Fourth line)

Because the suffix *sṛn* has been introduced here by the elision of the *tal*-suffix, for this very reason the word *ugra* is employed in the mantra "bhūyasam" (*ugro hrasaj jateṣu*) as a praise of the excellence of one's own caste (*jāti*). This is because, in that context, there is an absence of any term such as *sajāta* which could provide a correlate for the sense of "superior."

By the principle of the absence of limitation (*saṅkocābhāva-nyāya*), his status as the supreme of all—being greater than the universe—is established. The reason for this is given in the phrase *bhīmāya* (line 8): "Bhīma" means terrifying; according to the Vedic scripture, "From fear of him the wind blows," and thus, because he is terrifying even to the great-souled ones such as Indra and others, the sense is that the Lord, as their controller, is the most excellent of all. Furthermore, it is because he is the cause of victory over all enemies... (p. 81a, f. 77b, line 1).

The fifth [name] is intended to show that even by all those seeking that goal, the Blessed One alone is to be served. "Salutation to Agravadha" (*namo 'gravadhāya*): for one who has entered the arena of battle, being a devotee of his own, he effects the slaughter of enemies before him; thus he is *agrevadha*. Furthermore, even for those opposed to his devotees who remain far away from the battlefield, he effects the destruction of their strength and splendor while they are still at a distance; thus he is *dūre vadha*. Regarding his status as *agrevadha*, it is stated in the *Droṇaparvan*: [text follows].

Arjuna said: "In battle, while consuming the enemy host with showers of arrows, I perceive at my front a man of fiery luster, blazing and raising his trident toward every direction. Toward whichever direction he advances, my enemies there are shattered;
having seized them, I then burn all those foes from behind, and by him they are split asunder."
People consider the multitude of my ashes to be [the army]; and this matter is restated in the *Aśvamedhika* [Parvan]: "Then, when the night had turned to dawn, Arjuna arrived;

he struck down that army with his spear in the very presence of all the spectators. O Great King, who could even in thought assail that host, which was protected by Droṇa, Karṇa, and Kṛpa—those great archers and strikers—were it not for the God, the great archer of manifold forms, Maheśvara? (p. 77b, f. 74a, l. 1)

However, the fact that the killing of Arjuna was far off was stated by Śrī Kṛṣṇa in the *Mokṣadharma*. For there it is said: "Know him, O son of Kuntī, who goes at the head of those being praised when battle is imminent, to be Rudra. And: "By him, indeed, you previously slew your enemies;
therefore, with self-restraint, constantly worship the immeasurably powerful god, the lord of Umā, the imperishable Hara, the Lord of All."
In the *Gītā*, it is stated: "By me alone have these been slain already; be merely an instrument, O Savyasācin" (5th line).

Since Śrī Kṛṣṇa is non-different from the Supreme Lord by virtue of being His incarnation, there is no contradiction between the statements "by me alone have these been slain" and "they were slain by Him already" (6th line). Now, [it must be noted] that disregard for the Supreme Lord is the cause of great calamity (7th line).

The sixth [chapter] is intended to show that the worship of Him should be performed by everyone as well. With the words "Obeisance to the Destroyer" (*namo hantra*), [it refers to one who] would destroy with his own hands those who, out of pride—thinking "I alone am everything" or "I am the wind"—show him disrespect. Because he destroys them preceded by hatred and censure, he is a supreme destroyer; in this regard, Rāvaṇa is the exemplar of such destructiveness. He, indeed, through the pride of his power and sovereignty, [treated] the Supreme Lord... (as per page 82a, folio 78b, line 1).

It is well known in the Rāmāyaṇa and other texts that once, disregarding [the Lord], he extended his arms with the desire to shake Mount Kailāsa; then, due to the pain from his own arms being firmly struck by the slight vibration from the tip of the Blessed One’s big-toe nail, he lamented for a long time and was finally released by the Blessed One out of compassion. This is an example of his extreme insignificance. It is said that Dakṣa, enraged by the Blessed One’s conduct, began to perform a sacrifice. Him—

Vīrabhadra pursued [the sacrifice], severed the head of Dakṣa, set fire to the sacrificial hall, urinated into the ritual pits, destroyed the sacrificial fires, uprooted the sacrificial posts and struck all the deities with them, struck the hands of the officiating priests, plucked out the beard of Bhṛgu, broke the teeth of Pūṣan, and gouged out the eyes of Bhaga— oh, what great violence has been committed!

For at that time, there was no protector whatsoever for these [beings]; therefore, the disregard shown toward the Supreme Lord causes great misfortune. The intended meaning is that one must enter into the worship of Him. Not only is the state of being a worshiper of the Supreme Lord alone [necessary] out of fear of the subverting consequences in the case of the contrary position, but also because He is the means of accomplishing all sacrifices in this world through forms such as the *palāśa*, *bilva*, and *aśvattha* trees, and in the hereafter through forms such as the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*). (Page 82b, Folio 79a, Line 1)
The seventh [verse] is intended to show that because it provides the enjoyment of heaven, it should be resorted to by all who seek that goal.

"Salutation to the trees" (*namo vṛkṣebhyaḥ*): salutation to those trees whose hair consists of green-colored leaves. By the expression "golden-haired" (*harikeśa*), the majesty of the Supreme Lord’s manifestation is shown to reside not only in the leafiness resulting from their being trees, but also in the palāśa and other such [trees].

It has been shown that it indeed exists as the color of Brahman; for this very reason, when one removes the leaves and branches up to the roots, one removes them by means of Brahman itself. Thus, it appears as if the quality of being made from the *palāśa* tree is intended; therefore, there are three leaves on each of the three [branches] of the *palāśa*.
Its greatness is also heard of as being connected to its state of having three leaves, just as the sun is [associated] with the *bilva* tree.
From where it was born, from that [place] the *bilva* tree arose; the greatness of the *bilva* tree is heard of in the Purāṇas. In this manner, other examples may also be cited.
Now, the eighth [chapter] is intended to state that, just as [the Lord] is the means for attaining heaven, He alone is to be resorted to as the means for liberation (*mokṣa*).

"Salutation to Tāra" (*namas tārayai*): *tāra* is the *praṇava* (the syllable *oṃ*); salutation to Him who is of that form. For it is heard in the *Atharvaśiras*: "The *oṃkāra* is *tāra*," having introduced [the topic] with "He is the one Rudra."

"He is Īśāna"—thus it is stated even in the *Taittirīya*. Śiva is indeed the Praṇava; the Praṇava is remembered as Śiva. For there is a statement in the *Śiva Purāṇa*: "An absolute distinction between the signified and the signifier exists nowhere. And from the Śruti: "He who is higher than that which is merged in Prakṛti is the Great Lord (Mahādeśa).
Now, regarding the fruit of the twelve-potsherd sacrifice to Vaiśvānara—just as [the fruits] such as purification exist within the great ocean of unsurpassed bliss—[so too does this].

Indeed, because all fruits— whether pertaining to this world or the next— are included within the Supreme Self as its mere fragments, the ninth [chapter] is intended for all those who seek them, showing that He alone is to be resorted to.
In the phrase "Obeisance to Śambhu," *śam* refers to worldly happiness (*aihika-sukha*) and *bhava* refers to the happiness of heaven and so forth, which is not yet experienced.

He is called Śambhu because everything originates and manifests from him; he is likewise the source (*maya*) of all beings. Thus says the Śruti: "All other beings subsist upon a mere fraction of this bliss. It is not merely by virtue of being the sustainer of the world—like water situated within a reservoir—that the Blessed Lord is to be worshipped; rather, it is to demonstrate that he is also the sovereign agent who bestows worldly and transcendent happiness.

The tenth mantra: "Obeisance to Śaṅkara. Although this appears redundant because of the phrase "obeisance to Śambhu," there is a distinction: here [the former] refers to the direct agency of the Tantra, whereas here [the latter] refers to the traditional lineage. Now, [it is shown that] the Supreme Lord alone is the object of worship for the world, by virtue of being the bestower of all auspiciousness.

He [the author] declares the king of mantras, consisting of eleven syllables, which is the raft for crossing the shoreless net of all defects and the touchstone [for testing all doctrines], and which is to be venerated by Hari, Brahmā, and others:

*namaśśivāya*. The word *śiva* is derived from the root *śiv* with the causative suffix (*ṇic*) and the suffix *ac* (as in the *pacādi* group), signifying the state of being a bringer of auspiciousness (*śivaṃkaratva*).

Likewise, the *Atharvaśikhā* Śruti states: "Śiva alone is to be meditated upon; he is the maker of auspiciousness (*śivaṃkara*). For here, in order to explain the meaning of the word "Śiva," the phrase "endowed with all sovereignty" is employed, from which it is understood that the same applies there as well:
"All the Dānavas and those who are Suras approach me; I am Śiva for all beings. O Suras, [I am] your auspiciousness; salutations to me! (p. 84a, f. 80b, l. 1)

Furthermore, from the statement in the *Bhārata*: "Because he desires the welfare (*śiva*) of human beings, therefore he is remembered as Śiva," the etymological explanation of the word "Śiva" is also ultimately established as meaning "the one who brings about welfare. For the Blessed One, who creates the entire universe by mere will or thought alone, his very instrument is his desire. Likewise, there are other [scriptural passages] such as: "The lion is remembered as Śiva because he subdues (*vaśī-karaṇa*)," and "Therefore, may the Lord, the treasury of all auspicious qualities, be Śiva for you—so [it is said] by the wise who know the true meaning of the principle of Śiva."

The ancient etymological explanations of the word "Śiva" should be understood as culminating precisely in this quality of being "śivaṃkara" (the maker of auspiciousness), as stated in the *Atharvaśikhā*. Now, one might object that this quality of being "śivaṃkara" is seen in other contexts as well; for instance, in the world one says, "May Agni be auspicious (*śiva*) to us," or "May the paths be auspicious (*śivāḥ*) to you. Therefore, [the author] specifies [the Lord] as "to the most auspicious one" (*śivatamāya*).

The sense is this: among all those in the world who bring about auspiciousness (*śivaṃkara*), which one brings about auspiciousness even more excellently? It is the Blessed One alone who is to be worshipped. This very point is clearly stated in the *Atharvaśikhā Upaniṣad*. For there, in response to the questions "What is meditation? Who is the meditator? And what is the object of meditation?", it is said that Śiva alone is the object of meditation; he is the bringer of auspiciousness (*śivaṃkara*), and one should abandon everything else—having first abandoned all else—[and meditate upon him].

Having established that Śiva alone is the object of meditation by virtue of being denoted by the word "Śiva" and by his nature as the "Bestower of Auspiciousness" (*śivaṃkara*), his quality of being the supreme bestower of auspiciousness beyond all else is revealed as the cause [of that meditation]. This very [mantra] is the Great Mantra (*mahāmantra*) for the ritual application of the Rudra Upaniṣad, which serves as a garland of pearls for the entirety of the Vedas.
As they say: "Among the sciences, the Veda is supreme; among the Vedas, the Eleven Rudras; therein, the Five-Syllabled [Mantra]; and therein—"

The word "Śiva" consists of two syllables; thus, the usage of this term "Śiva" in the scriptures includes [the senses of] "that which possesses the two syllables 'Śi-va'" and "the jewel of living beings. All statements from the Śiva Purāṇas should be cited as authoritative evidence for this meaning of Brahman. In brief, He is the one to be worshipped by all through these mantras ending with "Obeisance to Soma."

The Blessed One has been honored for his excellence as the cause of the Dharma; now he is honored as the Inner Guide (*antaryāmin*) with the verses beginning "Homage to the Tīrtha" (line 9). He who exists in the *tīrthas*—such as the Gaṅgā and others—is the *Tīrthya*. He who exists on the banks is the *Kūla*. He who exists at the further shore (*pāra*), which is the supreme *tīrtha* among rivers and so forth, is the *Pārya*. He who exists at the near shore (*apāra*) is the *Avārya*. He is the *Prataraṇa*, the cause for crossing over sins by means of the excellent path (*mārga*), and is thus distinguished from that [other shore].

"Crossing over" (*uttaraṇa*) refers to the cause for crossing over ignorance by means of the path of knowledge; the salutation is made by identifying with that state. "The one who has crossed over" (*ātārya*) is he who exists therein [on the further shore]. "The one who eats" (*ālāda*) is the individual soul (*jīva*) who, in such a way that his *karma* is complete, consumes the fruit of *karma*. "The one who exists therein" is the "eater" (*ālādya*). "The one born in young grass" (*śaṣpya*) is he who exists in young grass (*śaṣpa*). "The one born in foam" (*phenya*) is he who exists in foam. "The one born in sand" (*sikatya*) is he who exists in sand. "The one born in flowing waters" (*pravāhya*) is he who exists in the currents.

He is to be carried forth (*pravāhya*). In the eighth [verse], the Blessed One is saluted as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) by means of the causes for the world’s worship. In the ninth, however, He is saluted as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*): "Obeisance to Hiraṇya" (*nama hiraṇyāya*). *Hiraṇya* refers to that which exists in *hiraṇa*, which is saline soil (*ūṣara*); thus, He is *hiraṇya*. *Prapathya* refers to that which exists on a *prapatha*, a trodden path; thus, He is *prapathya*.

*Kiṃśila* refers to a place where there are stones (*śilā*) scattered about (*kusthitāḥ*), or a dwelling-place (*kṣayaṇa*) suitable for habitation; the meaning is that He possesses the nature of both these forms. (8th line)

*Pulasti* is so called because he stands before his devotees, possessing matted locks (*jaṭājūṭa*) like those of *kapardin*. *Goṣṭhya* refers to one who exists in a *goṣṭha*, a place for cattle. *Gṛhya* refers to one who exists in a house (*gṛha*). *Talpya* refers to one who exists on a bed (*talpa*). *Gehya* refers to one who exists in a dwelling (*geha*) or palace (*prasāda*). *Kāṭa* is that which wanders about poorly; it is so called because it becomes difficult to enter due to being filled with thorns, creepers, and the like. *Kāṭya* refers to cows, buffaloes, and other such animals that exist there. *Gahvara* means a rugged or inaccessible place.

He who dwells in mountain caves and the like is *gahvareṣṭhaḥ*. He who exists in *hṛdaḥ*, that is, in unfathomable waters, is *hṛdaryaḥ*. He who exists there where the water of mist settles is *niveṣpyaḥ*. He who exists in *pāṃsavaḥ*, that is, in atoms of dust, is *pāṃsavyaḥ*. Regarding *rajas* as meaning clarity (*spaṣṭārthatā*), he who exists in the dust is *rajasyaḥ*. He who exists in dry wood is *śuṣkyaḥ*. [He who exists] in green, moist things... (line 6).

*bhavaḥ* means "born. *Lopaḥ* refers to a hard place, so called because grass and the like are cut off (*lūpyate*) therein. That which is born there is *lopya*. *Ulapāḥ* refers to *balbaja* grass and the like; that which is born there is *ulapya*. Regarding *sūrmyaḥ*: *urvī* means earth; *ūrvaḥ* is a Vedic form for "long" (*dīrgha*). Those rivers which have beautiful waves (*ūrmi*) are *ūrmyaḥ*; that which is born in them is *sūrmyaḥ*. That which is born among leaves is *parṇyaḥ*. [This refers to] dry leaves. (p. 86a, f. 82b, line 1)

The word *saṅghātaparṇa* means "that which exists there"; thus it is *saṅghātaparṇaśadya*. Now, with the two verses beginning with *namo ’paguramāṇāya*, the Rudras—who are portions of the Blessed One and the subduers of the world—are addressed and offered salutation. Among those to be subdued, the most wicked ones, [the Rudras] stand with weapons raised;
indeed, as they strike down and smite them according to their sins, some Daityas they merely gnaw upon slightly.

"Prakhkhidan" means causing exhaustion or distress in the act of drawing forth; that is to say, [causing it] to take on that form. This collection of thirty-one intermediate mantras consisting of *yajus* formulas, beginning with "namassomāya" (5th line) and taking the form of various salutations, constitutes a single mantra (6th line).
The Blessed One himself is its seer (*ṛṣi*), he alone is its deity, and [the attributes] such as "endowed with beauty and youth" (7th line) are stated in the *tritīyānuvāka*.

Thus are the verses on meditation. This mantra bestows fruits such as imperial sovereignty, lordship, the state of Jīva, and the state of Śiva. The mastery (*siddhi*) of this mantra is attained through fifty recitations preceded by the performance of two *kṛcchra* penances. With the five mantras beginning with "namo vaḥ kirikebhyaḥ," the hosts of Rudras, who exist in a hidden form and consist of the restraint of the world, are saluted. Their hidden nature is understood from the two qualifying adjectives [in the mantra] applied to the hearts of the gods.
"They abide in the hearts of the gods" means "we know. And this [phrase] is an epithet for all five, beginning with *kirika* (3rd line):

they are *kirikas* because they scatter or destroy according to their own will; they are *kṣīṇikas* because they variously exhaust or afflict. They are *vicinvatkaras* because, for the sake of restraint and favor, they investigate—thinking, "these are evildoers, these are doers of good"—with *āṅ* as a prefix denoting limit (5th line).

Salutation to you who, even toward the most wicked, certainly effect their destruction; [you] who possess the quality of making [them] unworthy [of happiness], that is, causing them suffering—those "unworthy ones" (*ānarhatas*). Salutation to you, O *Kirikā* and others, who manifest on all sides for the approach of the wicked from here and there, like a disease; indeed, desire (*kāma*) is of such a nature. This concludes the form of salutation directed elsewhere.
A collection of intermediate mantras consisting of *yajus* formulas constitutes a single mantra. Its seer (*ṛṣi*) is Agni, its deity (*devatā*) is Rudra.

One should meditate upon Śiva as a mass of splendor, blazing and holding aloft a trident, with hands and feet on all sides, and eyes, heads, and faces on all sides. Following the performance of the *parāka-kṛcchra* penance, through forty thousand recitations of this mantra, there is success (*siddhi*), characterized by sovereignty over the entire earth, a hundred thousand gold pieces, and a beautiful face.

This mantra bestows the fruit of the direct realization of liberation, which is characterized by the enjoyment of sovereignty. Thus, having propitiated [the Lord] with the first [anuvāka], the Blessed One is saluted through the second to the ninth anuvākas by way of His being the Lord of All, the Self of All, and the Inner Ruler of All.
Now, [the fifth line...]

In this tenth section (*anuvāka*), twelve mantras in the form of *ṛc* verses are requested. Among them, the first begins with "drāpi. (6th line) The word *drā* signifies something contemptible. That which causes one to attain such a state is *drāpiḥ*. Another [meaning] is that he is the master (*pati*) of food (*anna*) therein; thus he is *andhaspatiḥ*. He is not poor (*daridra*) nor destitute (*niṣkañcana*). Because half of his body is Umā, he is *nīlalohitaḥ*, meaning one whose half is blue (*nīla*) and half is red (*lohita*). (8th line)

Having addressed them with these words, safety is prayed for for them; that is to say, for these people of ours—our sons, grandsons, and so forth—and for these animals—cows, horses, and so forth—the meaning is: "Do not cause these to be afraid.
Furthermore, among these, let not even a single thing go to Māra, nor let it perish; likewise, let it not become afflicted by disease. In this context, [the phrase] is "do not fear" (*mā bhaiḥ*).

In the passage beginning with *māro mo āma* and including *drāpe andhasaspate*, this triad of vocatives contains a causal implication (*hetugarbha*). [The first vocative] refers to one who causes a contemptible state of existence through fear, disease, and so forth, because by not producing such fear and the like, he becomes the cause for their non-arising.

[The second vocative] refers to the Lord of Food (*andhasaspate*), because as the master of food, he is capable of protecting by providing sustenance. And by the term *nīlalohita*, there is the mention of his being accompanied by Umā.
It is shown that [bestowing] fearlessness, health, and so forth is appropriate for one whose form is adorned with the power of innate compassion.
(7th line) Thus, it should not be said that there is any loss of impartiality or cruelty on the part of the Blessed One who performs both restraint and favor;

this is shown by the word *daridra* ("poor"), which signifies one who is himself destitute of nothing (*niṣkiñcana*). The seer (*ṛṣi*) of this mantra is Pulastya; the deity (*devatā*) is Bhairava-Rudra. (p. 88a, f. 84b, 1st line)

The meter is Āstārapaṅkti. The Lord, the husband of Mṛḍānī, whose body is adorned with the attire of Bhairava, who wears a tunic reaching to the ankles, who is smeared with ashes from the *ḍamaruka* drum, whose neck is radiant, who bears a trident, whose ears are encircled by earrings, who is marked with beautiful *tilaka*, whose anklets jingle sweetly, and who appears white due to the rays emanating from his rows of teeth as dark as sapphire— this Lord, the master who destroys the fear of all beings, is to be meditated upon.

This mantra, which brings about the direct realization of Bhairava and the attainment of the wealth of peace, achieves mastery (*mantrasiddhi*) through ten thousand recitations (*ayuta-japa*) preceded by a one-day fast.
Now, the second [mantra]: *yā te rudra*. O Rudra, that which is yours—your auspicious and peaceful [nature]... (line 6).

By that body of yours which is most auspicious and peaceful, being propitiated (*tatvānaḥ*), [be gracious] so that we may live (*jīvase*)—the suffix *se* is used in the Veda in the sense of the infinitive marker *tumun*.
"Be merciful" (*mṛḍaya*) means "so that we may live healthy and immortal," that is, "grant us happiness. How is it propitiated? To this he says:
"She is the healer of all days" (*viśvāha bheṣajī*). She is the remedy for disease, poverty, and so forth, on all (*viśveṣu*) days (*ahaḥ*).
Because she is the cause of the destruction of speech [and worldly bondage], therefore Śivā is not called "Śiva" merely by virtue of bestowing worldly happiness;

rather, she is so called because she bestows the bliss of liberation. Thus he says: "O Śivā of Rudra. She is the medicine belonging to you, Rudra—the physician for the disease of saṃsāra—acting as a divine elixir that removes the disease of saṃsāra. Therefore, O Śivā, protect me.
The seer (ṛṣi) and deity of the mantra are Rudra in the form of Skanda. One should meditate upon Śiva in the form of Skanda— six-faced, resembling molten gold, and mounted upon his peacock vehicle.

Preceded by one hundred and eight breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*), five thousand recitations of this mantra bring about its perfection (*mantrasiddhi*). It pacifies malevolent magic, demonic disturbances, evil dreams, and the like; it bestows excellent sons, rain, health, and prosperity. Herein, the third [verse] is: *imā rudrāya tavase tapo...* (RV 2.33.1).

The suffix expressing possession (*matvarthīya*) is elided after *balavat*. To Kapardin—the one possessing matted locks (*jaṭā*) and a topknot (*jūṭa*)—to that Rudra for whom the opposing heroes (*vīra*) are wasting away (*kṣayantaḥ*), i.e., perishing, we offer this prayer (*mati*). [The term] *kūrma* means "in the manner of" or "continuously. In response to the inquiry as to what kind of prayer it is, he says: "Just as... That is, just as those men who, thinking themselves to be superior, have been made [low] by our action. Our... [third line].

May there be well-being for our relatives—both bipeds and quadrupeds, such as sons, grandsons, and so forth—and for our livestock, the four-footed animals. From this [root], the fifth verbal suffix (*leṭ*) occurs; the augment *aṭ* is applied according to the rule *leṭo yāḍāvaḥ*. Not only is there happiness for those belonging to us alone, but we offer our prayers so that every living being dwelling in our village may be well-nourished and free from disease. Thus [ends the sixth line].

"In whatever village or even city one who recites the Rudrādhyāya may dwell, there affliction from disease, famine, thieves, or mental anguish shall not arise"—this Purāṇic statement is to be considered here. In this regard, the four words beginning with "Rudrādhyāya" contained in the second half of the verse provide the reason for its quality of bestowing happiness. Among them, by the word "Rudrādhyāya," the capacity to draw away (destroy) either sorrow or suffering is expressed.

By the word *tapas* (asceticism), he is shown to possess the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), according to the Vedic scripture which states, "His austerity consists of knowledge. By the term *kapardinaḥ* (the one with matted hair), his capacity to accomplish tasks that cannot be achieved by others is indicated. Etymologically, *kaparda* refers to that which protects (*pardayati*) or sustains (*pālayati*) the water of the Gaṅgā (*kaṃ*); thus, *kapardī* means "one who possesses a mass of matted hair" (*jaṭājūṭa*). Through this analysis of the meaning of the words, it is understood that he is the bearer of the Gaṅgā, a task impossible for anyone else.

O King, the earth will not be able to endure the descent of the Gaṅgā; indeed, O hero, I see no one other than you who can sustain her. Since, through such statements from the *Rāmāyaṇa* and other texts as "the wielder of the trident" (*śūlī*), it is understood that the bearing of the Gaṅgā is impossible for anyone else, the intention [of the verse] is that by the phrase "to the one whose heroes perish" (*kṣayadvīrāya*), his possession of heroic power is expressed—[that is, he alone is capable of such a task].

Now the fourth [verse]: "O gracious Rudra" (*mṛḍāno rudra*). O Rudra, homage to you! Be gracious to us; gladden us by granting our desired objects. And furthermore, bestow upon us *maya*—that is, the bliss of liberation (*mokṣa-sukha*). [Objection: But how can the bliss of liberation be given to you, who are most wicked? To this he says: "To the one whose heroes perish" (*kṣayadvīrāya*). To you, for whom our sins have been destroyed, we shall pay homage with salutation (*namasā*); that is to say, we shall serve you. (2nd line)

The sense is this: for me, whose sins have been destroyed by prostrating before you, even the removal of ill-repute (*nirvāda*) constitutes the qualification for liberation, according to the Vedic scripture which states, "By these, indeed, one becomes immortal. And this goal, consisting of both worldly enjoyment and final release (*bhoga-apavarga*), is to be accomplished through your grace. It is not something attained at present, but rather something attained through a lineage; thus he says: "He who is the father of the moving and the unmoving, Manu, and those who are known as our younger brothers."

O Rudra, by that very instruction on the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśrama*) through which you have protected the subjects—[you] whose greatness is renowned in the *Śruti* and other scriptures—when there is affection and grace in your ordinance, whatever [you] bestowed as the happiness of enjoying sense-objects and liberation (*mokṣa*), which consists in the complete separation from suffering; all that, O Rudra, may we obtain through your ordinance and by your grace. The two *ṛc*s beginning with "Rudra" constitute a single mantra. (p. 90b, f. 87a, l. 1)
The seer is Mārkaṇḍeya; the meter is Jagatī; the deity is Śrī Rudra.
One should meditate upon Soma, who sits upon a divine lion-throne, being praised by the great seers, with a gracious countenance and the crescent moon as his crest-ornament.

The accomplishment of my *puraścaraṇa* is achieved by reciting nine thousand [times] preceded by the performance of one *kṛcchra* penance. This mantra bestows peace upon cows, horses, animals, and so forth.
Now, the fifth: "Mā no mahāntam... (4th line).

O Rudra, do not harm our great, aged man; do not afflict him with disease and the like. And furthermore, do not harm our small child—this applies to all cases. And furthermore, [do not harm] our son who is capable of procreation; and furthermore, our [others].

"Do not kill our son who dwells in the womb, nor our father, nor even our mother; do not harm our dear bodies and limbs. (8th line) The word *mā* is used in each instance to express prohibition due to an excess of affection (*ādarātiśayāt*). The plural number (*mārirīṣaḥ*) is used in reference to one's own offspring.
Thus, the meaning is: "Do not harm my great ones, the small ones, and so forth. The seer (*ṛṣi*) of this mantra is Bhṛgu. (2nd line)
Rudra, whose nature is Nandīśvara, is the deity; the Jagatī is the meter.
One should meditate upon the Lord who has the crescent moon as his crown and a body like the rising sun.
Having the form of Nandīśvara and surrounded by the lords of the Gaṇas.
This mantra is primarily for the purpose of pacification (*śānti*). Accomplishment of the mantra is attained through five thousand recitations preceded by three days of fasting.
Now begins the sixth [mantra]: *mā nastoke*. O Rudra, you who are provoked to anger by the non-performance of prescribed duties...
Do not cause harm to our triple-born offspring—our children, our mere progeny, and our descendants.

And as for us, do not slay our heroic servants. How could you fail to harm them while you are moving among them? To this, he replies: "We are possessed of oblations. Oblations consist of cooked rice, sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*), and so forth, as well as offerings presented through devotion to Śiva.

"What indeed can be done by a man for that which is eternal and perfect? But as it is said by the Blessed One: "O Goddess, I indeed accept the state of being [offered] with my whole self" (p. 91b, f. 88a, 1st line); and from the *Gītā*: "I accept what is offered with devotion by one of purified soul" (2nd line). Therefore, those who are devoid of such an oblation, we worship you with salutation—that is, with prostration; we shall serve you, for prostration is the remedy against the onset [of suffering]. (3rd line)

According to the maxim "of the great-souled ones," the sense is that even I, though most sinful, am worthy of being seen. The seer (*ṛṣi*) and deity (*devatā*) of this mantra are the Blessed One himself;
the meter (*chandas*) is Jagatī.
[He] bears a body divided into eleven parts, shining like pure crystal.
One should always meditate here upon Rudra, who is composed of light, wielder of the trident, and crowned with the moon.
The fruits of this mantra include the increase of longevity,

the increase of royal glory, excellent nourishment, invincibility in messengership and legal disputes, the gain of a thousand gold pieces, the cessation of great sins, success in vision, and victory over one's own people and others— such are its results in the oceans and other [sacred sites].
These have been explained. That which brings about the accomplishment of mantras should also be seen in that very place.

Now begins the seventh [chapter]. Regarding the phrase "ārātta" (*ārāt ta*): O God, [this applies] to the slayer of a cow (*goghna*)—that is, to one who has killed a cow—and furthermore, to the slayer of a human (*puruṣaghna*)—here the dative case is used in the sense of the genitive—meaning one who destroys all living beings.

And he says that for this one who withdraws the entire world, there is no object [of destruction]: "To the Kṣayadvīra" means for the one who is the hero of destruction. Among gods, asuras, humans, and others, those warriors possessed of immeasurable strength—all of them go to their prior destruction; thus he is the Kṣayadvīra.
To that Kṣayadvīra—this is the meaning of "to the Kṣayadvīra. For whom both Brahman and Kṣatriya are the food of the Blessed One, and for whom death is the condiment.

"Who indeed knows where he is?"—so says the Śruti. Of you, who are such as this, that *sumnam* which is non-terrible (*aghora*) and has the form of the head—that form has become manifest to us. The meaning is: "May it be near; let the terrible form not remain at a distance.
The sense is: "Be present in a gracious form. And having become present, [protect] us...

"Protect [us] from all misfortune; guard us. To this, one might ask: "How is this most sinful person to be protected? If the gods should then inquire, you must speak on their behalf, saying, "This is mine," and thus offer words of support. Furthermore, protection does not consist merely in the cessation of calamity; moreover, O *dvibarhas*—O increaser (*barhayitā*, *vardhaka*) of the two, namely the happiness of worldly enjoyment and liberation—for us.
And that which is *śarma*, the bliss of worldly enjoyment and liberation; the deity (*devatā*) of this mantra is Śambhu; the meter (*chandaḥ*) is Triṣṭubh;
[the mantra] describes the Lord performing the dance of bliss (*ānandatāṇḍava*) in the presence of the Goddess.
One should meditate upon the fire-eyed one, resembling molten gold.
This mantra bestows longevity and sovereignty. Through three days of fasting followed by uninterrupted recitation for three nights, there is accomplishment of the mantra.
Now, the eighth: "Praise! (stuhi). Here, one's own self is being addressed: "O Self, you..."

"Pray, or rather, praise this speech"—thus [the text] shows that the cause for this is the "gold from the far shore" (*pāraja*). "Renowned" (*śruta*) means it is well-known throughout all the worlds by virtue of being the Supreme Lord. [One might ask: "If He is such [a being], how will my hymn approach Him?"—because He is "seated in the pit" (*gartasada*), meaning He dwells or sits within the cavity of the heart. "Seated in the pit" refers to the Lord who resides in the region of the hearts of all beings.

The *Smṛti* records this. His worthiness to be praised does not rest on his supreme status alone; rather, it is also due to his being exceedingly wonderful by virtue of possessing a divine and auspicious form. Thus he says: "the youth," meaning one beautiful with perpetual adolescence. Demonstrating the attainment of desired and undesired results from performing or not performing the aforementioned praise, he first states the undesirable consequence of non-performance: "to offer," [referring to] the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśrama*).

The meaning is: "one who brings harm to my devotees by transgressing my own command through the performance of [forbidden] religious rites. (6th line) Here he provides an illustration: the particle *iva* is used for the purpose of comparison; [he says] "like a deer," meaning as terrifying as a deer [is to a lion], or rather, for the purpose of tearing apart an elephant, [he adopts] a vow. (7th line) He takes the example of a deer that is exceedingly terrifying like a lion; the word "deer" (*mṛga*) refers to the lion, which is superior to himself. (8th line)

One might raise the doubt that even the Blessed One could be overcome by some being of greater strength than himself, such as a *śarabha*; therefore, to dispel this [doubt], it is said that he is "fierce" (*ugra*), meaning he cannot be overcome by anyone. Furthermore, it is stated: "His power is declared to be truly manifold—innate wisdom, strength, and action"—or else, "O Rudra, you are not [merely] powerful."

The sense is this: since [the Lord] is celebrated in hundreds of such scriptural passages as "He is the established one among lords, the supreme Maheśvara," and is exalted by a great power that is peerless and unsurpassed, it is impossible for any lord of the entire world to effect his subjugation. Having thus stated the undesirable consequence of not offering praise, the Lord is now entreated while demonstrating the desirable outcome resulting from such praise: "O Rudra, be gracious! (mṛḍa). 6th line.
O You whose horses are being praised, be gracious toward those—whether established or unestablished—who abide in this decaying body of mine;

grant that I may be free from disease and possess firm limbs (*māriṣā*), and thereafter, that I may be liberated, free from old age and death—this is the meaning of "make me happy. Those armies of Yours which are adverse to this, namely the thirty-three [deities] whom we shall address later with the words "Salutation to the Rudras" (p. 94a, f. 90b, l. 1).

In such [mantras] as "triyañca gaṇino rujanta," those armies are well-known; may they strike down (*nibarhantu*)—that is, destroy for the sake of our ruin—another than us, namely our enemy (*asmat... anyaṃ... asmad-vairiṇam*). For this mantra, the seer (*ṛṣi*) is Vaiyyāghra, the meter (*chandaḥ*) is Triṣṭubh, and the deity (*devatā*) is Śrī Rudra.

One should meditate upon Rudra, who is praised by hosts of gods, who moves through the sky, who is terrifying yet possesses the brilliance of ten million rising suns, and who grants fearlessness while appearing fearful.

Success in the *puraścaraṇa* rite is attained by reciting [the mantra] continuously for three nights, preceded by a fast of one night. This mantra is primarily intended for the destruction of enemies.
Now, the ninth [mantra]: "pari no rudrasya..."—may the *heti*, the weapon, spare us (*naḥ*). May it avoid us.

"May he avoid [him] at all times" means "may he never strike. Since it is impossible to avoid striking when the intent to kill is present, that very intention is requested to be avoided. Regarding the phrase *paritveṣasya*: *aghāyuḥ* refers to one who desires (*ā-yu*) evil (*agha*, i.e., sin) by means of anger; his [intention] is that of Rudra, who is *taveṣa*, blazing with wrath. His *durmati* is the malicious intent, the thought of killing.
May that wrath of the Supreme Lord—which consists of the non-performance of what is enjoined and the performance of what is censured—also strike us.

From that arises the cognition of being an object to be slain; from that, by means of the weapons of the Supreme Lord in the form of various entities such as place, time, and persons, which are the instruments for manifold sufferings pertaining to this world and the next; and from that [weapon], the experience of suffering [arises].

The sequence here is such that even the left [hand], ending with the experience of suffering from sin and so forth, becomes desired. Now, [one might object]: "My weapon is unfailing" (5th line), and my intellect is likewise;

how then could there be an avoidance of that? To this he says: "Unsteady... (6th line). O *mīḍhvah* (6th line)—O showerer of the desires of those who bow down! This is the reason for addressing the *garbha*. "Your weapon and intellect are steady and unfailing" (7th line).

For the sake of us who have committed sins, for the sake of the bounteous ones (*maghavadbhyaḥ*), extend—make descend—your weapons and your wisdom, which take the form of praise, prostration, and so forth; let them be made effective for our benefit.
O you whose weapons and wisdom are never in vain, it is your duty as the protector of those who bow before you to withhold [these from us].
Furthermore, O Bountiful One (*mīḍhvaḥ*), bestow happiness upon our offspring in general and especially upon our sons.
The Blessed One himself is the seer (*ṛṣi*) and the deity (*devatā*) of this mantra; the meter (*chandas*) is *triṣṭubh*.
One should meditate upon the God, the piercer of elephants, whose body is clad in elephant hide, who is radiant with flashing weapons, and who removes all sins. (Verse 3)
This mantra bestows fruits such as the attainment of excellent sons. Mantra-siddhi is achieved by performing one *kṛcchra* penance followed by five thousand recitations daily for nine days.
Now, the tenth [mantra]: "O most bountiful one" (*mīḍhuṣṭama*). "O most bountiful one" (*he mīḍhuṣṭama*).

O you who rain down boons with excellence, O most auspicious one (*śivatama*), [the vocative] "O you who bring about supreme welfare" (*atiśayena śivaṃ karoti*) is an address containing a reason. And for us, may Bhava—the one who brings about welfare (*śivaṃkaraḥ*), the benevolent (*sumanāḥ*), the one of beautiful countenance (*śobhanamukhaḥ*), and the father—be [our protector].
He states that this is the characteristic of you, the Father, in the verse beginning with *parivṛkṣa*. In the highest, most exalted tree, such as the *vaṭa* and so forth... (line 8).

For it is heard: on Mount Kailāsa, there is the divine banyan tree (*divyavaṭavṛkṣa*), the abode of the Blessed One, rising one hundred *yojanas* high and measuring seventy-five hundred and odd *yojanas* in extent. With a height of one hundred *yojanas* and a length of one hundred and seventy-five less a quarter [of a *yojana*], its pure shade forms a circular canopy; it is unstained and free from heat. In that tree, which consists of great yoga and is a refuge for those seeking liberation, the gods beheld Śiva seated. Upon that supreme tree is your mind.
Having set aside His terrifying weapon where it was placed so that we do not see it, He stands there; come near!

Come close! Wearing a tiger skin as a garment, clad in it, bearing the Pināka bow for the sake of ornament, holding that bow in His hand—come near! With the Pināka in His hand, clothed in a tiger skin, the Lord of Life.
Based on such scriptural passages as "Clad in a hide" and "Wielder of the Pināka bow," that very form of Yours is praised for its great excellence.

This is the underlying meaning: the Supreme Lord’s wearing of animal skins is due to the lack of [fine] garments. For it would be a source of ridicule to say that the Blessed One—who bestows all sovereignty upon Brahmā, Indra, and others, and who has attendants such as Kubera, the bringer of treasures—lacked clothing. Rather, it is [a manifestation of] His own bliss...

In order to demonstrate the repulsiveness of objects that are pursued for the sake of fulfillment, the wearing of skins is prescribed in place of the divine garments favored by those who are greedy for sense-objects; this very point is set forth in the *Bhāgavatapurāṇa*: "Those unfortunate ones indeed laugh at the conduct of one who knows the truth within himself and desires it; yet they nourish as their own self the dog's food [of worldly life] with golden garments, garlands, ornaments, and ointments."

Thus, those proponents of the doctrine that the body is the self— unfortunate, ill-fated, and born of a mixed womb (meaning born from a corrupt source)— being ignorant of the Lord’s intended purpose, which was to clarify the repulsiveness of sense objects for one who delights in his own Self, mock the Supreme Lord, who is covered in garments of skin, skull-bones, and ashes as bodily unguents; such is the meaning of the verse.

It is also illustrated in the *Mahimnastava*: "The great bull, the skull-topped staff, the axe, the deerskin, the ashes, and the serpent—these are the extent of Your means for granting boons. The gods possess various prosperities bestowed by You; indeed, the deer of the senses do not cause one to wander through thirst for objects when they are fixed upon the earth [of Your feet]. Thus, for one who delights in the Self (*svātmārāma*), wearing the deerskin is a characteristic mark indicating the cessation of all sensory objects.

By the phrase "bearing the Pināka," the word *pināka* is intended to signify a vessel; for this is established by the rule [Pāṇini 3.2.178] regarding the suffix *-aka* in words such as *pināka*, and by the addition of the augment *nuṭ*. Thus, it refers to the bearing of the Pināka, which is the instrument of protection and concentration. It is the symbol of bliss (*prīti*). The seer (*ṛṣi*) of this mantra is Vairāja, the meter (*chandas*) is Triṣṭubh, and the deity (*devatā*) is Śambhu.

One should meditate upon the God who is the abode of auspiciousness, youthful and exceedingly beautiful— the wielder of the Pināka bow— approaching in the form of a forest-dweller. Thus [ends the section on] fear of kings.
This mantra is primarily for those facing calamities such as the harassment of thieves and life-threatening dangers.
Now begins the eleventh [chapter].

"Vikirida" means that which scatters (*vividhaṃ kiranti*) or destroys (*hiṃsanti*), namely, evil, disease, saṃsāra, poverty, and so forth; it is that which pierces (*dyati*) or shatters them. O Vikirida! O Vilohita! [This refers to] one whose color is as white as camphor. For this very reason, in the meditation on the five syllables, the Tantrikas [describe Him thus]. (Tantrikāḥ, p. 97a, f. 93b, l. 1)

They remember You as the one whose radiance is like a mountain struck by the nectar-essence free from all taints—that is to say, as the embodiment of pure *sattva*. O Blessed One, endowed with the sixfold sovereign powers (*ṣaḍguṇaiśvarya*), salutations be to You. These three vocatives contain within them the reasons for what is to be established in the subsequent chapter.
Having offered salutation with the words "Icchan," he makes his request: "yāsta iti. Those thousands of weapons, those infinite armaments that exist—all of them [turn away] from us to another.

"May they cast away and destroy evil, but not us"—this is the meaning. Now, for this mantra: Pulastya is the seer (*ṛṣi*); *triṣṭubh* is the meter (*chandaḥ*); (fifth line) Śambhu is the deity (*devatā*).
[He is] one with a gracious countenance, peaceful, whose conduct is a source of adornment.
One should meditate upon [the deity] together with Ambā, praised by the hosts of Surasas.

The fruits of this practice shall include the removal of enmity with great men, victory over enemies, the bearing of burdens, and so forth. Preceded by a meal of *caru* for three nights, there should be ten thousand recitations (*japa*), followed by ten thousand circumambulations of Śiva. Such are the limits of the preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*) for this mantra.

Now the twelfth [verse]: "Thousands" (*sahasrāṇi*). Here, although the dual form "in the two arms" (*bāhvoḥ*) is used, it is intended to mean "in the arms" (*bāhuṣu*). O Blessed One (*bhagavan*), [this refers to] your two arms—or, since you possess infinite arms—intending each pair of arms occupied with bow and arrow.

The word *hetayaḥ* is in the dual number. Weapons (*āyudhāni*) exist by the thousands, and the word *sahasra* expresses infinity. (Third line) By way of the distinction between different types of weapons—such as the bow, sword, and trident—there are infinite [weapons]; and even among those, because each one has many subdivisions, they bring about infinite results. For it is heard [in scripture]: "From his trident, thousands of other tridents issue forth by his splendor. (Fifth line)
Turn the faces of those weapons away from us;
turn their tips away. The sense is that you are the Lord, the Sovereign of all, capable of withdrawing even those [weapons] that have been discharged.
Nārada is the seer (*ṛṣi*) of this mantra; Śrī Rudra is the deity (*devatā*).
"One should meditate upon the Great Lord (Maheśvara) in all worlds—the God who removes all sins, adorned with all ornaments, and bearing all weapons. Thus [it is said].
This mantra is primarily intended for the warding off of calamities. One *kṛcchra* [penance]... [p. 97b, f. 94a, l. 1]

Preceded by the *cāraṇa* [recitation], the perfection of the mantra is attained through one thousand recitations (*sahasrajapa*). In the tenth section (*anuvāka*), the Blessed Lord is entreated; in the eleventh, however, the Rudras, who are His partial manifestations (*aṃśabhūta*), are entreated. For indeed, as lords of all worlds, they are partial manifestations of the Lord Śiva, the father of Ambā and Brahmā, existing as the respective lords of those worlds for the sake of punishing or favoring the various living beings residing in those worlds according to their respective karmas.

Established by the Blessed One as the presiding forms over the entire circle of the Brahmāṇḍa, they are great oceans of unsurpassed majesty. (5th line) Regarding Rudra, one Rudra is spoken of, yet in the Mahābhārata they are augmented to innumerable thousands.
(6th line) He is the eternal Mahādeva, the god of all beings; there are innumerable thousands of Rudras. (7th line)

The place is imperishable. And in the Śaiva Purāṇas it is said: "He who is the one Rudra presides over the universe. "Becoming Rudras, [he pervades] countless thousands of the entire world. Likewise: "The forms that are eternally liberated, the pairs of forms that flow forth, together with their powers and their attendants—those are worshipped by all the worlds."
They are capable of both the creation and the dissolution of all the worlds;
they are mutually affectionate and pay homage to one another;
they are eternally beloved by Śiva and are characterized by the attributes of Śiva.
Gentle, fierce, and likewise mixed, consisting of two intermediate types;
deformed and beautiful, assuming various forms—
these are the attendants of that Lord, bearing diverse divine forms for their Master.
Some were dwarfish, some had matted hair, and some were shaven-headed; they had necks like conch shells and large bellies.
With spears and swords in hand, their crowns were raised high above all, these slayers of enemy armies possessed irresistible prowess.
The perfected ones who act according to their will are the lords of the three worlds;
by whom— the Blessed One and the Great Lords— acting through their own essential natures, he, the sovereign of the past,
the future, and the present, enjoys [the world] together with the hosts of elemental beings.

(8th line) Here, by the phrase "gentle, terrible, and likewise mixed," [it refers to] the mantra: "Obeisance to you from the non-terrible ones, from the terrible ones, from all, from all-sharers, O Rudra, to those who are forms of Rudra" (p. 99a, f. 95b, 1st line). Thus it is stated at the end of the Rudra [section]. Likewise, in the Sāmaveda, there is that which is called the Devavrata, beginning with "sātniyadiviṣa... (2nd line).

By such statements as these, the various Rudras residing in those respective worlds are established and further elaborated upon in the Śaiva Purāṇas. Indeed, they are shown to be dwellers of heaven, dwellers of the intermediate space, and likewise dwellers of the earth. Furthermore, their essential nature as characterized by restraint and grace, as well as their forms of both terrible and non-terrible aspects, are set forth in the Laiṅga Purāṇa; for therein, by mere remembrance—
Beginning with the words, "O Rudra, these lords of the Gaṇas have arrived before you; they are innumerable and high-souled," it is said:
(line 6) "Those lords of the Gaṇas, possessed of great strength and masters of the lords of all worlds, having bowed down to the God and the Goddess, spoke these words:
(line 7) 'For what purpose, O God, have we been remembered by you, O Great Lord?'"
"Shall we dry up the oceans, or shall we slay Yama with his servants?
Shall we kill Death, or even the immortal Sun-born Brahmā,
having bound the eternal Viṣṇu along with Indra and the other gods?"
Or else, being enraged, we shall subdue the Daityas along with the Dānavas;
by your command, whom today shall we subject to terrible calamity?
Or whom, O Lord, shall we today bestow upon a festival endowed with every object of desire?

"His assembly consists of divine beings assuming various forms"—by this statement from the *Mahābhārata*, it is shown that there are ancient divine hosts of many forms. Likewise, the Rudras mentioned in the *Śruti* are clearly seen;
similarly, in the *Sāmaveda*, in the two Sāmans named *Devavrata*, by the passage beginning with "the gods and so forth," those residing in their respective worlds [are indicated].

The Rudras have been established [in the Vedas] and further elaborated upon in the Śaiva Purāṇas. For they are indeed praised by the gods as observers of divine vows (devavrata), dwelling in heaven, dwelling in the intermediate space, and likewise dwelling on earth. And among these Rudras, who are the lords of their respective worlds, there stand the divine abodes of the sons of Amṛta; such is well known from the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad and other sources.
Those *yāmas*, their respective names, and their activities numbering in the tens of millions of their hosts—all this is elaborated upon in the *Śaiva Purāṇas* and other texts;

however, for fear of prolixity, it is not written here. With reference to these very *mudrās*, there is this *anuvāka*. In this section, there are thirteen mantras, of which the first is as follows: "Sahasrāṇi... By this [verse], there is a transformation into the number of thousands, and they exist by the thousands. Having become a thousand times a thousand—

Thus situated—those Rudras who are upon the earth, in a region far above it, separated by a thousand human settlements—we bow down to them; that is, we perform prostrations through hymns of praise and salutations. The sense is: "May they not string their bows in order to strike us."
Now the second [verse]:
"In this great..."— in this visible great ocean and in the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), you Rudras exist above, presiding over both the ocean and the intermediate space.
"Let their bows sink down a thousand *yojanas*," "let them [sink] at a *yojana*," and "here, in this great ocean, in the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*).

(8th line) This statement regarding the greatness of the ocean and the intermediate space as perceived through direct observation is as they say: "The sky is like the sky; the ocean is comparable to the ocean. (p. 100b, f.
