97a, 1st line) By this, the extraordinary greatness of the Rudras who preside over them is manifested. Beginning from this mantra— (2nd line)

In the mantras ending with the ninth, the phrase "sahasrayojanam" (a thousand yojanas) is to be supplied to them; and precisely to indicate that supply, the words "teṣām" and so forth are recited again in the tenth mantra. Now, the third [mantra]:

"Blue-necked" (*nīlagrīva*) refers to those whose nature is that of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) following the swallowing of the *kālakūṭa* poison; they are "blue-necked" for that reason. Prior to that, they were of a white-necked nature (*śvetagrīva*).
The states of being "blue-necked" and "dark-throated" (*śitikaṇṭha*) have already been explained according to the distinction of occasion.
Such are the Śarvas and Rudras who move upon the earth below; they dwell in the subterranean worlds (pātālaloka) as their lords.
"Of them," and so forth, as before. Now, the fourth [section].
"Those with blue necks" (*nīlagrīvāḥ*) have heard [this] from heaven; now, through self-restraint, they have attained the celestial realm (*svarga*).

The remaining [mantras] are as before. Now, beginning with "Thousands upon thousands" (*sahasrāṇi sahasra*) and ending with this, these four mantras constitute a single mantra. Its seer (*ṛṣi*) is Dūrvāsas; its deity (*devatā*) is Śrī Rudra.
One should meditate upon him who has a face made terrible by fangs, who is fearsome, four-armed, three-eyed, blazing with a trident, and adorned with serpents.
This mantra bestows the fruit of destroying enemies. Through five thousand recitations preceded by the Cāndrāyaṇa vow, the success of the *puraścaraṇa* is attained.
Now, the fifth [mantra].

Those Rudras who abide as lords over the worlds, even so they abide in the trees. Now, among those trees, some are tawny like young grass, while others are deep red; specifically, those who are of such a red color and have blue necks, for them it is as stated previously.

Now the sixth [chapter]. Regarding the verse beginning with *ye bhūtānām*: among those Rudras who are the lords of the hosts of spirits (*bhūta*)—such as the child-seizing spirits (*bālagraha*) and others—some are "shaven-headed" (*viśikha*), meaning devoid of a topknot; some are "wearing matted locks" (*kapardinaḥ*), meaning endowed with a mass of matted hair. Of them... [the rest follows].

Now the seventh [chapter]: "Those who, in foods"— that is, in edible substances, remaining hidden— those Rudras who pierce [the body], who, through the inequality of food, afflict people by producing various diseases, and likewise [those who remain] in vessels, that is, in things to be drunk.

Regarding the phrase "of those who, remaining hidden in buttermilk and other substances, pierce people even while drinking [them]": here, the single mantra beginning with "ye vṛkṣeṣu" and ending with "tisraḥ" consists of three verses; the seer (*ṛṣi*) and other details for these are as before.
Now follows the eighth [section].

Regarding the phrase *ye pathām*, here the word *pathi* (in the fourth line) refers to the worldly and Vedic paths; thus, [the compound] is *pathirakṣayaḥ*. The entire word *rakṣayaḥ* is to be construed with *pathām* (in the fifth line).
Thus, *pathāṃ rakṣayati* means "those who protect the paths," i.e., the protectors of the worldly and Vedic paths. (Sixth line)
Thus, he establishes this quality of being a protector as a qualifying attribute: "ailabrudāyavyudha" (the one who drives away the *ailabrudas*).

The word *irā* denotes food; a collection of *irās* is *aira*. That which sustains (*bibharti*) the *aira* is *ailabhṛt*; these very ones are the *ailabṛdas*. [The change occurs] from *ja* to *sa*, from *bha* to *bha*, and from *ta* to *da*. [The change] of the vowel *a*— (Note: The text fragment provided ends mid-sentence regarding the phonetic transformation.)
*Andasaḥ* means "givers of food. *Vayau timi śrī bhagavatī pāpena iti yuḥ*—the most sinful one is *yuḥ*;

those who fight with such [sinful ones] are *yavyudhaḥ*. The etymological derivation (*rūpaniṣpatti*) of *andasirūpa* is thus: they are the restrainers of the most sinful. In this way, their nature as protectors of the worldly and Vedic paths consists in engaging in those paths among the virtuous and [providing for them] with their fruits, such as food and other necessities.
The meaning is that it consists of the very form of the cessation of the fetters of the most wicked ones there. "Of those Rudras who are such" (fifth line).
Now, the ninth [chapter].

"Those who go to the sacred fords (*tīrthāni*)"—this refers to those possessing *sṛka* (spears), known as *sṛkāyinaḥ*; the lengthening [of the vowel] is Vedic (*chāndasa*). "Those with quivers" (*niṣaṅgiṇaḥ*) means those possessing swords. Those Rudras who wander about to protect sacred fords such as the Gaṅgā and others—for some to grant the fruit of the sacred fords, and for others to obstruct it—[they are addressed by] the two verses beginning with "those who go to the sacred fords. These two verses constitute a single mantra.
Devala is the seer (*ṛṣi*) of this [mantra]; Rudra is the deity; the meditation (*dhyāna*) is as before. This mantra bestows the fruit of excellent sons. (p. 102b, f.

99a, 1st line) The preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) is accomplished by reciting it five thousand times preceded by the performance of the *kṛcchra* penance. All else is to be understood as stated in the passage beginning "thousands upon thousands. (2nd line)
Now the tenth [section]:

"Those who are so many," beginning with "thousands by the thousands" (3rd line), refers to as many Rudras as there are, and even more than these— far more numerous— existing beyond this limit (4th line).

To those Rudras who have spread through all directions, pervading and remaining in every quarter—to them we extend our bodies [in prostration] even unto a thousand *yojanas*. Here, the *ṛṣi* and other details are as before. With the mantras beginning with "Salutation to the Rudras who are on the earth," one should pay homage to the Rudras residing in the worlds of earth, the intermediate space, and heaven, for the sake of one's own well-being and against those who harbor enmity.

And suffering is sought after. In this regard, the division of the three mantras is as follows: "Homage to the Rudras who are on earth; their food is arrows—to them [ten in the east, ten in the west, etc.]"—this is the first mantra. "Homage to the Rudras who are in the intermediate space; their arrows are the wind—to them I offer [oblations]"—this is the second mantra. "Homage to the Rudras who are in heaven; their arrows are rain—to them... [the third mantra].

"I place [thee]," thus the third [verse]. Herein, this is the meaning of the first [verse]: "Let there be obeisance to the Rudras who abide upon the earth; and their food is arrows. For the consumption of unwholesome food is, as it were, in the position of an arrow. Having caused them to eat in measured portions, they afflict some by producing diseases through that [food], and others by means of hunger through the deprivation of food.

Having produced [crops], they afflict some by causing them to commit theft and other crimes for the sake of food, leading them to death and the like. Thus, in the most wicked violence, food is the cause. To those Rudras for whom that very [food] is the object of desire, I extend my ten fingers forward—meaning with the palms joined and facing eastward. By means of joining the palms while facing east, the ten fingers [are extended].

The tips [of the fingers] point toward the east; in this manner, they should be understood for the south and so forth, up to the zenith. The meaning is that I perform salutations characterized by fingers in the form of such joined palms (*añjali*). By this, bodily salutation is shown; "homage to them" is mental salutation;
and the salutation at the beginning of the mantra is verbal salutation. Thus, while we pay homage through the three doors of action, whomsoever we hate—
And him who hates us—him, our enemy, the embodiment of that enmity, its fruit, and its instruments—I entrust to you.
O Rudras, I place him in your jaws (*jambhe*), in your wide-open mouth (*viritāsye*); the meaning is: "devour him.
This same construction should be applied to the second and third [verses] as well. Those Rudras who dwell in the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), their arrows are the wind (*vāta*).

The meaning is that the arrows [of Rudra] harm the sinners by means of various diseases produced by the transformations of the wind, as well as through the impelling of exceedingly violent winds. Those Rudras who abide in the sky—[their] arrows being the rains—the meaning is that they harm [beings] through excessive rain, drought, and so forth.
The remainder is as before; thus, everything here is beautiful. This triad of *yajus* mantras beginning with "Obeisance to the Rudras" and ending with "the end" constitutes a single mantra.
In this context, the meditation (*dhyāna*) upon Rudra as the god and the seer (*ṛṣi*) is to be understood exactly as it has been stated in the passage beginning with "sahasraśaḥ.

This mantra bestows abundance of food. The methods for the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*), as well as the specific fruits such as the accomplishment of one's tasks, the attainment of the memory of past lives (*jātismaratva*), and so forth, are to be seen explained in detail in the *Rudrakalpa* and other such works. Thus ends the inquiry concerning the *Śrī Rudrādhyāya*. [Thus, the Paramahaṃsa...]

The *Śrī Rudrabhāṣya*, composed by the venerable Abhinava Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda—the sovereign among wandering mendicants (*parivrājaka*) and the glorious establisher of the non-dualistic science (*advaitavidyā*)—is hereby complete. Om. Salutations to Sumīnākṣi and Sundareśa.
Om. May this be an offering to Śiva. Salutations to the venerable Gurus. Hariḥ Om. May there be auspiciousness. Together with Mahāgaṇapati. Salutations to Śiva.
